text:
🇺🇦 Elon Musk and SpaceX deserve genuine thanks for what Starlink has done for Ukraine. When Mykhailo Fedorov appealed for help two days after Russia launched its full-scale invasion, Musk responded quickly. The first terminals arrived on 28 February 2022. In February this year, SpaceX worked with Ukraine to block Russian forces from using unauthorised terminals. Both decisions mattered.

That record makes it all the more important to get a straight answer about Starshield.

Musk says Ukraine wants to use commercial Starlink for offensive operations and that military use of Starshield is a matter for the US government. The question Ukraine is asking is more specific. Why are restrictions on Starshield interfering with drones used to intercept Russian attacks?

Ukrainian personnel say speed restrictions can cut connectivity to interceptors as they pursue faster Russian attack drones. On 12 November, President Zelenskyy said the restrictions meant more Russian strikes were getting through and Ukrainian civilians were dying. An interceptor trying to stop a drone before it reaches a block of flats is performing air defence. Any policy that affects it should account for the people it is there to protect.

Who authorised the restrictions? The public accounts conflict. The Wall Street Journal pointed to Musk. Reuters reported that officials pointed to the White House. The Trump administration denied involvement, and SpaceX disputed reports of fresh changes in November. On 13 November, US senators asked Musk and SpaceX to preserve records that could establish who made the decision and whether the consequences for Ukraine’s air defences were considered.

There is also a question about access. In December 2024, Bloomberg reported that Pentagon contracts provided Starshield service for 3,000 terminals in Ukraine, a figure confirmed by a US government agency. That establishes access under those contracts. Which terminals were affected by the restrictions is a separate question. An accusation that Zelenskyy is lying doesn’t answer it.

Musk also repeated the claim that Washington organised a coup in Ukraine in 2014. The Maidan began as a popular protest after Viktor Yanukovych’s government abandoned preparations to sign an agreement with the European Union. After months of protests, in which dozens of demonstrators were killed, Yanukovych left Kyiv. Parliament declared that he had ceased to exercise his constitutional duties and called an early election. The constitutional procedure and the role of foreign diplomacy are open to scrutiny. Musk offered no evidence that Washington organised a coup.

Finally, Musk asks us to have empathy for everyone killed in war, including Russian soldiers. Every human life matters. That includes the civilians asleep in a building an interceptor is trying to protect. If a communications restriction prevents that interception, the danger falls on them.

So the questions are simple. Who authorised the restrictions? What assessment did they make of the risk to civilians? And what are they doing, in consultation with Ukraine, to ensure its air defences can keep working?

Gratitude for what SpaceX did in 2022 is entirely compatible with asking for accountability now. I mean both sincerely.

text:
A potential future conflict between Taiwan and China would be shaped by novel methods of drone warfare involving advanced underwater drones and increased levels of autonomy, according to a new war-gaming experiment by the think tank Center for a New American Security (CNAS). 

The report comes as concerns about Beijing’s aggression toward Taiwan have been rising: China sent dozens of surveillance balloons over the Taiwan Strait in January during Taiwan’s elections, and in May, two Chinese naval ships entered Taiwan’s restricted waters. The US Department of Defense has said that preparing for potential hostilities is an “absolute priority,” though no such conflict is immediately expected. 

The report’s authors detail a number of ways that use of drones in any South China Sea conflict would differ starkly from current practices, most notably in the war in Ukraine, often called the first full-scale drone war. 

Differences from the Ukrainian battlefield

Since Russia invaded Ukraine in 2022, drones have been aiding in what military experts describe as the first three steps of the “kill chain”—finding, targeting, and tracking a target—as well as in delivering explosives. The drones have a short life span, since they are often shot down or made useless by frequency jamming devices that prevent pilots from controlling them. Quadcopters—the commercially available drones often used in the war—last just three flights on average, according to the report. 

Drones like these would be far less useful in a possible invasion of Taiwan. “Ukraine-Russia has been a heavily land conflict, whereas conflict between the US and China would be heavily air and sea,” says Zak Kallenborn, a drone analyst and adjunct fellow with the Center for Strategic and International Studies, who was not involved in the report but agrees broadly with its projections. The small, off-the-shelf drones popularized in Ukraine have flight times too short for them to be used effectively in the South China Sea. 

An underwater war

Instead, a conflict with Taiwan would likely make use of undersea and maritime drones. With Taiwan just 100 miles away from China’s mainland, the report’s authors say, the Taiwan Strait is where the first days of such a conflict would likely play out. The Zhu Hai Yun, China’s high-tech autonomous carrier, might send its autonomous underwater drones to scout for US submarines. The drones could launch attacks that, even if they did not sink the submarines, might divert the attention and resources of the US and Taiwan. 

It’s also possible China would flood the South China Sea with decoy drone boats to “make it difficult for American missiles and submarines to distinguish between high-value ships and worthless uncrewed commercial vessels,” the authors write.

Though most drone innovation is not focused on maritime applications, these uses are not without precedent: Ukrainian forces drew attention for modifying jet skis to operate via remote control and using them to intimidate and even sink Russian vessels in the Black Sea. 

More autonomy

Drones currently have very little autonomy. They’re typically human-piloted, and though some are capable of autopiloting to a fixed GPS point, that’s generally not very useful in a war scenario, where targets are on the move. But, the report’s authors say, autonomous technology is developing rapidly, and whichever nation possesses a more sophisticated fleet of autonomous drones will hold a significant edge.

What would that look like? Millions of defense research dollars are being spent in the US and China alike on swarming, a strategy where drones navigate autonomously in groups and accomplish tasks. The technology isn’t deployed yet, but if successful, it could be a game-changer in any potential conflict.  

A sea-based conflict might also offer an easier starting ground for AI-driven navigation, because object recognition is easier on the “relatively uncluttered surface of the ocean” than on the ground, the authors write.

China’s advantages

A chief advantage for China in a potential conflict is its proximity to Taiwan; it has more than three dozen air bases within 500 miles, while the closest US base is 478 miles away in Okinawa. But an even bigger advantage is that it produces more drones than any other nation.

“China dominates the commercial drone market, absolutely,” says Stacie Pettyjohn, coauthor of the report and director of the defense program at CNAS. That includes drones of the type used in Ukraine.

For Taiwan to use these Chinese drones for its own defenses, it would first have to make the purchase, which could be difficult because the Chinese government might move to block it. Then Taiwan would need to hack them and disconnect them from the companies that made them, or else those Chinese manufacturers could turn them off remotely or launch cyberattacks. That sort of hacking is unfeasible at scale, so Taiwan is effectively cut off from the world’s foremost commercial drone supplier and must either make its own drones or find alternative manufacturers, likely in the US. On Wednesday, June 19, the US approved a $360 million sale of 1,000 military-grade drones to Taiwan.

For now, experts can only speculate about how those drones might be used. Anthropic, the company behind Claude, is now a listed company, and it was the biggest IPO on record.

Shares were priced at US$83, opened on the Nasdaq at US$111.50 (+34%), briefly passed US$115, then closed at US$97.17, still up 17% on day one. It raised US$81.3 billion, ahead of SpaceX's US$75 billion in June.

The Australian angle: ABC News says Aussie investors were among the few outside the US offered shares before the debut. But the good mood didn't spread. Wall Street fell about 2% overnight, and the ASX 200 opened almost 1% lower this morning, with tech leading the drop.

What stood out to me were the prospectus numbers ABC pulled out: revenue went from US$41 million in 2023 to US$16.3 billion in just the first half of 2026, yet the company is still losing money and has huge computing bills ahead.

My learner take: a great product and a great share price are two different questions. One fund manager told ABC she thinks it's a great company but isn't buying because "it's just too expensive". That kind of honest, split view taught me more than the day-one hype.

Not financial advice, just a learner reading the news.

Russian documents Set out 'tectonic weapon' research
Carl Levitin

Moscow. The first official details have emerged in Moscow of ambitious research into 'tectonic warfare' carried out by the former Soviet Union and subsequently by the government of Russia, and involving atte mpts to stimulate 'artificial' earthquakes as weapons of destruction. According to documents obtained by the newspaper Moscow News, two research programmes, the first known as ' Mercury ' and the second as ' Volcano', were aimed at creating new earthquake epicentres by using underground nuclear explosions . Geophysicists are aware that impending earthquakes may be triggered by underground nuclear explosions . But Western geophysicists remain sceptical about tectonic warfare and have all but abandoned research after two unsuccessful phases of activity in the 1960s and 1980s, says Roger Clark, a lecturer in geophysics at the University of Leeds. Clark is not at all surprised that th e Russians tried to create earthquakes and control their location electromagnetically, however. "This sort of science is very much part of their heritage. We don't think it is impossible, or wrong , but past experience suggests it is very, very unlikely. "

The programme , which was secretly launched by the Communist rulers of the former Soviet Union in 1987, and has been unofficially known to Western geophysicists for several years, is now believed to have been abandoned. It would certainly contravene the terms of the Comprehensive Test Ban Treaty, which Russia signed at the United Nations in Geneva last month . The Mercury project was launched in the former Soviet republic of Azerbaijan, but came to a halt when the republic became independent. It was superseded by the Volcano project. Three underground nuclear tests are believed to have taken place at sites in Kyrgyzstan.

According to the documents, the Mercury project was launched by a secret decree of the Central Committee of the Communist Party and the Council of Ministers of the Soviet Union. The objective was to "develop a methodology for remote operation on an earthquake epicentre by using weak seismic fields and research possibilities of transferring the seismic energy of an explosion ".

The documents say that the Mercury project involved 22 scientific and industrial organizations, including the Geological Institute of the Azerbaijan Academy of Sciences in Baku. The remit extended to developing the electronic equipment to be installed aboard space satellites that would control the tectonic weapon. The scientists were given three years to complete research, with testing planned for 1990.

During the research phase, Azerbaijani scientists grew increasingly confident and, according to the documents, were sure that " after [a] nuclear explosion, subterranean energy may accumulate at huge distances from the epicentre and reach massive capacity, after which the next directed explosion can release it all ".

Underground testing began at the town of Batken in Kyrgyzstan, and was directed by lkram Ke rimov , of the Azerbaijan Academy of Sciences. The documents say that scientists detonated an underground nuclear charge and tried to control the direction of seismic energy release d using British-built equipment known as 'system 9690 ' .

A report prepared by the Mozhaisky Military Engineering Institute concluded that the test had been a success. But progress slowed considerably following Azerbaijan's independence from the Soviet Union. At about this time , Russia embarked on a more comprehensive tectonic warfare programme known as the Volcano project. The Earth Physics Institute of the Russian Academy of Sciences (RAS) became the project headquarters .

Research was scheduled to be completed in 1992, with underground testing beginning the following year. The final test was carried out at a place code-named S36NZ-0Kh; Moscow News believes the letters 'NZ' refer to Novaya Zemlya, where Soviet nuclear testing began in the 1950s."

Russian documents Set out 'tectonic weapon' research
Carl Levitin

Moscow. The first official details have emerged in Moscow of ambitious research into 'tectonic warfare' carried out by the former Soviet Union and subsequently by the government of Russia, and involving atte mpts to stimulate 'artificial' earthquakes as weapons of destruction. According to documents obtained by the newspaper Moscow News, two research programmes, the first known as ' Mercury ' and the second as ' Volcano', were aimed at creating new earthquake epicentres by using underground nuclear explosions . Geophysicists are aware that impending earthquakes may be triggered by underground nuclear explosions . But Western geophysicists remain sceptical about tectonic warfare and have all but abandoned research after two unsuccessful phases of activity in the 1960s and 1980s, says Roger Clark, a lecturer in geophysics at the University of Leeds. Clark is not at all surprised that th e Russians tried to create earthquakes and control their location electromagnetically, however. "This sort of science is very much part of their heritage. We don't think it is impossible, or wrong , but past experience suggests it is very, very unlikely. "

The programme , which was secretly launched by the Communist rulers of the former Soviet Union in 1987, and has been unofficially known to Western geophysicists for several years, is now believed to have been abandoned. It would certainly contravene the terms of the Comprehensive Test Ban Treaty, which Russia signed at the United Nations in Geneva last month . The Mercury project was launched in the former Soviet republic of Azerbaijan, but came to a halt when the republic became independent. It was superseded by the Volcano project. Three underground nuclear tests are believed to have taken place at sites in Kyrgyzstan.

According to the documents, the Mercury project was launched by a secret decree of the Central Committee of the Communist Party and the Council of Ministers of the Soviet Union. The objective was to "develop a methodology for remote operation on an earthquake epicentre by using weak seismic fields and research possibilities of transferring the seismic energy of an explosion ".

The documents say that the Mercury project involved 22 scientific and industrial organizations, including the Geological Institute of the Azerbaijan Academy of Sciences in Baku. The remit extended to developing the electronic equipment to be installed aboard space satellites that would control the tectonic weapon. The scientists were given three years to complete research, with testing planned for 1990.

During the research phase, Azerbaijani scientists grew increasingly confident and, according to the documents, were sure that " after [a] nuclear explosion, subterranean energy may accumulate at huge distances from the epicentre and reach massive capacity, after which the next directed explosion can release it all ".

Underground testing began at the town of Batken in Kyrgyzstan, and was directed by lkram Ke rimov , of the Azerbaijan Academy of Sciences. The documents say that scientists detonated an underground nuclear charge and tried to control the direction of seismic energy release d using British-built equipment known as 'system 9690 ' .

A report prepared by the Mozhaisky Military Engineering Institute concluded that the test had been a success. But progress slowed considerably following Azerbaijan's independence from the Soviet Union. At about this time , Russia embarked on a more comprehensive tectonic warfare programme known as the Volcano project. The Earth Physics Institute of the Russian Academy of Sciences (RAS) became the project headquarters .

Research was scheduled to be completed in 1992, with underground testing beginning the following year. The final test was carried out at a place code-named S36NZ-0Kh; Moscow News believes the letters 'NZ' refer to Novaya Zemlya, where Soviet nuclear testing began in the 1950s."

text:
On New Year’s Eve a Real Housewives couple from South Africa posted “America is good to us!” from their new life in Florida. Ten weeks later police were knocking on their door over $5,302 worth of groceries from the local Publix, and in an interview room the wife told a detective it was all her, “it wasn’t my husband.” A few weeks after that, the husband reportedly stood up in court and said the same thing.

In the video below, Boca Raton police find Mel Viljoen at home in her bathrobe while Peet is being handcuffed next to their Range Rover, and later a detective sits her down and explains exactly what he thinks they did, “instead of you buying your San Pellegrino for $23.99, you’re getting your San Pellegrino for $0.79.” Mel says “maybe there’s a misunderstanding,” and when he asks why Peet walked out with carts that weren’t paid for, she tells him “he probably thought it was paid for,” and then, “it’s an interesting question, I’m not sure.”

The police affidavit tells it very differently. It says that from August 2025 to March 2026 the couple went through Publix self-checkouts 52 times, scanning cheap seasoning packets while 392 other items went through unpaid, with Peet chatting to staff while Mel did the scanning. Three times, it says, he walked out with a full cart while her cards were declining at the till. Mel told police she was in “survival mode” because she couldn’t legally work in the US.

They were arrested on 10 March 2026 for aggravated grand retail theft, made bail, and were picked up by ICE straight away because their tourist visas had run out. After nearly three months in detention Mel left for South Africa in May, Peet was deported in June, and he was arrested the moment he landed at OR Tambo airport on more than 400 counts of commercial crime.

This is the same couple who ran the Tammy Taylor nail franchise in Africa, until a US court awarded the company $4 million in damages for counterfeiting its trademarks, and who in January 2025 offered a sheriff diamonds worth more than R2.7 million to cover their debts.

I think the part I can’t stop thinking about is that she sat in that room and took all of it on herself, calmly, to protect him, and then had to watch him do the opposite in front of a judge. And she’s still raising money for his lawyers. That’s not survival mode, that’s love making terrible decisions.

Florida still has warrants out for both of them, so if they ever come back, the Publix case is waiting.

Ladies, is Mel the most loyal wife on reality TV, or just the easiest one to leave holding the bag?

When betting #NFL Thursday Night Football, it is important to separate the expected winner from the betting value.

Houston may be favored to win, but Indianapolis +12.5 gives the Colts a sizable cushion. A Colts spread bet can still cash even if Indianapolis loses, as long as the final margin is 12 points or fewer.

The projected score of Houston 24, Indianapolis 17 would produce a 7-point margin, meaning Indianapolis +12.5 would cover.

The Under 44 angle works the same way. A 24-17 final score produces 41 total points, which would finish below the posted total of 44.

Host: After Republicans mid-term wipeout, the 2028 race to succeed President Trump appears to be wide open. CNN has learned that there is a growing push by Republicans for Secretary of State Marco Rubio to join the field, and they may get their wish. Until now Rubio has avoided discussing the looming presidential race, but allies say that he's now more seriously weighing a run. We're joined now by CNN White House reporter Adam Cancryn. So Adam, what more are you learning about the push for Rubio to run and his own thinking? Yeah,

Adam Cancryn: Absolutely. This is something that we've seen change and evolve over the last seven or eight months. People close to Rubio now telling us that he is seriously considering a 2028 presidential run, and that's a change from earlier this year when he was telling allies, one, I don't even want to run for president at all, and two, that after he was done at the State Department, he wanted to go into the private sector and make some money. He's been a politician for several, for years. So this would be a new chapter for him. Now, no longer saying that. In public, he's no longer saying that he will defer to J.D. Vance, the vice president, if Vance decides to run. And so these are some subtle changes that we've seen just over the last few months. At the same time that there's this broader context of a renewed push in the Republican Party writ large for somebody that might run, that's an alternative to Vance, especially after these post midterm losses where now folks are starting to wonder is Vance too closely tied to Donald Trump and to these losses to be able to successfully run in 2028. So you're seeing this real groundswell of people who already liked Rubio now think he's a little bit more open to it. We talked to Newt Gingrich, who's a former Republican House speaker and really ingrained in Trump world. He said this about Marco. He said, Marco is the most frequent name I hear from everybody. He said, it's striking to me how many people, even before the election, were saying that they really wanted him. And so you're seeing this energy now, especially post those midterms for anybody there who might say, you know, be able to capture some of the MAGA based energy and at the same time kind of chart their own territory. They see Rubio as a potential candidate for doing that. Wow. And if he decides to run, the next two years for him would look very different. Yeah, this is the crucial decision. And the sources told us that he's truly undecided here. It's a matter of how best to spend the next couple of years. So there's plenty of things, as we all know, foreign policy wise that need to be taken care of in the next two years. He would have to leave that at some point if he's going to run for president. The main issue there is Cuba. He's been working toward some kind of political regime change. This has been really a lifelong effort for him. So the question is, does he believe that in the next couple of years he can make real progress and it's worth staying at the State Department? Or at some point, do you decide, hey, I'm going to try to do this on my own as president and launch a campaign in the next several months? And potentially wind up eating a lot of fair food in Iowa. Adam Cancryn, thank you so much. Appreciate that. I think some things

Rick Tyler: Need to happen. One is Trump's base of support is uniquely uninheritable. So this idea that who's he going to give his base to, that's not going to happen because Trump's base is like fan girls. I mean, they're for him, they're for nobody else. And we've seen that over 10 years. The other thing is the Republican Party has to decide who it wants to be because Rubio and Vance are, which I think is why Rubio is considering it, because they're running for totally different party nominations ideologically. Vance is an isolationist. Vance doesn't support Israel to the extent that Rubio does. Rubio is more of an internationalist, a foreign policy interventionist. He's not a globalist, but those are two different things. And the Republican Party has to decide what is the coalition? So Reagan's had three. He had the three, like economic conservatives, Christian conservatives, and national security conservatives. I don't know that that's the three, but what is the three? And Vance and Rubio have totally two different threes.

Host: And one of them, one of the three is not MAGA. I wonder, Sabrina, how you see it.

Sabrina Singh: Yeah, you know, I think you're right. Like I think just whoever is the party nominee, whether it's Vance, Rubio, or someone else in the Republican wing, I don't necessarily think it is an automatic inheritance of what Donald Trump created with the MAGA movement. And I think the conversation in the Republican Party is something similar to what Democrats had in 2016 when we lost, you know, it was like, what is the direction that the party is going to go? And then similarly in 2024, we had to sort of decide, are we going to swing more to the progressive wing or charter path forward with more moderates? And I think, you know, given the election results of the midterms, I think you saw more moderate candidates prevail. Of course, we can talk about some of the DSA candidates, but they're not the overwhelming majority in the party. So I do think Rick is right that you are going to see some fracturing and who can kind of, you know, Hungry Hippo all of those coalitions together,

Host: That remains to be seen. Which hippo would Democrats most prefer to go up against?

Sabrina Singh: I think the hippo today would be J.D. Vance. He comes in so closely aligned with the president, who, you know, we've talked about their approvals many times before. I mean, sinking approval ratings in the 30s, even though he tried to distance himself from Donald Trump with that, you know, ex post the day after the elections, he's still so tied to this administration. And that's really the problem and struggle that all vice presidents had, including Kamala Harris, to distance themselves from the president.

Host: I wonder, Rick, if you think there's still time for Vance to do more distancing from Trump or do you think his stock is tied to the president?

Rick Tyler: Look, I think they are. I think, look, I think the MAGA movement's effectively over as a political force because they belong to Trump. They don't belong to anybody else. Somebody else is going to have to make their way forward. I do think you're right that J.D. Vance would have an awful hard time as vice president to distance himself from Trump. It remains to be seen if Rubio can do that. He seems to have done it even within the administration. But the question is, how long is he going to stick in the administration? Because running a campaign and being secretary of state, I think, are fairly incompatible.

Host: And the war chest, too, the comparability. I mean, Rubio has not been fundraising like J.D. Vance has. So he would have to leave pretty quickly.

Rick Tyler: There's not one person that I have ever met that wants an endless war. Who will say the president's got to keep fighting no matter what? So that is another straw man argument that this guy puts up. I'm talking about the vice president of the United States. He never should have been vice president. And then what he said last week, two weeks ago, after the loss of the midterms, any honest conversation about what went wrong in the midterms for Republicans has to start with the Iran war. Really? So you're telling me how I have to argue something? And my beliefs, if I don't argue the way you want me to, it's not worth your time?

Kasie Hunt: All right. My panel's back. David Urban, what is your sense of the 2028 landscape on the Republican side right now? Because I mean, listen, I will say I hear a lot about Rubio in sort of general conversations I have with sources, frankly, on both sides of the aisle. Democrats wonder if he's going to run, too, because some of them will argue that it may be harder for them to win if he actually were to be the GOP nominee. But what are you hearing? What do you know? Listen, I don't

David Urban: Know anything. Okay. I'll just be frank. Like everybody else, I guess. I think, look, the vice president is a really good, I think he's a much better retail politician than he is wholesale, large gems. He does great one-on-one. There's a lot of advantages that the vice presidency offers, right? You get to fly around in a big plane. You have all the pomp and circumstance where you roll up to a donor's house, you get a motorcade. All those things matter to raising money. He's been out during this election cycle meeting with donor after donor after donor. He's got the base. To run for president of the United States, you need to have a large operation. You can't just pop up out of nowhere. So I think it's his to kind of lose or give up at some point, but the donor base may reject him at the outset. Both, I think, J.D. Vance and Marco Rubio have the same problem in that, do people really want a third term of Donald Trump? So they're going to have to figure a way to distance themselves from Donald Trump. You see Marco Rubio in these shots with Putin. He's going to be asked, do you support this? What do you think about NATO? All these very tough questions, right? Vance has already kind of put a little distance there, I think. So Rubio's going to have to answer that and people are going to have to answer the question, does the Republican Party want another Trump 3.0 after this 2.0? I think it's an open question. I think that gives room for people like Ron DeSantis and Glenn Youngkin and Dave McCormick and lots of other people, new faces, Spencer Cox in Utah. I remember after Charlie Kirk, everybody was loving Spencer Cox. There are a lot of people, I think, if they decided to pop up are very interesting. So I think it might be a wide open race. We'll

Kasie Hunt: See. Jonah, what do you think?

Jonah Goldberg: I think that Vance's post-election autopsy thing was a spectacular blunder. He wanted to carve out, like there was no, there was nothing that required him to do it. The actual analysis was garbage. And he has this theory that he can run as the president's chief booster and chief critic simultaneously, which is hard. In the United States, only, basically since 1804, only two sitting vice presidents have ever been elected president directly. And the reason for that is you have to want, as David was saying, four more years. The idea that Vance has the skills to convince, you know, if Trump's approval rate is at 36 percent or 40 percent, to convince people above into double digits that he should get four more years who don't want, who don't approve of the president now is just a huge lift. So I think Rubio is in a much better position, but I think there's going to be a lot of people just want to turn the page on the Trump years entirely.

text:
OttoGeoGraphica
August, 1999
Lassen Volcano
Lassen Volcanic National Park
Redding, California
(film camera photo)

To the west, there is Whiskeytown and the Coastal range, and beyond, the Pacific. To the south, there is the Sacramento valley, and beyond, thirty-five million people pursuing and promoting the latest trend. To the east, there are alpine lakes, cascading streams, the northern Sierra’s, and beyond; Nevada’s great basin, the great Salt Lake, the I-80 corridor through Union Pacific rail towns, dusty and transient, across Wyoming and Nebraska, and on to Chicago. With the exception of relatively small urban centers like Salt Lake City, Omaha and Des Moines, this is the vast Western wilderness, from the Rockies to the Heartland. But, to bring focus back to Lassen, the north, there is deep evergreen forest, and beyond, the cascade range of Oregon. Oh, and yes, just slightly to the northwest, a stone’s throw relatively speaking is Shasta.

Shasta is spectacular, majestic, and California’s northern sentinel. Other superlatives abound to describe one of the single most magnificent mountains in North America, standing alone, capped in snow, and usually with a small cloud hovering near its peak.

At three-thousand feet below Shasta’s fourteen, Lassen offers the ultimate panoramic visual of northern California. Also snowcapped, Lassen summit shows the barren remnants of a still active volcano. Picas scurry out for some windblown plant or the crumbs of a discarded granola bar, complete with the shiny silver and red wrapper; so disheartening. At eleven thousand the wind stings off the drifts and the air is scarce.

After the four-hour trek, some lunch, and an extended period of relaxation and contemplation upon a bed of snow, there is the ethereal moment, when Shasta seems so close, reachable, touchable, requiring just one leap from peak to peak. The moment transcends the hiker for the rest of the afternoon. The wind dies and one returns from meditation to the gently hum of a weather station, sheltered just below the peak, north side, near where the old fire observation tower stood. The cabin was absorbed by lava one- hundred years ago, after Lassen’s last eruption. There is a sign nearby that shows a picture of the fire watcher, an old timer sharing the cabin with his dog. The descent to parking is treacherous through the drifted melting snow.

The next morning, heading south on I-5, some eighty miles south, and still seeing Shasta from the rear-view, the feeling of almost touching that hovering cloud from Lassen’s summit just the day before, leaves me with a smile.

text:
Anthropic opened at $111.50 today, 34% above its $83 offer. The filing says safety can come before shareholder returns.

The numbers: 980 million shares sold for $81.3 billion, the largest IPO on record. At the $83 offer the company was worth about $1.4 trillion fully diluted. At the $111.50 open, about $1.9 trillion. By the afternoon it had faded to the high $90s, still roughly 17% above the offer.

Do not mix up the two $81 billion figures today. $81.3 billion is the money raised. About $81 billion is also the run-rate revenue on October 31, but that figure extrapolates 28 days of data. Reported Q3 revenue was $16.96 billion, up from $1.38 billion a year earlier. The first 10-Q is the real test of the run rate.

Here is the part that matters if you build on Claude. Anthropic is a Delaware public benefit corporation. Its directors must balance shareholder returns with the interests of people affected by its conduct and its stated purpose: the responsible development of advanced AI for the long-term benefit of humanity. The risk factors say plainly that decisions to slow a release or forgo revenue for safety reasons may not maximize stockholder value. And public buyers get economics, not control: the Long-Term Benefit Trust elects a board majority, and the founders hold 50.1% of the vote.

So the market just priced a frontier lab that can legally choose safety over returns, and paid a premium for the privilege. I read that as good news for builders: the vendor your product depends on cannot be voted into cutting safety corners for a quarterly number.

Tonight, do the boring check anyway. List every place Claude is load-bearing in your stack and write down the fallback for each one, plus how long the switch takes. A charter protects the mission. It does not protect your uptime.

Would you rather your most critical vendor answer to its shareholders or to its charter?

text:
Are We Heading Toward Another FInancial Crisis Like 2008?

In this episode of the Investing in Real Estate Show, I’m discussing the current state of the real estate market, whether we’re heading toward another financial crisis similar to 2008, and which real estate investment strategies I believe offer the best opportunities in today’s market.

I’ll also explain why I believe certain Florida real estate markets have already experienced significant price corrections, why fixing and flipping houses has become riskier, and why strategies like wholesaling, buying rental properties, seller financing, and creative financing could present substantial opportunities for investors over the next few years.

I started investing in real estate in 2003, more than 23 years ago. At that time, the Federal Reserve had been lowering interest rates following September 11, 2001, and the real estate market was booming.

Mortgage rates were low, real estate prices were rising rapidly, and just about everyone wanted to get involved in real estate investing.

During 2003, 2004, and 2005, we were doing extremely well. I started by purchasing rental properties using what is commonly called the Buy, Repair, Rent, and Refinance strategy or the BRRR Method.

One of my first rental properties was purchased for $50,000. I spent another $25,000 renovating the house, bringing my total investment to $75,000. After the renovation, the house appraised for $163,000.

Another house I purchased in a lower-income neighborhood cost a little over $15,000. I spent less than $10,000 getting it rent-ready, and that property appraised for $115,000.
Those were incredible numbers, and real estate prices continued climbing (and so did my wealth).

I remember people approaching me and telling me they wanted to quit their jobs and become full-time real estate investors.

One individual was an architect working for a prominent architectural firm. He wanted to leave his career and start flipping houses full-time.

That’s the kind of enthusiasm you see when a market becomes overheated like it did in 2006.

Everyone was buying houses, everyone could qualify for mortgages, and everyone thought real estate prices would continue going up forever.

By 2007 prices started coming down and by 2008 we were in a full blown financial crisis and the real estate market was collapsing.

During the financial crisis, I started my real estate education company (Lex Levinrad Real Estate Training because I saw an incredible opportunity for new investors to buy properties for pennies on the dollar. The banks were literally giving properties away – and smart buyers were buying them.

Properties that had previously sold for $225,000 in Port St. Lucie, Florida, were now being listed by banks for as low as $50,000.

By March 2009, I was purchasing some of those same three-bedroom, two-bathroom houses for as little as $35,000 to $36,000.

Over the following decade, those properties appreciated dramatically.

Some of the houses purchased for $35,000 eventually became worth $350,000.
Think about that for a moment.

Imagine purchasing a house for $35,000 in 2009 and watching its value increase to $350,000 by 2021 or 2022.

That’s a tenfold increase in value!

text:
Venerable Philippine Duchesne, by G. E. M. Part 2
.
Chapter 5 – Serious Crosses.
.
God’s saints have never been spared the cross of contradiction, and Mother Duchesne was no exception to the rule. Mother Barat heard from various persons that she was too austere, too narrow, too unwilling to adapt herself to the requirements of the times; and this, it was said, was why the houses in Missouri were not progressing. By these critics, their backwardness was contrasted with the flourishing condition of the Southern houses. There were numerous reasons for this difference. Louisiana had been colonized a century earlier; its people were wealthy and prosperous; nearly all spoke the French language, and as yet there was little or no competition; whereas entirely opposite conditions prevailed in Missouri. Mother Barat, however, heard these charges so often that she began to fear they were true, and to consider that it was time to place the government of the Saint Louis house, at least, in the hands of a younger superior, who would have a clearer understanding of the needs of the times. But before taking a step which was very much against her inclination, she consulted Bishop Rosati, in 1832. His answer was that the removal of Mother Duchesne from her office would result in the collapse of the houses in Missouri, as there was no one else capable of bearing the burden of governing them; that the slowness of success for which she was blamed, was due to difficulties inherent in the situation, while her recognized sanctity gave her an influence for good that no one else would wield. This was not Mother Duchesne’s opinion of herself. On the contrary, she thought herself an encumbrance and a drawback upon God’s work; and again and again, ever since she had been in America, she had begged to be replaced by some one who would possess the virtues and abilities in which she thought herself entirely lacking. Bishop Rosati’s reply was a great relief to the heart of Mother Barat, and Mother Duchesne remained in office for the time being.
.
The years immediately following brought the holy Mother many crosses, of which we can only name the most notable. Mother Régis Hamilton, the dearest of her American daughters, had to undergo a severe operation, according to the rude surgical methods of the time. The ravages of the cholera in France filled her with anxiety for the fate of the French houses, as also for that of her own relatives and friends, and letters were long in coming.
.
The cholera broke out with great violence in Saint Michael’s, where it carried away five of the community, and finally it reached Saint Louis. One morning, after her brief rest, she arose to find every one in the community ill except herself. Happily the disease had appeared among them in a milder form, known as cholerine. No one died, but during three months all the sick suffered from continual relapses. The devoted Mother seemed to multiply herself to be able to attend to them all, and at the same time to look after the house. Often she was up the whole night with those who were the more seriously affected. Fortunately, the orphans were spared, and so were the houses of Florissant and Saint Charles, but Mother Duchesne heard, with great desolation of heart, that besides the five religious already mentioned, the pestilence had carried off her old friends, the Abbé Martial, Mgr. de Neckere, first Bishop of New Orleans after the division of the diocese, and twenty priests–an immense loss to the Church and to souls.
.
She had been compelled to dismiss all her pupils except the orphans, and was consequently obliged to borrow from the bank to meet ordinary expenses. Under the pressure of so many sorrows and trials, Mother Duchesne determined to appeal to Heaven by a day of fasting and penance, ending with an expiatory procession. She and the older orphans made it barefoot and with a rope around their necks, in the old medieval fashion. A few days later all the sick were well, and the following week she was able to reopen the school. Another great sorrow was the intense sufferings of Mother Octavie Berthold, one of her first companions, whom a cruel malady was now hurrying to the grave, and who died a holy death in November of that same year. During these years, likewise, she heard of the closing of her beloved convent of Sainte Marie d’en Haut, in Grenoble, while at the same time there was question of closing those of Florissant and Saint Charles. Under the weight of these crosses and many others, her affliction was indescribable. In a letter to Mother Barat she gives vent to the anguish of her soul, and with touching humility expresses the fear that her sins are the cause of so many calamities.
.
But Mother Duchesne was too heroic a soul ever to be discouraged. She set herself to work anew with unflinching fortitude, and went on with the building of an addition to her house. The next year, 1834, had opened prosperously with thirty-two boarders, when the cholera broke out afresh, and the bankruptcy of several business houses in Saint Louis reduced their number to one-third. Just at this time Mother Audé was called to France, and received orders to visit all the houses before leaving, that of Saint Louis included. A few months later Mother Duchesne was removed to Florissant, while Mother Thieffry took her place at Saint Louis. We may mention here that the new Superior did not find a way of overcoming the difficulties of the situation, and several years more went by before the Saint Louis house entered upon an era of prosperity.
.
Mother Duchesne resumed her old life at Florissant–a life of prayer, toil and self-immolation. She could be seen engaged in the hardest labor of the house, the stables and the grounds, cooking, washing the dishes, scouring the kitchen utensils, chopping wood, working in the garden with hoe and spade, like an industrious field laborer, sweeping and cleaning in the house, and, in fact, taking upon herself, according to her invariable custom, all that was hardest and most repulsive to nature. She took care of the sick herself, and would let no one else sit up with them at night, on the plea that the others needed their rest more than she did. She took entire charge of the sacristy, which, like the care of the sick, was for her a labor of love. She made the morning call and night visit, directed the different schools, and took a share in the teaching. Her correspondence was usually done at night, and it was also at that time she made up her accounts and prepared the church for great feasts. During the night, likewise, she spent long hours in prayer, in her usual motionless attitude before the Tabernacle. Her thoughts were all upon God, and her prayer was unceasing. When returning from Holy Communion a nimbus of light was sometimes seen around her head. The mere sight of her recalled the presence of God; her intercessory power was universally recognized, and her words had a wonderful efficacy for strengthening, consoling and enlightening souls.
.
Her hands were rough and hard, like those of an old farm laborer, and in winter time they were swollen, cracked and bleeding with chilblains. To avoid offending the eyes of the children, she used to wear, during the cold season, mittens which she made of scraps of calico or other stuff, sewed together so as to cover them only on the backs, and thus leave them free for work. She wore the same clothes in winter as in summer; her habit was so patched with different shades of black, that the original material could not be distinguished; her shoes were made of pieces of old carpet, and everything that she made use of for herself bore the stamp of her love of poverty, and gave evidence of her contempt for all that the world loves and seeks after. In fact, she presented an appearance which, in others, would have seemed grotesque, but which in her inspired veneration and awe. The pupils wondered and looked upon her as a supernatural being. They were very fond of her, and when they caught sight of her during their recreation hours, they flew to meet her like a flock of birds, and were delighted when they could offer her the least service.
.
For her scanty meals she gathered up the scraps and leavings from the children’s refectory; and wherever she lived at any time, she would have no other cell than the closet under the stairs. Her mattress was barely two inches thick, and she was never known to have any other covering for her bed but an old funeral pall. She ruled the children with a firm hand, but with the affectionate solicitude of a loving and prudent mother. She trained them to be strong Christians and lovers of duty. Those of her pupils who were called to move in the higher ranks of society, were noted, not only for their prudence and Christian reserve, but also for their refinement and distinction of manners and language. The poorer children came in for an equal share of her kindness and care, and her motherly solicitude followed them after they had gone forth into the world. She had warm friends among the most notable families of Saint Louis, but Mother Duchesne was no respecter of persons, and the poor were equally welcome, even more so, perhaps, to her time, her counsels, her prayers, her sympathy, and her services.

text:
As soon as Google launched its latest video-generating AI model at the end of May, creatives rushed to put it through its paces. Released just months after its predecessor, Veo 3 allows users to generate sounds and dialogue for the first time, sparking a flurry of hyperrealistic eight-second clips stitched together into ads, ASMR videos, imagined film trailers, and humorous street interviews. Academy Award–nominated director Darren Aronofsky used the tool to create a short film called Ancestra. During a press briefing, Demis Hassabis, Google DeepMind’s CEO, likened the leap forward to “emerging from the silent era of video generation.” 

But others quickly found that in some ways the tool wasn’t behaving as expected. When it generates clips that include dialogue, Veo 3 often adds nonsensical, garbled subtitles, even when the prompts it’s been given explicitly ask for no captions or subtitles to be added. 

Getting rid of them isn’t straightforward—or cheap. Users have been forced to resort to regenerating clips (which costs them more money), using external subtitle-removing tools, or cropping their videos to get rid of the subtitles altogether.

Josh Woodward, vice president of Google Labs and Gemini, posted on X on June 9 that Google had developed fixes to reduce the gibberish text. But over a month later, users are still logging issues with it in Google Labs’ Discord channel, demonstrating how difficult it can be to correct issues in major AI models.

Like its predecessors, Veo 3 is available to paying members of Google’s subscription tiers, which start at $249.99 a month. To generate an eight-second clip, users enter a text prompt describing the scene they’d like to create into Google’s AI filmmaking tool Flow, Gemini, or other Google platforms. Each Veo 3 generation costs a minimum of 20 AI credits, and the account can be topped up at a cost of $25 per 2,500 credits.

Mona Weiss, an advertising creative director, says that regenerating her scenes in a bid to get rid of the random captions is becoming expensive. “If you’re creating a scene with dialogue, up to 40% of its output has gibberish subtitles that make it unusable,” she says. “You’re burning through money trying to get a scene you like, but then you can’t even use it.”

When Weiss reported the problem to Google Labs through its Discord channel in the hopes of getting a refund for her wasted credits, its team pointed her to the company’s official support team. They offered her a refund for the cost of Veo 3, but not for the credits. Weiss declined, as accepting would have meant losing access to the model altogether. The Google Labs’ Discord support team has been telling users that subtitles can be triggered by speech, saying that they’re aware of the problem and are working to fix it. 

So why does Veo 3 insist on adding these subtitles, and why does it appear to be so difficult to solve the problem? It probably comes down to what the model has been trained on.  

Although Google hasn’t made this information public, that training data is likely to include YouTube videos, clips from vlogs and gaming channels, and TikTok edits, many of which come with subtitles. These embedded subtitles are part of the video frames rather than separate text tracks layered on top, meaning it’s difficult to remove them before they’re used for training, says Shuo Niu, an assistant professor at Clark University in Massachusetts who studies video sharing platforms and AI.

“The text-to-video model is trained using reinforcement learning to produce content that mimics human-created videos, and if such videos include subtitles, the model may ‘learn’ that incorporating subtitles enhances similarity with human-generated content,” he says.

“We’re continuously working to improve video creation, especially with text, speech that sounds natural, and audio that syncs perfectly,” a Google spokesperson says. “We encourage users to try their prompt again if they notice an inconsistency and give us feedback using the thumbs up/down option.”

As for why the model ignores instructions such as “No subtitles,” negative prompts (telling a generative AI model not to do something) are usually less effective than positive ones, says Tuhin Chakrabarty, an assistant professor at Stony Brook University who studies AI systems. 

To fix the problem, Google would have to check every frame of each video Veo 3 has been trained on, and either get rid of or relabel those with captions before retraining the model—an endeavor that would take weeks, he says. 

Katerina Cizek, a documentary maker and artistic director at the MIT Open Documentary Lab, believes the problem exemplifies Google’s willingness to launch products before they’re fully ready. 

“Google needed a win,” she says. “They needed to be the first to pump out a tool that generates lip-synched audio. And so that was more important than fixing their subtitle issue.”

Nuland and various other senior US and EU officials and politicians also publicly supported Euromaidan by visiting the Maidan. Putin and the Russian Foreign Minister Lavrov suggested that Obama pushed for signing a deal between Yanukovych and the Maidan leaders but that the Maidan opposition broke the deal and seized the power the next day (see Obama, 2019). The US and other Western governments blamed the Yanukovych government and his forces for the massacre of the Maidan protesters. They also immediately recognized the new Maidan government after the seizure of the presidential administration and the parliament by the Maidan Self-Defense and the parliament vote to remove Yanukovych even though such actions violated the agreement signed on February 21, 2014 by Yanukovych, the Maidan opposition leaders, and representatives of France, Germany, and Poland which stipulated withdrawal of the government forces from downtown Kyiv, disarmament of the Maidan activists, early presidential elections, and the investigation of the Maidan massacre with involvement of the Council of Europe.

There is no publicly available evidence of the direct involvement of the US or other Western governments and forces in the Maidan massacre. But these governments de facto backed the overthrow of the Ukrainian government in spite of evidence that this overthrow was perpetrated by the elements of the Maidan oligarchic and far-right opposition by means of the false-flag mass killing of the Maidan protesters and assassination attempts against Yanukovych.

Ukraine becoming a US client state right after the Maidan is indirect evidence of the US-led regime change. The Ukrainian media, Ukrainian and US officials, and a declassified transcript of a meeting of the National Security and Defense Council of Ukraine also revealed that the US and other Western governments told the Maidan government leaders not to use military force during the Russian annexation of Crimea in order to avoid a war with Russia (See Chapter 4; Katchanovski, 2015; U.S., 2015). The nearly perfect alignment of the Ukrainian and US government policies after the Maidan is also consistent with Ukraine becoming a US client state and remaining during the Russia-Ukraine war. The US administration was involved in the Maidan government decision to use force in the separatist conflict in Donbas (Chapter 5). The use of Ukraine as a proxy for a proxy war with Russia after the Russian invasion of Ukraine on February 24, 2022 and the US and UK blocking of a peace deal to end the war in April 2022 also show that Ukraine was a client state.

Then a member of the Ukrainian parliament from the Poroshenko’s ruling party and the current adviser to President of Ukraine Zelenskyy stated in 2015 that “Pyatt and the U.S. administration have more influence than ever in the history of independent Ukraine.” A rare report in the US media noted that “Americans are highly visible in the Ukrainian political process. The U.S. embassy in Kiev is a center of power, and Ukrainian politicians openly talk of appointments and dismissals being vetted by U.S. Ambassador Geoffrey Pyatt and even U.S. Vice President Joe Biden.” (See Bershidsky, 2015).

Jeffrey Sachs, a world-renowned American economist who was invited to serve as an economic advisor to new prime minister Arsenii Yatseniuk right after the Yanukovych government overthrow, stated that the US government “definitely contributed to the overthrow of Yanukovych… I know this from inside, not just from outside. I know from top people involved in these issues.” (Jeffrey, 2023). Renowned American investigative journalist Seymour Hersh said based on his insider sources in the US intelligence and the government: “We certainly did overthrow [of the Ukrainian government] with a lot more American involvement than the press knows about right now.” (CN, 2023).

Various evidence shows US administration involvement in appointments and dismissals of top Ukrainian government officials and in key policy decisions in Ukraine since the Maidan. For example, the Ukrainian media reported that then US Vice President Joe Biden requested to put Arsenii Yatseniuk, Valentyn Nalyvaichenko, and foreigners in the Ukrainian government (Mostovaia, 2015). Yatseniuk became the prime minister, Nalyvaichenko the head of the Security Service of Ukraine, and the former president of Georgia and his former Georgian government officials occupied various positions in the Ukrainian state. Ukrainian media reports and tapes of phone calls between then US Vice President Joe Biden and President of Ukraine Petro Poroshenko revealed that he had say in Poroshenko’s decision to dismiss Yatseniuk as prime minister and in appointing his successor. The tapes, Ukrainian media reports, and public admission by Biden showed that he was involved in dismissal of the Prosecutor General of Ukraine and approval of his successor’s appointment (See FLASHBACK, 2019; Listen, 2020; Mostovaia, 2015, 2016).

The declassified transcript of the Trump and Zelenskyy phone call shows the same client-patron relationship between Ukraine and the United States (Read, 2019). The client-patron relationship between Ukraine and the US enabled the use of Ukraine as a US proxy during the Russia-Ukraine war (See Chapter 9)."

text:
National Pop-Tarts Day! I bet you thought I would miss it.

Few breakfast foods are as closely associated with American childhood as Pop-Tarts. Those rectangular toaster pastries, with their sweet fillings, frosting, and colorful sprinkles, have been part of American grocery stores and kitchen cupboards for more than sixty years.

The story began in Battle Creek, Michigan, where two breakfast cereal giants, Kellogg's and Post, were competing to develop a new kind of convenience food.

Post announced its Country Squares toaster pastries, but Kellogg's moved quickly to bring its competing product to market. In 1964, Pop-Tarts arrived in grocery stores in four original flavors: Strawberry, Blueberry, Brown Sugar Cinnamon, and Apple Currant.

Interestingly, the first Pop-Tarts were unfrosted. Frosted varieties didn't arrive until 1967.

And that brings us to a rather unusual Hollywood interpretation of the story.

In 2024, Jerry Seinfeld directed and starred in the Netflix comedy *Unfrosted*, a movie about the battle between Kellogg's and Post to invent the toaster pastry.

The film features Melissa McCarthy, Jim Gaffigan, Amy Schumer, and Hugh Grant, who plays an outrageous version of the actor behind the voice of Tony the Tiger.

The actual corporate rivalry was real, but the movie takes enormous liberties with history. Seinfeld's character, Bob Cabana, is fictional, as are many of the events portrayed. The film turns the competition into an absurd comedy involving corporate intrigue, eccentric executives, and an unlikely collection of characters.

It's an entertaining example of how an everyday packaged breakfast food became the subject of a Hollywood movie.

The real Pop-Tarts story is also an interesting chapter in American food history.

During the 1960s, convenience foods were changing American eating habits. Breakfast cereals, frozen waffles, and toaster pastries offered alternatives to traditional breakfasts, while television advertising helped turn packaged foods into household names.

Pop-Tarts eventually became more than breakfast. They were snacks, lunchbox treats, and something people could eat straight from the package without ever going near a toaster.

For my photograph, I assembled a collection of whole and broken frosted toaster pastries, exposing the fruit filling beneath the pastry and icing.

More than sixty years after their introduction, Pop-Tarts remain an unmistakable part of American food culture.

And not many breakfast pastries can claim to have inspired a Jerry Seinfeld movie!

Happy National Pop-Tarts Day!

There is a lot more of my food photography and other projects to see at https://t.co/SCX5zrvlMS

🟨SNF PULSE™          EVENING

THE BIGGEST AI IPO IN HISTORY COULDN'T STOP A 1,100 POINT SELLOFF.

Thursday, November 19, 2026

Wall Street began Thursday looking for a recovery.

Anthropic's historic public offering generated extraordinary demand. Technology futures rallied before the opening bell, and investors had another opportunity to rebuild confidence in the AI trade.

By the close, that optimism had disappeared across the broader market.

The Dow lost more than 1,100 points. The S&P 500 fell for a sixth consecutive session. Every major sector declined.

Even Anthropic surrendered much of its initial surge.

Wednesday suggested buyers were returning selectively. Thursday showed how fragile that buying really was.

⚪ THE EVENING TAPE

🔴 S&P 500: 7,175.83 | −2.02%
🔴 Nasdaq: 23,879.20 | −2.25%
🔴 Dow: 49,097.06 | −2.19%
🔴 Russell 2000: Approximately −2.2%
🟠 VIX: Near 28
🔴 Philadelphia Semiconductor Index: −2.4%

The most revealing figures were beneath the indexes.

🔴 NYSE declining stocks outnumbered advancing stocks by more than four to one.
🔴 Nasdaq decliners outnumbered advancers by approximately 3.6 to one.
🔴 The NYSE recorded 796 new 52-week lows against just 21 new highs.
🔴 All eleven S&P 500 sectors finished lower.

Energy and utilities held up relatively better, but neither provided a broad defensive refuge. Consumer discretionary and communication services were among the weakest areas.

This was not a rotation into a new group of market leaders. It was widespread selling, with only pockets of relative resilience.

🟨 THE AI TEST

Anthropic's first trading day captured the market's contradiction.
🟢 IPO price: $83.
🟢 Opening trade: $111.50.
🟡 Closing price: $97.17, approximately 17% above the offering price but nearly 13% below its opening trade.

The historic offering demonstrated substantial investor demand for direct AI exposure.

But it did not restore confidence across the existing technology complex.

🔴 Nvidia declined 3.3%, extending its losing streak to six sessions despite its exceptionally strong earnings forecast.
🔴 AMD lost approximately 7.7% amid a new short selling disclosure.
🔴 CoreWeave declined 6.1%.
🔴 Nebius fell 9.4%.
🟢 Palo Alto Networks gained 6.4% after raising its fiscal year outlook.

That divergence matters.

Investors remain willing to reward specific businesses and new investment opportunities. But enthusiasm for 

AI technology is no longer translating automatically into confidence across the companies financing and constructing its infrastructure.

The market still believes AI can generate extraordinary demand. It is becoming more demanding about valuation, financing and returns.

🟠 THE CROSS-ASSET SIGNAL

🟡 U.S. 10-year Treasury yield: Approximately 5.04%, lower on the day.
🟠 U.S. dollar index: Near 103.8.
🔴 Gold: Around $3,674 per ounce, at a 14-month low.
🔴 Bitcoin: Under pressure around $62,000 after trading below that level.
🟡 Brent crude: $91.98 per barrel.
🟡 WTI crude: $83.21 per barrel.

Oil finished essentially unchanged as concerns about excess supply competed with Middle East disruption risks.

The larger story was elsewhere.

Treasury yields declined, but stocks continued falling. 

Gold failed to attract sustained defensive demand. Bitcoin remained under pressure.

These markets are responding differently, but they share an important vulnerability: increasingly restrictive financial conditions and uncertainty about future liquidity.

The Federal Reserve remains central to that pressure.

Traders are assigning a very high probability to another December interest rate increase.

And Thursday's economic data complicated the picture further.

Initial jobless claims rose to 203,000, while the Philadelphia Fed's manufacturing activity index weakened from 20.9 to 6.3.

Yet the survey's prices paid index climbed to 58.2, indicating broader input cost increases among respondents.

Manufacturing momentum weakened while pricing pressure intensified. That is an uncomfortable combination for a central bank still focused on inflation.

🟨 WHAT SNF IS WATCHING

🟡 FRIDAY, NOVEMBER 20 | 10:00 AM EST

The final University of Michigan consumer sentiment report and its inflation expectations readings.

Consumer confidence matters ahead of holiday spending. Inflation expectations matter because the Federal Reserve is already confronting renewed price pressure.

🟡 FRIDAY | MARKET BREADTH

Watch whether the S&P 500 can interrupt its six-session decline.

A rebound confined to Nvidia, Anthropic or another handful of major names would not establish a broad recovery.

More convincing evidence would include stronger participation in small caps, financials, industrials and consumer discretionary.

🟡 AI LEADERSHIP

Watch Anthropic's second trading session, Nvidia's response to its earnings, semiconductor suppliers, and financing dependent infrastructure companies.

A stable IPO alone is insufficient. Investors need evidence that demand can spread across the wider AI ecosystem.

🟡 RATES, GOLD AND BITCOIN

Monitor whether declining Treasury yields finally support equities and whether gold and Bitcoin stabilize.

Continued weakness across these markets would suggest the pressure is not confined to technology valuations.

🟡 NOVEMBER 25 | PCE INFLATION AND GDP

Wednesday's scheduled October PCE inflation report and third quarter GDP revision will be important tests of the growth and inflation balance heading into the December Fed meeting.

🟨 THE TWO SCENARIOS

🟢 CONSTRUCTIVE

Friday's inflation expectations are contained, Treasury yields remain orderly and investors begin rebuilding exposure beyond a narrow group of technology stocks.

Anthropic stabilizes, semiconductor selling moderates, and market breadth improves.

That would suggest the recent decline is transitioning from broad liquidation toward more selective positioning.

🔴 RISK

Inflation expectations remain elevated, the dollar stays firm, and the Federal Reserve's tightening outlook continues pressuring valuations.

Selling persists across Nvidia, AI infrastructure, small caps and consumer sensitive stocks while gold and Bitcoin fail to recover.

Under that scenario, occasional earnings winners and isolated rallies may not be enough to reverse the broader retreat.

🟨 SNF LENS™

🟢 SIGNAL: Thursday's closing breadth confirmed that selling extended far beyond the AI trade. Anthropic's successful offering did not translate into stronger demand across the market.

⚪ NOISE: Confusing a 17% gain from an IPO offering price with a positive signal for the entire technology sector, or assuming lower Treasury yields automatically restore risk appetite.

🟡 CONFIRMATION: Improving participation across sectors, stabilization in Nvidia and Anthropic, less pressure on gold and Bitcoin, and consumer inflation expectations that do not intensify concerns about further tightening.

🔴 RISK: Persistent inflation, restrictive financing conditions, increasingly concentrated exposure, weak market breadth and additional selling in capital intensive AI businesses.

🟨 THE BOTTOM LINE

Thursday was a significant setback for the market's recovery attempt.

Wednesday's selective buying offered the possibility that investors were beginning to separate strong businesses from weaker market segments.

Thursday rejected that optimism, at least temporarily.

The largest AI IPO in history attracted enormous demand.

But the broader market continued falling.

Treasury yields eased.

Gold and Bitcoin remained weak.

Every major equity sector finished lower.

The lesson is not that AI demand has disappeared. 

Nvidia's earnings and Anthropic's offering suggest otherwise.

The question is whether investors can regain confidence in valuations, financing structures and broader economic conditions while inflation remains elevated.

Friday's consumer sentiment report and the market's reaction will provide the next test.

THE BIGGEST AI IPO EVER FOUND BUYERS.

THE BROADER MARKET DID NOT.

UNTIL BREADTH RECOVERS, STRONG HEADLINES ARE NOT STRONG CONFIRMATION.

text:
Closing DD, Thu Nov 19

This morning I asked whether Nvidia and Micron would still be up an hour into trading. They were. Both gave back those gains by the bell.

The selling spread beyond chips. Anthropic also made its Nasdaq debut and finished above the offer price after giving back much of its opening jump.

1. How the market finished
$SPY $QQQ $DIA $IWM

The S&P 500 and Nasdaq-100 funds were up early. By the bell, they were down 2.0% and 2.2%, respectively. The Dow fund and the fund that tracks smaller U.S. companies each fell 2.2%.

I'd check the smaller-company fund tomorrow to see whether any bounce reaches beyond big tech.

2. Chip gains faded
$NVDA $MU $INTC $SOXX

An hour into regular trading, Nvidia was up about 1.7% and Micron was up 3.7%. Nvidia finished down 3.3%. Micron, which I'm watching, finished down 2.1%. Intel, also on my list, rose 1.9%. The iShares chip fund fell 2.7%.

I'd compare any early Nvidia rebound Friday with the chip fund to see whether it moves higher, too.

3. Anthropic's first day
$ANT

Anthropic, the company behind Claude, priced its IPO at $83 a share. Its first trade on Nasdaq was $111.50 at 11:48am ET. It closed at $97.17. That's about 17% above the offer and 13% below the first trade.

The offer and the first trade give you two very different starting points for the day.

4. SpaceX finished below $143
$SPCX

SpaceX closed at $138.43, down 3.5%. Yesterday it recovered after dipping below $143 late in the day.

Friday's check is whether SpaceX can get back above $143 and stay there into the close.

5. More purchases at Walmart
$WMT

Walmart says U.S. comparable sales rose 2.9% from a year earlier, excluding fuel. The number of purchases rose 1.5%, and the average purchase was 1.4% larger in dollars. Walmart shares fell 1.0% in the regular session.

6. Intuit agrees to sell Mailchimp
$INTU

Intuit, the company behind QuickBooks, reported a 12% rise in quarterly revenue to $4.4 billion. QuickBooks Online Accounting revenue rose 19% to $1.4 billion. Intuit agreed to sell Mailchimp, its email marketing business, to Bending Spoons for about $3.68 billion, subject to closing conditions.
Around 5:17pm ET, Intuit shares were down about 9.8% from their regular-session close in after-hours trading.

If the deal closes, QuickBooks is one place to look for growth in the business Intuit plans to keep.

Around 5:17pm ET, $BTC was near $61,730, down about 2.0% since midnight UTC, and $ETH was near $1,746, down about 1.6% on the same basis.

On deck
The University of Michigan releases its final November consumer sentiment survey at 10am ET Friday.

Walmart showed more purchases and slightly bigger bills. The survey checks how households feel about their finances heading into the holidays.

If Nvidia and Micron bounce again Friday morning, are they still up by lunchtime?

David Schwartz once put it simply about XRP: it can’t stay dirt cheap. That doesn’t make sense for a token meant to move real value.

If a large payment required a million tokens at a dollar each, the cost is a million dollars. If the token itself was worth a million, you’d only need one. Either way, the utility forces the price higher once real volume shows up. The math doesn’t care about the ticker.

I’ve held XRP for years and still see the potential in that logic. But when I look at what Telcoin is actually building right now, the same principle applies with even stronger structural pressure.

Telcoin isn’t just a token sitting on a network. It has a Nebraska-chartered Digital Asset Bank that issues eUSD (Digital Cash), takes deposits, and offers on-chain bank accounts inside the Telcoin Wallet. That bank is already live. At the same time, Telcoin Network is moving into mainnet: code freeze is done, genesis is set for December 2, and public launch follows mid-month. The network is EVM-compatible and validated exclusively by GSMA mobile operators who stake TEL and earn fees.

Think about what that combination actually means. You have regulated banking rails that can issue and move dollars on-chain, plus a settlement layer secured by the same telecom companies that already run the world’s most trusted communication infrastructure. Banks get hacked. Pure software validators can be gamed. Here the validators are the mobile operators themselves—entities with existing licenses, customer bases, and skin in the game across dozens of countries.

When money starts moving at the speed and scale of mobile networks, through a bank that already holds a charter, the token that pays for that movement and secures the network can’t stay priced like a pure speculative asset. The same Schwartz math applies: once real volume hits (carrier settlements, vendor payments, remittances, on-chain bank activity), the unit of account has to carry more value or the system becomes inefficient.

This isn’t another “blockchain will change banking” pitch. The bank already exists. The network is launching with the actual mobile operators as the security layer. The internet of money and the mobile networks that already connect billions of people are being wired together under one regulated roof.

That combination is rare. And rare things with real utility don’t stay cheap for long once the volume arrives.
The towers that carry voice and data are about to carry value the same way. For anyone who has watched this space for years, this is one of the cleaner setups where the infrastructure, the regulation, and the token utility are finally lining up at the same time.

Russian documents Set out 'tectonic weapon' research
Carl Levitin

Moscow. The first official details have emerged in Moscow of ambitious research into 'tectonic warfare' carried out by the former Soviet Union and subsequently by the government of Russia, and involving atte mpts to stimulate 'artificial' earthquakes as weapons of destruction. According to documents obtained by the newspaper Moscow News, two research programmes, the first known as ' Mercury ' and the second as ' Volcano', were aimed at creating new earthquake epicentres by using underground nuclear explosions . Geophysicists are aware that impending earthquakes may be triggered by underground nuclear explosions . But Western geophysicists remain sceptical about tectonic warfare and have all but abandoned research after two unsuccessful phases of activity in the 1960s and 1980s, says Roger Clark, a lecturer in geophysics at the University of Leeds. Clark is not at all surprised that th e Russians tried to create earthquakes and control their location electromagnetically, however. "This sort of science is very much part of their heritage. We don't think it is impossible, or wrong , but past experience suggests it is very, very unlikely. "

The programme , which was secretly launched by the Communist rulers of the former Soviet Union in 1987, and has been unofficially known to Western geophysicists for several years, is now believed to have been abandoned. It would certainly contravene the terms of the Comprehensive Test Ban Treaty, which Russia signed at the United Nations in Geneva last month . The Mercury project was launched in the former Soviet republic of Azerbaijan, but came to a halt when the republic became independent. It was superseded by the Volcano project. Three underground nuclear tests are believed to have taken place at sites in Kyrgyzstan.

According to the documents, the Mercury project was launched by a secret decree of the Central Committee of the Communist Party and the Council of Ministers of the Soviet Union. The objective was to "develop a methodology for remote operation on an earthquake epicentre by using weak seismic fields and research possibilities of transferring the seismic energy of an explosion ".

The documents say that the Mercury project involved 22 scientific and industrial organizations, including the Geological Institute of the Azerbaijan Academy of Sciences in Baku. The remit extended to developing the electronic equipment to be installed aboard space satellites that would control the tectonic weapon. The scientists were given three years to complete research, with testing planned for 1990.

During the research phase, Azerbaijani scientists grew increasingly confident and, according to the documents, were sure that " after [a] nuclear explosion, subterranean energy may accumulate at huge distances from the epicentre and reach massive capacity, after which the next directed explosion can release it all ".

Underground testing began at the town of Batken in Kyrgyzstan, and was directed by lkram Ke rimov , of the Azerbaijan Academy of Sciences. The documents say that scientists detonated an underground nuclear charge and tried to control the direction of seismic energy release d using British-built equipment known as 'system 9690 ' .

A report prepared by the Mozhaisky Military Engineering Institute concluded that the test had been a success. But progress slowed considerably following Azerbaijan's independence from the Soviet Union. At about this time , Russia embarked on a more comprehensive tectonic warfare programme known as the Volcano project. The Earth Physics Institute of the Russian Academy of Sciences (RAS) became the project headquarters .

Research was scheduled to be completed in 1992, with underground testing beginning the following year. The final test was carried out at a place code-named S36NZ-0Kh; Moscow News believes the letters 'NZ' refer to Novaya Zemlya, where Soviet nuclear testing began in the 1950s."
