Once the State of Israel was born, the fate of Jerusalem and the holy places continued to be an issue of Vatican concern, together with the evolution of the Arab-Israeli conflict, the fate of Christian communities in the Middle East, and the question of recognition or non-recognition of the new state. As Vatican expert Henry Bocala pointed out, the Holy See viewed the question of Jerusalem as a religious issue (protection of the holy places) with a political dimension (the legal status of the city). Here, Rome saw itself as a party to the dispute and, consequently, not only asked for a resolution but also demanded a say over the outcome. Initially, it asked for the internationalization of Jerusalem and the holy places, and from 1967 onwards modified its position in pursuit of an internationally guaranteed special status. The Arab-Israeli conflict was seen as a political problem (a clash between two nationalisms) with a religious component (the diminished Christian presence in the Holy Land). Here, Rome saw itself in the role of a conciliator and asked for a resolution without proposing details for it.3

This did not prevent the Papacy from adopting a pro-Palestinian position. The Holy See propagated the idea that the Palestinians were the main victims of the conflict, that the Israelis were responsible for their condition, as well as the notion that without a solution to their cause there could be no peace in the region. Rome’s stand on the Arab-Israeli conflict was reflected in this phrase by the President of the Pontifical Mission for Palestine, Monsignor John Nolan: “If the Palestinians have no voice, we are their voice.”4

Rome’s endorsement of Palestinian national aspirations did not echo its lack of support for Jewish national yearnings before 1948, and once the Jewish state was established it took the Vatican decades to establish diplomatic ties. An Israeli official based in Rome expressed Jerusalem’s annoyance thus: “Our position was clear: we are always ready. If you truly wish to normalize relations, you have only to say the word. Our address is the same as it was 2,000 years ago.”5

As the first Israeli ambassador to the Holy See, the late Shmuel Hadas, observed, early recognition of Israel could have been a historic opportunity for the Catholic Church to rectify – albeit partially – its past hostility toward Jews and its silence during the Holocaust.6 Rome chose to see things in a different way. Only after the PLO agreed to formally recognize Israel in September 1993 did the Holy See decide to do the same, two months later. By then, the State of Israel had lived through forty-five years of sovereign life.

In December 1993, the Fundamental Agreement was signed between the parties and in June 1994, Israel and the Holy See exchanged ambassadors. A new horizon in relations between the two emerged, and the bond between Rome and Jerusalem was finally normalized.

I believe the genie in a bottle concept may have roots in the Middle Eastern stories about jinn, particularly traditions that associate King Solomon with controlling and imprisoning them. However, I haven't been able to establish the exact original source of the familiar genie in a bottle story.
What I did find interesting is an ancient extra-biblical text called the Testament of Solomon. Although traditionally attributed to Solomon, its actual author is unknown, and it is generally dated to the first several centuries AD.
It contains two particularly interesting accounts:
1. Chapter 16, verses 1–7 The sea demon
Solomon captures a demon called Kunopegos (also spelled Kynopegos). He orders the demon placed inside a broad, flat bowl, adds ten containers of seawater, seals the opening with marble, asphalt, pitch and hemp rope, and has it stored in the Temple.
2. Chapters 119–121 -A demon inside a flask.
This account is even closer to the genie in a bottle story. Solomon sends a servant to Arabia with a leather flask and his signet ring. The servant captures a spirit inside the flask, seals it, and brings it back to Solomon.
Of course, these are extra-biblical accounts, and whether the events actually happened is another matter entirely.
Personally, I put far greater trust in Scripture than in these later writings. That doesn't mean I think we can never learn anything from historical writings outside the Bible. They can offer interesting insight into what people believed, the traditions that developed around biblical figures, and the historical context of different periods.
But I distinguish between historical accounts and Scripture, and I wouldn't give an extra-biblical story the same authority or credibility as God's Word. Just because something was written about a biblical figure doesn't automatically make it true.

Published: 10 October 1996
Russian documents Set out 'tectonic weapon' research
Carl Levitin

Moscow. The first official details have emerged in Moscow of ambitious research into 'tectonic warfare' carried out by the former Soviet Union and subsequently by the government of Russia, and involving atte mpts to stimulate 'artificial' earthquakes as weapons of destruction. According to documents obtained by the newspaper Moscow News, two research programmes, the first known as ' Mercury ' and the second as ' Volcano', were aimed at creating new earthquake epicentres by using underground nuclear explosions . Geophysicists are aware that impending earthquakes may be triggered by underground nuclear explosions . But Western geophysicists remain sceptical about tectonic warfare and have all but abandoned research after two unsuccessful phases of activity in the 1960s and 1980s, says Roger Clark, a lecturer in geophysics at the University of Leeds. Clark is not at all surprised that th e Russians tried to create earthquakes and control their location electromagnetically, however. "This sort of science is very much part of their heritage. We don't think it is impossible, or wrong , but past experience suggests it is very, very unlikely. "

The programme , which was secretly launched by the Communist rulers of the former Soviet Union in 1987, and has been unofficially known to Western geophysicists for several years, is now believed to have been abandoned. It would certainly contravene the terms of the Comprehensive Test Ban Treaty, which Russia signed at the United Nations in Geneva last month . The Mercury project was launched in the former Soviet republic of Azerbaijan, but came to a halt when the republic became independent. It was superseded by the Volcano project. Three underground nuclear tests are believed to have taken place at sites in Kyrgyzstan.

According to the documents, the Mercury project was launched by a secret decree of the Central Committee of the Communist Party and the Council of Ministers of the Soviet Union. The objective was to "develop a methodology for remote operation on an earthquake epicentre by using weak seismic fields and research possibilities of transferring the seismic energy of an explosion ".

The documents say that the Mercury project involved 22 scientific and industrial organizations, including the Geological Institute of the Azerbaijan Academy of Sciences in Baku. The remit extended to developing the electronic equipment to be installed aboard space satellites that would control the tectonic weapon. The scientists were given three years to complete research, with testing planned for 1990.

During the research phase, Azerbaijani scientists grew increasingly confident and, according to the documents, were sure that " after [a] nuclear explosion, subterranean energy may accumulate at huge distances from the epicentre and reach massive capacity, after which the next directed explosion can release it all ".

Underground testing began at the town of Batken in Kyrgyzstan, and was directed by lkram Ke rimov , of the Azerbaijan Academy of Sciences. The documents say that scientists detonated an underground nuclear charge and tried to control the direction of seismic energy release d using British-built equipment known as 'system 9690 ' .

A report prepared by the Mozhaisky Military Engineering Institute concluded that the test had been a success. But progress slowed considerably following Azerbaijan's independence from the Soviet Union. At about this time , Russia embarked on a more comprehensive tectonic warfare programme known as the Volcano project. The Earth Physics Institute of the Russian Academy of Sciences (RAS) became the project headquarters .

Research was scheduled to be completed in 1992, with underground testing beginning the following year. The final test was carried out at a place code-named S36NZ-0Kh; Moscow News believes the letters 'NZ' refer to Novaya Zemlya, where Soviet nuclear testing began in the 1950s."

Defense Primer: Directed-Energy Weapons
Both the 2022 National Defense Strategy and the House Armed Services Committee’s bipartisan Future of Defense Task Force Report have identified directed energy as a technology that could have a significant impact on U.S. national security in the years to come. As the Department of Defense (DOD) continues to invest in directed-energy (DE) weapons, Congress may consider implications for defense authorizations, appropriations, and oversight. Overview DOD defines DE weapons as those using concentrated electromagnetic energy, rather than kinetic energy, to “incapacitate, damage, disable, or destroy enemy equipment, facilities, and/or personnel.” DE weapons include high-energy lasers (HEL) and high-powered microwave (HPM) weapons; other DE weapons, such as particle beam weapons, are outside the scope of this In Focus. HELs might be used by ground forces in short-range air defense (SHORAD), counter-unmanned aircraft systems (C-UAS), or counter-rocket, artillery, and mortar (C-RAM) missions. The weapons might be used to “dazzle” (i.e., temporarily disable) or damage satellites and sensors. This could in turn interfere with intelligence-gathering operations; military cmmunications; and positioning, navigation, and timing systems used for weapons targeting. In addition, HELs could theoretically provide options for boost-phase missile intercept, given their speed-of-light travel time; however, experts disagree on the affordability, technological feasibility, and utility of this application. In general, HELs might offer lower costs per shot and— assuming access to a sufficient power supply—deeper magazines compared with traditional munitions. (Although a number of different types of HELs exist, many of the United States’ current programs are solid state lasers, which are fueled by electrical power. As a result, the cost per shot is equivalent to the cost of the electrical power required to fire the shot.) This could in turn produce a favorable cost exchange ratio for the defender, whose marginal costs would be significantly lower than those of the aggressor.

FOR IMMEDIATE RELEASE

**COWBOYS ANNOUNCE DEFENSIVE COORDINATOR WILL NO LONGER COORDINATE THE DEFENSE ON THE DAYS IT MATTERS**

FRISCO, Texas — The Dallas Cowboys proudly announced Wednesday that Christian Parker remains the team's defensive coordinator in every way except the one that happens during football games.

Parker, hired in January as the youngest defensive coordinator in franchise history, will continue to run meetings, lead walkthroughs, and build game plans that someone else will call. Play-calling duties transfer to senior defensive assistant Mike Pettine, who was hired five weeks ago as a "consultant" and has now completed the fastest hostile takeover in franchise history. Pettine previously employed Parker as a quality control assistant in Green Bay, meaning the student has become the teacher's assistant again.

The move comes after a rigorous evaluation process that began Tuesday, when owner Jerry Jones told a radio station the team was "talking about" Parker's future, and ended roughly 24 hours later.

The results demanded action. Through ten games, the Cowboys defense ranks last in the NFL in total yards (393.8 per game), last in rushing yards, last in third-down defense, and 30th in points allowed (28.2). On Sunday, the unit surrendered 584 yards to San Francisco — the most ever allowed at AT&T Stadium — in a 46-40 loss that head coach Brian Schottenheimer described as part of the search for "answers and solutions."

Parker addressed the media Thursday in his regularly scheduled press conference, which the team stresses he was always going to do. He confirmed he pushed back against the decision, admitted he considered resigning, and summarized the arrangement as "not an ideal situation for me personally." Asked about his long-term future in Dallas, the defensive coordinator offered the organization's new unofficial motto: "We'll cross that bridge when we get there."

Schottenheimer insisted Parker is "a huge part of the solution" and has "an incredibly bright future" with the team, remarks he delivered while explaining why Parker will not be allowed to call plays.

Pettine makes his debut Sunday against the 1-8 Tennessee Titans, a matchup the organization selected for its difficulty setting.

The Cowboys are 4-6.

text:
🇺🇲 The Pentagon is racing to rebuild its missile and shell stockpiles after the Iran war. Its own watchdog says nobody is in charge of the plan, because there is no plan

The United States spent the Iran war firing interceptors, cruise missiles and bombs faster than factories could replace them. On Thursday the Government Accountability Office said the Pentagon still has no overall plan for getting the stockpiles back.

"DoD does not have an overarching plan that links munitions production and funding to requirements," the congressional watchdog wrote in a new report. Defense officials told investigators that without one, the department and the services "can be reactive to global events rather than driven by total requirements."

GAO offers a concrete example. The Army's push to ramp up 155 millimeter artillery shell production, launched to cover shortages made worse by US support to allies and partners, was not driven by the Pentagon's total munitions requirement. Defense News, which first reported the findings, noted that the same effort has been dogged by factory problems, including a new Texas plant that cost nearly 500 million dollars and failed to produce any shell components.

The risk cuts both ways, the report warns. Without a plan, the military may fail to fix chronically low inventories, or end up investing in munitions projected to exceed what it needs.

The Pentagon also has a data problem. Its department-wide tracking tool, the Munitions Readiness Initiative, pulls from 37 separate data sources, some updated by hand. GAO found that the acquisition and sustainment office does not regularly reconcile that tool against the services' own inventory systems, and has no data management plan explaining how the numbers are combined. That leaves open how far senior leaders can trust the stockpile figures in front of them.

Then there is leadership. Authority is spread across several Pentagon offices and the services' program executive offices, and the working groups meant to tie them together lack authority and accountability. GAO says the department has never named a single office with the power to drive improvements and answer for the results.

The watchdog made four recommendations: write an overarching munitions plan with goals and metrics, put one office in charge of it, set regular timelines for reconciling inventory data, and have the Pentagon's chief digital and AI officer document how that data is assembled. The Pentagon generally concurred.

What the public cannot see may matter most. The report is the unclassified version of a study GAO delivered in September, stripped of inventory trends, persistent shortfalls and how those shortfalls have affected support to war plans.

It lands as Congress fights over defense money and as the Navy's acting secretary, Hung Cao, has acknowledged the service "recoded" expired munitions so it could keep firing them during the Iran war. Factories are getting orders. GAO's question is whether anyone is checking that they are the right ones.

BREAKING: MEMPHIS WAFFLE HOUSE LOVE TRIANGLE EXPLODES INTO FIVE-WAY BREAKFAST BRAWL OVER ONE MAN WITH THREE GIRLFRIENDS
MEMPHIS, TN — Police responded to a Waffle House on Elvis Presley Boulevard early Thursday morning after three Memphis women allegedly turned a routine breakfast date into a full-blown episode of Jerry Springer, complete with flying purses, airborne hair extensions, and enough screaming to wake up Elvis.

The fight reportedly started around 1:47 a.m., just as the cook was finishing a fresh batch of scattered, smothered, and covered hashbrowns.

According to witnesses, 32-year-old Shanika "Hot Sauce" Williams, 29-year-old Tiffany "Big Trouble" Jenkins, and 35-year-old Latoya "The Situation" McBride all showed up at the restaurant believing they were on a romantic date with the same man.

That man was identified as 27-year-old DeAndre "D-Train" Washington, who apparently thought he was running a dating service when, in reality, he was operating a traveling disaster.

Investigators say D-Train had separately invited all three women to "meet me at Waffle House. We can chill and see where things go."

Unfortunately, all three women arrived at approximately the same time.

And apparently, none of them were interested in sharing the All-Star Special.
WITNESSES DESCRIBE THE CHAOS
Patrons say the trouble started when all three women spotted D-Train sitting in a booth, drinking a Mountain Dew and eating hashbrowns like a man who had absolutely no idea his life was about to become a documentary.

"He just froze," said one customer. "I've seen deer react better when headlights are coming at them. That boy knew he was in trouble."

The women allegedly confronted each other, then D-Train, then each other again, before the situation escalated into what one employee described as "a breakfast buffet at the gates of hell."

Witnesses reported:
- One purse being swung so hard it knocked over three coffee mugs and a bottle of Texas Pete.
- Someone screaming, "I GOT RECEIPTS, HO!"
- A set of expensive hair extensions landing directly in a stranger's cheese eggs.
- One woman throwing a plate of scattered hashbrowns like she was competing in the Olympic discus event.
- A waitress calmly stepping over two fighting women while asking if anybody needed more coffee.
Meanwhile, D-Train reportedly attempted to hide underneath the booth, repeatedly insisting, "I didn't know y'all knew each other."

Police later described this statement as technically true but spectacularly stupid.
POLICE ARRIVE — D-TRAIN DISCOVERS CONSEQUENCES
When officers arrived, the three women were still arguing, one had lost a shoe, another was missing an eyelash, and D-Train was reportedly still underneath the booth holding a half-eaten waffle.

One officer asked him what happened.

His response?

Japanese people are often called polite and considerate. We value that.

But there’s something I admire about Americans, something I think we can learn from.

I’m Japanese, born and raised in Tokyo. It’s the courage to stand up for someone else.

“On a New York subway, a stranger was yelling at a young woman. Everyone stayed quiet until a man sat beside her and said, ‘She’s not alone.’ The stranger got off at the next stop.” (Office worker, 34)

“At a Texas gas station, an older man was counting coins, short on gas money. A woman offered her card. When he refused, she said, ‘Someday my dad might need help too.’” (Traveler, 29)

“A Japanese boy at a California school ate lunch alone because he barely spoke English. An American boy sat beside him with his tray. They didn’t understand much, but ate together every day.” (Teacher, 43)

“A customer was insulting a waitress in Chicago. A woman at another table stood and said, ‘She’s not your servant.’ The room fell silent. Then someone clapped.” (Restaurant owner, 55)

“In a Florida downpour, a man in a wheelchair was stuck at a crosswalk. When the light changed, a young driver got out and pushed him across, getting soaked. Nobody honked.” (Nurse, 38)

“At an Ohio high school, a student mocked a boy’s accent. Another asked, ‘He speaks two languages. How many do you speak?’ The room went quiet. The boy wasn’t alone after that.” (International student, 21)

“A neighbor shouted that a dog was trapped in a burning house. A firefighter went in without hesitation and came out minutes later holding the little dog. Its owner cried and thanked him repeatedly.” (Veterinarian, 47)

“At a Boston station, an elderly woman struggled with a suitcase on the stairs. A student offered help. When she hesitated, he said, ‘If she were my grandma, I’d hope someone helped her.’” (Professor, 62)

“At a youth baseball game, a boy was hit in the face by a ball and fell. The first to reach him was the opposing batter. He forgot the game and held the boy’s hand.” (Baseball coach, 49)

“At an LA bus stop, a homeless man shivered in the cold. A woman gave him her coat. ‘Won’t you be cold?’ he asked. ‘I have a home to go to,’ she said.” (Social worker, 41)

“At an American airport, an elderly Japanese couple who spoke no English nearly missed their connection. A young woman ran with them to the airline counter, helped them, then walked back toward her own gate.” (Travel agent, 36)

One more thing. My mother is 58.

She’s always cared about people’s feelings, but when someone needs help, she acts before she can overthink it.

Once, talking about Americans helping strangers, she told me:

“In Japan, we’re raised not to trouble others. That’s important.

But I don’t think we should stand back when someone needs help just because we’re afraid to get involved.

That’s what I admire about Americans. They’ll approach a stranger and offer help without worrying what people think.

Kind people exist everywhere. But actually doing something with that kindness? That’s special.”

Her words stayed with me.

Kindness exists in Japan, America, everywhere. But acting on it takes courage.

Courage to approach a stranger. To speak up when something is wrong. To move first when everyone else stands still.

So, America, however harshly you judge your country, remember the people who deserve respect.

Not celebrities, politicians, or billionaires. Ordinary people who step forward for someone else at school, at work, or on the street.

Real courage isn’t never being afraid. It’s stepping forward even when you’re scared because someone needs you.

From Japan, across the ocean, I have so much respect for those Americans.

text:
No forms, no weekly log

Coaching mitigation clauses are written in broad legal language, and schools almost never police them the way an unemployment office would.

What the clause requires

The usual wording asks the coach to make a “good faith” or “reasonable and diligent” effort to find comparable work. Whatever he earns in the new job is then subtracted from what the old school still owes him. The idea comes from contract law in general: the side that took the loss has to take reasonable steps to keep it down.

Proof of the job search

Some contracts let the school ask for proof. James Franklin’s Penn State deal required him to show evidence that he’s looking for work if the university requests it. Nothing gets turned in on a schedule, and most contracts don’t require regular reporting at all.

Where the clause matters

1. The offset. Once he’s hired somewhere, his new salary reduces what the old school pays.

2. The definition of “comparable.” At Wisconsin, Luke Fickell’s contract counts any NFL or Division I coaching job, not just head coaching jobs. He can’t turn down a coordinator offer and say nothing comparable came along.

3. Rules against gaming it. Some coaches try to avoid the offset by taking a cheap short-term job or volunteering while the buyout keeps paying. Bo Pelini’s contract barred him from structuring his pay to dodge mitigation. Franklin’s requires him to pursue the highest reasonable salary in his next job.

How it plays out

Proving that a coach didn’t try hard enough is hard and expensive, so schools rarely sue over it. More often the two sides negotiate a lump-sum settlement. A coach who sits out a year usually gets paid. A coach who takes a new job sees the offset kick in.

Not every contract has the clause at all. Jimbo Fisher had no duty to mitigate at Texas A&M, and Billy Napier’s Florida deal has no offset.

It sounds like she needs to find another job if her current position doesn't meet her financial needs or career expectations. At some point, personal responsibility has to enter the conversation.

Walmart isn't responsible for ensuring that every employee earns the income they want or achieves the lifestyle they desire. The company offers a position at a stated wage, and individuals have the choice to accept it, negotiate for more, or pursue other opportunities.

If the job doesn't provide the income she needs, the solution is to develop additional skills, pursue advancement, seek better-paying employment, or make a career change.

This generation has developed an unfortunate tendency to blame employers for circumstances that they as individuals have the power, and ultimately the responsibility, to change. Employers should provide fair compensation for the work performed, but employees also have a responsibility to increase their own value in the marketplace.

A job is an opportunity, not a lifetime guarantee of financial satisfaction. At some point, you have to take ownership of your own future rather than expecting someone else to improve it for you.

Host: An historic judgment from the International Court of Justice today, ruling that Myanmar committed genocide against its Rohingya minority. Stephanie Sy details how the ruling comes years after Myanmar's Muslim minority was forced to flee. And a warning. This report contains images that some viewers may find disturbing.

Stephanie Sy: Today, a sliver of justice for the Rohingya Muslims of Myanmar.

Judge: The Republic of the Union of Myanmar has committed genocide against the Rohingya group.

Stephanie Sy: The landmark nine-to-six decision is the first of its kind. Before today, the International Court of Justice, a United Nations body, had never held a state responsible for genocide.

Judge: The only reasonable inference that can explain Myanmar's actions is an intention to destroy a substantial part of the protected group, namely the Rohingya population in Northern Rakhine State.

Stephanie Sy: Today's ruling comes seven years after the case was first brought by Gambia.

Dawda Jallow: The victory belongs to the Rohingya. They survived, they testified, and today they were believed.

Stephanie Sy: Rohingya survivors reacted after the decision.

Yasmin Ullah: It didn't feel real to me. I'm still kind of delirious from the decision that was read to us.

Stephanie Sy: Yasmin Ullah is the executive director of Rohingya Women's Collaborative Network.

Yasmin Ullah: It is also for them to feel like they can be heard, that their experience was real. It all validates the experience of the Rohingya.

Stephanie Sy: As the decision was announced in The Hague, Netherlands, thousands of miles away in Bangladesh, Rohingya refugees watched with anticipation.

Mohammad Rofik: Today, all courts recognize and, I mean, give the victory to the Rohingya community, not only Rohingya community. It is the victory of the whole community of the Myanmar. Those are suffering for a long time in the hands of the Myanmar military.

Stephanie Sy: The Rohingya are a Muslim minority from Buddhist majority Myanmar. Almost a decade ago, Myanmar's military executed what it called clearance operations in Rakhine state in response to a Rohingya insurgency that killed more than a dozen officers. The military burned entire villages, systematically raped victims, and, by conservative estimates, killed nearly 7,000 Rohingyas.

Hosna Ara: I have five children. One daughter was thrown in the fire by soldiers, and two are missing. I left my native village with my two children. But before I left, three soldiers entered my house and raped me. At the time, I was bleeding and I was crying. Then the military caught my youngest child and threw her in the fire. Another soldier beat me with a gun, and I continued to cry.

Stephanie Sy: 700,000 Rohingya civilians fled in the immediate aftermath to Bangladesh. But as the atrocities continued, more than 1.2 million Rohingya refugees left Myanmar.

Sayed Ullah: We are satisfied. So, what can we do in the future? We are satisfied, but yet we can't go back home.

Stephanie Sy: While today's ruling gives recognition, many are now wondering what comes next. To unpack what the genocide verdict means for international law and the future of the Rohingya people, we turn now to Rutgers law professor Adil Haque, author of "Law and Morality at War." Mr. Haque, thank you so much for joining the "NewsHour." Before we dive into what led the court to make this decision, I want to get into what those 1.2 million displaced Rohingya people can now expect. Can they expect reparations? Can they expect restitution? Is there a safe way for them to go home?

Adil Haque: Thanks very much for having me. So, certainly, that is what the court has ordered, restitution and compensation, to the extent that the Rohingya can return to their homes, they must be returned to their homes, and monetary compensation must be offered where interest cannot be repaired. That process will take several years to determine the form and amount of restitution and compensation. And then we have to see if Myanmar will comply. The United Kingdom has already called a meeting of the U.N. Security Council to hopefully support the court's orders and to ensure that Myanmar complies with those obligations. And then we have to wait and see if Myanmar does, in fact, do what it must do.

Stephanie Sy: The military -- the junta that rules Myanmar has not responded at all to the court. Have they cooperated at all in this process? Is there any reason to believe that the Rohingya will have a pathway to go back?

Adil Haque: So, the government of Myanmar has participated in the proceedings from the beginning, both under the prior government and now under the military government. So that creates some hope that the new government will comply with the court's directives and will comply with their legal obligations. Hopefully, the new government does not want to be a pariah or an outcast. They want to be a member of the international community and rejoin it, despite the terrible acts they have committed.

Stephanie Sy: As you mentioned, the United Kingdom's Foreign Office did issue a very harsh statement condemning Myanmar, calling for more sanctions. They are also dismissing the country's defense attache from the U.K. But other than that, we haven't heard much international response. Would you expect the U.N. Security Council to do anything? Would you expect any further international pressure?

Adil Haque: I certainly hope so. I certainly think that the United Kingdom, France and other -- some of the elected members of the Security Council will push for that. And then we have to wait and see what the United States, Russia and China, how they will do. But, certainly, states can take action outside of the Security Council, although it's less than ideal. There are other fora where they can coordinate their efforts to try to ensure that Myanmar does what it can, though it certainly can't undo what it has done, but perhaps offer something to its victims.

Stephanie Sy: How did Gambia, a third-party country that is not directly involved in this conflict in any way, manage to pull off this legal victory? Genocide is notoriously difficult to prove and prosecute.

Adil Haque: Thanks. Well, first, the Gambia did something quite extraordinary. It brought a case under the Genocide Convention on behalf of a minority group in another state. And the court, in an earlier proceeding, said that this is proper, this is something that states can do under the Genocide Convention. And that really opens the door to whole new pathways for accountability, that it was not clear were available before this case. So that's really to the credit of the Gambia. As for how they were able to achieve this result, it really turns on the evidence that they were able to present to the court, not only witness testimony, but relying heavily on UN fact-finding mission reports and independent investigative mechanism reports. And these really documented many of the atrocities that you described earlier, the mass killing, the commission of sexual violence on a large scale, the destruction of homes, mass displacement. And it was from all of that conduct that the court was able to infer genocidal intent to destroy a substantive...

Stephanie Sy: Sorry, Adil, the U.S. has expressed concern. This is a controversial decision in some quarters, because the U.S. has always feared that a decision like this would lower the threshold for proving genocide. Does this judgment do that? And what could it portend for other genocide cases before this court, including the one that South Africa has brought against Israel, as it relates to the war in Gaza?

Adil Haque: So, no, this decision does not change the court's interpretation of genocide or the applicable standard of proof. The standard remains very high. Genocide must be proven by fully convincing evidence and must be the only reasonable inference that can be drawn from the evidence. But in this case, the court found that, indeed, this is the only reasonable inference, and Myanmar's alternative theories of the case were simply not credible.

Stephanie Sy: That is Adil Haque, the author of "Law and Morality at War," joining us. Thank you for your insights.

Adil Haque: Thank you for having me.

SOURCE: PBS NewsHour, Nov. 19, 2026

Resident Dumping.

"Resident dumping" in congregate care is the illegal or unethical practice of discharging a vulnerable resident from a group living facility—such as a nursing home, assisted living center, or residential treatment facility—without proper notice, a safe discharge plan, or consent. [1, 2, 3]
While congregate care settings are legally required to ensure a safe transition and appropriate follow-up care, facilities sometimes abandon residents to avoid high care costs or make room for higher-paying private-insurance patients. [1, 2, 3]

Common Forms of Resident Dumping

Hospital dumping. A facility sends a resident to an emergency room for an acute issue and then refuses to readmit them once they are stabilized, often claiming their bed is no longer available. [1]
Unsafe shelter or motel discharges. Facilities drop medically fragile or cognitively impaired residents off at homeless shelters, bus stops, or unequipped motels with little warning and no ongoing care arrangements. [1, 2, 3]
Improper eviction notices. Staff pressure residents or families to leave immediately when short-term insurance (like Medicare) ends, rather than helping them transition to long-term coverage like Medicaid or giving legally mandated advance notice. [1, 2, 3]

Legal Protections & Resident Rights

Under federal and state regulations (especially for Medicare- and Medicaid-certified nursing facilities), facilities cannot simply evict a resident at will: [1, 2]
Valid reasons only. A facility can generally only initiate an involuntary discharge if the resident’s needs can no longer be met there, their health has improved enough that they no longer need care, they pose a direct danger to others, or they have failed to pay after reasonable notice.
30-day written notice. Facilities are typically required to provide at least 30 days' written notice before a discharge, including instructions on how to appeal the decision.
Bed-hold and readmission rights. If a resident is hospitalized, facilities must hold their bed for a state-mandated period (often up to 7 days) or offer them the next available bed once they are cleared to return.
Safe discharge planning. Facilities are legally obligated to prepare a safe, appropriate post-discharge care plan rather than releasing a dependent resident onto the streets. [1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6]

Where to Get Help

If you or someone you know is facing an improper discharge or eviction from a congregate care setting:
Contact the Long-Term Care Ombudsman. Every state has an independent Ombudsman program that advocates for residents in nursing homes, assisted living, and adult foster care at no cost. In Minnesota, you can reach the Minnesota Office of Ombudsman for Long-Term Care to intervene immediately during an active eviction threat.
File an official appeal. If you receive a written discharge notice, follow the appeal instructions immediately—filing a timely appeal often pauses the eviction until a hearing takes place. [1]
Review your rights. Organizations like the AARP Foundation provide step-by-step guides on challenging illegal nursing home discharges. [1]
Are you looking into this for general research, or is someone currently facing an eviction or unsafe discharge? If you share the type of facility (e.g., nursing home, assisted living, group home) and state, I can give you specific rules and contact resources.

Thousands of U.S. judges who broke laws or oaths remained on the bench
In the past dozen years, state and local judges have repeatedly escaped public accountability for misdeeds that have victimized thousands. Nine of 10 kept their jobs, a Reuters investigation found – including an Alabama judge who unlawfully jailed hundreds of poor people, many of them Black, over traffic fines.

By MICHAEL BERENS and JOHN SHIFFMAN in MONTGOMERY, ALABAMA Filed June 30, 2020, noon GMT
Judge Les Hayes once sentenced a single mother to 496 days behind bars for failing to pay traffic tickets. The sentence was so stiff it exceeded the jail time Alabama allows for negligent homicide.

Marquita Johnson, who was locked up in April 2012, says the impact of her time in jail endures today. Johnson’s three children were cast into foster care while she was incarcerated. One daughter was molested, state records show. Another was physically abused.

“Judge Hayes took away my life and didn’t care how my children suffered,” said Johnson, now 36. “My girls will never be the same.”

Fellow inmates found her sentence hard to believe. “They had a nickname for me: The Woman with All the Days,” Johnson said. “That’s what they called me: The Woman with All the Days. There were people who had committed real crimes who got out before me.”

In 2016, the state agency that oversees judges charged Hayes with violating Alabama’s code of judicial conduct. According to the Judicial Inquiry Commission, Hayes broke state and federal laws by jailing Johnson and hundreds of other Montgomery residents too poor to pay fines. Among those jailed: a plumber struggling to make rent, a mother who skipped meals to cover the medical bills of her disabled son, and a hotel housekeeper working her way through college.

Hayes, a judge since 2000, admitted in court documents to violating 10 different parts of the state’s judicial conduct code. One of the counts was a breach of a judge’s most essential duty: failing to “respect and comply with the law."

Despite the severity of the ruling, Hayes wasn’t barred from serving as a judge. Instead, the judicial commission and Hayes reached a deal. The former Eagle Scout would serve an 11-month unpaid suspension. Then he could return to the bench.

Until he was disciplined, Hayes said in an interview with Reuters, “I never thought I was doing something wrong.”

This week, Hayes is set to retire after 20 years as a judge. In a statement to Reuters, Hayes said he was “very remorseful” for his misdeeds.

Community activists say his departure is long overdue. Yet the decision to leave, they say, should never have been his to make, given his record of misconduct.

“He should have been fired years ago,” said Willie Knight, pastor of North Montgomery Baptist Church. “He broke the law and wanted to get away with it. His sudden retirement is years too late.”

Hayes is among thousands of state and local judges across America who were allowed to keep positions of extraordinary power and prestige after violating judicial ethics rules or breaking laws they pledged to uphold, a Reuters investigation found.

Judges have made racist statements, lied to state officials and forced defendants to languish in jail without a lawyer – and then returned to the bench, sometimes with little more than a rebuke from the state agencies overseeing their conduct.

Recent media reports have documented failures in judicial oversight in South Carolina, Louisiana and Illinois. Reuters went further.

In the first comprehensive accounting of judicial misconduct nationally, Reuters identified and reviewed 1,509 cases from the last dozen years – 2008 through 2019 – in which judges resigned, retired or were publicly disciplined following accusations of misconduct. In addition, reporters identified another 3,613 cases from 2008 through 2018 in which states disciplined wayward judges but kept hidden from the public key details of their offenses – including the identities of the judges themselves.

All told, 9 of every 10 judges were allowed to return to the bench after they were sanctioned for misconduct, Reuters determined. They included a California judge who had sex in his courthouse chambers, once with his former law intern and separately with an attorney; a New York judge who berated domestic violence victims; and a Maryland judge who, after his arrest for driving drunk, was allowed to return to the bench provided he took a Breathalyzer test before each appearance.

The news agency’s findings reveal an “excessively” forgiving judicial disciplinary system, said Stephen Gillers, a law professor at New York University who writes about judicial ethics. Although punishment short of removal from the bench is appropriate for most misconduct cases, Gillers said, the public “would be appalled at some of the lenient treatment judges get” for substantial transgressions.

Among the cases from the past year alone:

In Utah, a judge texted a video of a man’s scrotum to court clerks. He was reprimanded but remains on the bench.

In Indiana, three judges attending a conference last spring got drunk and sparked a 3 a.m. brawl outside a White Castle fast-food restaurant that ended with two of the judges shot. Although the state supreme court found the three judges had “discredited the entire Indiana judiciary,” each returned to the bench after a suspension.

In Texas, a judge burst in on jurors deliberating the case of a woman charged with sex trafficking and declared that God told him the defendant was innocent. The offending judge received a warning and returned to the bench. The defendant was convicted after a new judge took over the case.

“There are certain things where there should be a level of zero tolerance,” the jury foreman, Mark House, told Reuters. The judge should have been fined, House said, and kicked off the bench. “There is no justice, because he is still doing his job.”

Judicial misconduct specialists say such behavior has the potential to erode trust in America’s courts and, absent tough consequences, could give judges license to behave with impunity.

“When you see cases like that, the public starts to wonder about the integrity and honesty of the system,” said Steve Scheckman, a lawyer who directed Louisiana’s oversight agency and served as deputy director of New York’s. “It looks like a good ol’ boys club.”

That’s how local lawyers viewed the case of a longtime Alabama judge who concurrently served on the state’s judicial oversight commission. The judge, Cullman District Court’s Kim Chaney, remained on the bench for three years after being accused of violating the same nepotism rules he was tasked with enforcing on the oversight commission. In at least 200 cases, court records show, Judge Chaney chose his own son to serve as a court-appointed defense lawyer for the indigent, enabling the younger Chaney to earn at least $105,000 in fees over two years.

In February, months after Reuters repeatedly asked Chaney and the state judicial commission about those cases, he retired from the bench as part of a deal with state authorities to end the investigation.

Tommy Drake, the lawyer who first filed a complaint against Chaney in 2016, said he doubts the judge would have been forced from the bench if Reuters hadn’t examined the case.

“You know the only reason they did anything about Chaney is because you guys started asking questions,” Drake said. “Otherwise, he’d still be there.”

Bedrock of American justice

State and local judges draw little scrutiny even though their courtrooms are the bedrock of the American criminal justice system, touching the lives of millions of people every year.

The country’s approximately 1,700 federal judges hear 400,000 cases annually. The nearly 30,000 state, county and municipal court judges handle a far bigger docket: more than 100 million new cases each year, from traffic to divorce to murder. Their titles range from justice of the peace to state supreme court justice. Their powers are vast and varied – from determining whether a defendant should be jailed to deciding who deserves custody of a child.

Each U.S. state has an oversight agency that investigates misconduct complaints against judges. The authority of the oversight agencies is distinct from the power held by appellate courts, which can reverse a judge’s legal ruling and order a new trial. Judicial commissions cannot change verdicts. Rather, they can investigate complaints about the behavior of judges and pursue discipline ranging from reprimand to removal.

Few experts dispute that the great majority of judges behave responsibly, respecting the law and those who appear before them. And some contend that, when judges do falter, oversight agencies are effective in identifying and addressing the behavior. “With a few notable exceptions, the commissions generally get it right,” said Keith Swisher, a University of Arizona law professor who specializes in judicial ethics.

Others disagree. They note that the clout of these commissions is limited, and their authority differs from state to state. To remove a judge, all but a handful of states require approval of a panel that includes other judges. And most states seldom exercise the full extent of those disciplinary powers.

As a result, the system tends to err on the side of protecting the rights and reputations of judges while overlooking the impact courtroom wrongdoing has on those most affected by it: people like Marquita Johnson.

Reuters scoured thousands of state investigative files, disciplinary proceedings and court records from the past dozen years to quantify the personal toll of judicial misconduct. The examination found at least 5,206 people who were directly affected by a judge’s misconduct. The victims cited in disciplinary documents ranged from people who were illegally jailed to those subjected to racist, sexist and other abusive comments from judges in ways that tainted the cases.

The number is a conservative estimate. The tally doesn’t include two previously reported incidents that affected thousands of defendants and prompted sweeping reviews of judicial conduct.

“If we have a system that holds a wrongdoer accountable but we fail to address the victims, then we are really losing sight of what a justice system should be all about.”

Arthur Grim, retired judge

In Pennsylvania, the state examined the convictions of more than 3,500 teenagers sentenced by two judges. The judges were convicted of taking kickbacks as part of a scheme to fill a private juvenile detention center. In 2009, the Pennsylvania Supreme Court appointed senior judge Arthur Grim to lead a victim review, and the state later expunged criminal records for 2,251 juveniles. Grim told Reuters that every state should adopt a way to compensate victims of judicial misconduct.

“If we have a system that holds a wrongdoer accountable but we fail to address the victims, then we are really losing sight of what a justice system should be all about,” Grim said.

In another review underway in Ohio, state public defender Tim Young is scrutinizing 2,707 cases handled by a judge who retired in 2018 after being hospitalized for alcoholism. Mike Benza, a law professor at Case Western Reserve University whose students are helping identify victims, compared the work to current investigations into police abuse of power. “You see one case and then you look to see if it's systemic,” he said.

The review, which has been limited during the coronavirus pandemic, may take a year. But Young said the time-consuming task is essential because “a fundamental injustice may have been levied against hundreds or thousands of people.”

‘Special rules for judges’

Most states afford judges accused of misconduct a gentle kind of justice. Perhaps no state better illustrates the shortcomings of America’s system for overseeing judges than Alabama.

As in most states, Alabama’s nine-member Judicial Inquiry Commission is a mix of lawyers, judges and laypeople. All are appointed. Their deliberations are secret and they operate under some of the most judge-friendly rules in the nation.

Alabama’s rules make even filing a complaint against a judge difficult. The complaint must be notarized, which means that in theory, anyone who makes misstatements about the judge can be prosecuted for perjury. Complaints about wrongdoing must be made in writing; those that arrive by phone, email or without a notary stamp are not investigated, although senders are notified why their complaints have been summarily rejected. Anonymous written complaints are shredded.

These rules can leave lawyers and litigants fearing retaliation, commission director Jenny Garrett noted in response to written questions.

“It’s a ridiculous system that protects judges and makes it easy for them to intimidate anyone with a legitimate complaint,” said Sue Bell Cobb, chief justice of the Alabama Supreme Court from 2007 to 2011. In 2009, she unsuccessfully championed changes to the process and commissioned an American Bar Association report that offered a scathing review of Alabama's rules.

In most other states, commission staff members can start investigating a judge upon receiving a phone call or email, even anonymous ones, or after learning of questionable conduct from a news report or court filing. In Alabama, staff will not begin an investigation without approval from the commission itself, which convenes about every seven weeks.

By rule, the commission also must keep a judge who is under scrutiny fully informed throughout an investigation. If a subpoena is issued, the judge receives a simultaneous copy, raising fears about witness intimidation. If a witness gives investigators a statement, the judge receives a transcript. In the U.S. justice system, such deference to individuals under investigation is extremely rare.

“It’s a ridiculous system that protects judges and makes it easy for them to intimidate anyone with a legitimate complaint.”

Sue Bell Cobb, former chief justice of the Alabama Supreme Court

“Why the need for special rules for judges?” said Michael Levy, a Washington lawyer who has represented clients in high-profile criminal, corporate, congressional and securities investigations. “If judges think it’s fair and appropriate to investigate others for crimes or misconduct without providing those subjects or targets with copies of witness statements and subpoenas, why don’t judges think it’s fair to investigate judges in the same way?”

Alabama judges also are given an opportunity to resolve investigations confidentially. Reuters interviews and a review of Alabama commission records show the commission has met with judges informally at least 19 times since 2011 to offer corrective “guidance.” The identities of those judges remain confidential, as does the conduct that prompted the meetings. “Not every violation warrants discipline,” commission director Garrett said.

Since 2008, the commission has brought 21 public cases against judges, including Hayes, charging two this year.

Two of the best-known cases brought by the commission involved Roy Moore, who was twice forced out as chief justice of the Alabama Supreme Court for defying federal court orders.

Another Alabama justice fared better in challenging a misconduct complaint, however. Tom Parker, first elected to the state’s high court in 2004, pushed back when the commission investigated him in 2015 for comments he made on the radio criticizing the U.S. Supreme Court's decision legalizing gay marriage.

Parker sued the commission in federal court, arguing the agency was infringing on his First Amendment rights. He won. Although the commission had dropped its investigation before the ruling, it was ordered to cover Parker’s legal fees: $100,000, or about a fifth of the agency’s total annual budget.

In 2018, the people of Alabama elected Parker chief justice.

These days, Parker told Reuters, Alabama judges and the agency that oversees them enjoy “a much better relationship” that’s less politically tinged. “How can I say it? It’s much more respectful between the commission and the judges now.”

Taxpayer-funded COLA Benefits for Government Employees 

Washington State Legislative Select Committee on Pension Policy pushes COLA for retired teachers, public government employees

Nov. 19, 2026

Thousands of retired teachers and public employees in Washington are once again fighting for a boost in benefits because the older pension plans they are enrolled in do not provide annual increases like other state plans.

This week the Select Committee on Pension Policy voted to support legislation giving a 3% cost-of-living-adjustment to the eligible members of the Public Employees’ Retirement System and the Teachers’ Retirement System. 

As envisioned, retirees would receive the 3% boost on July 1, 2027 with a maximum monthly increase of $150, up from the previously approved cap of $110. At least 50,000 retirees could see an increase if the legislation were to pass.

The bump would cost the state an estimated $20.1 million in the next budget and add roughly $11 million in expenses for local governments, according to a report presented to the committee.

The 20-member committee is composed of House and Senate members from both parties, representatives of the public and private sectors, and retirees. It acted Tuesday following a public hearing in which retirees shared the difficulties they have paying their bills and their disappointment in having to beg for assistance after decades of public service. 

They also said that they’d appreciate the one-time increase but want changes made to lock in an annual boost in benefits as a matter of fairness.

Democrat state Sen. Steve Conway of Tacoma, who is the committee chair and is retiring from the Legislature at the end of the year, called the lack of a cost-of-living-adjustment “probably the greatest weakness” of the employee plans. The draft legislation, he said, is intended to ensure something is provided until the larger issue is addressed.

It is no slam dunk. Gov. Bob Ferguson is forecasting a $4 billion shortfall in the fiscal year that starts next July. He recently directed state agency leaders to find more places to cut spending, thus making new investments a tough sell. 

Noticeably absent for Tuesday’s vote were four committee members who are also integral to crafting and passing the next spending plan: Ferguson’s budget director, K.D. Chapman-See; Sen. June Robinson, D-Everett, the lead Democratic budget writer in the Senate; Rep. Joe Fitzgibbon, D-West Seattle, who is House Majority Leader, and Nicole Macri, D-Seattle, a vice chair of the House Appropriations Committee.

This is an old issue. 

Prior to October 1977, most public employees who were eligible for a pension benefit were enrolled in Plan 1 of the Public Employees’ Retirement System (PERS) or the Teachers’ Retirement System (TRS).  After that date, newer plans were created that offer annual increases.

Those in Plan 1 of PERS or TRS did not automatically receive post-retirement adjustments, but lawmakers often did approve one-time bumps on an ad-hoc basis.

In 1995, the Legislature established a uniform cost-of-living-adjustment, referred to as the UCOLA, that did lock in annual increases. The UCOLA was repealed in 2011.

Since then, members of the two plans have regularly sought adjustments and did receive increases from the Legislature in 2018, 2020, 2021, 2023, 2024 and earlier this year.

In the 2026 session, the Legislature approved and Ferguson signed Senate Bill 5862, which provided a 3% increase on July 1, 2026. It capped the increase at $110 per month. On average, eligible members were expected to receive $80 more per month. Overall, nearly 70,000 people received an increase, the Department of Retirement Systems estimated.

Rep. Cyndy Jacobsen, R-Puyallup, serves on the committee but is unlikely to return because she is losing her re-election bid.

She Leads America (SLA) is a faith-based 501(c)(3) nonprofit that functions as a national network and honor society for Christian women leaders.⁠

Mission and Purpose: 
It honors, equips, and empowers exemplary Christian women who lead with faith, wisdom, and courage. Grounded in biblical principles, it unites leaders across sectors to collaborate, offer faith-based solutions to modern challenges, and strengthen communities and the nation. The organization emphasizes peer support, relationship-building, independent thinking, mutual respect, and biblical values.⁠

Its stated mission is: “She Leads America is a dynamic and diverse national network that honors, equips, and empowers exemplary Christian women who lead with faith, wisdom, and courage. Grounded in biblical truth, we unite and mobilize leaders across every sphere of influence to advance collaboration, catalyze solutions to the challenges of our time, and strengthen our communities and our nation for generations to come.”⁠

Founding and Leadership:
It was founded by Dr. Elizabeth “Liz” Doyle (also referred to as Rev. Liz Doyle). She is a Michigan/Ohio native who began speaking ministry in Belfast, Northern Ireland, in 1972, later pastored churches in England with her husband Syd, and moved to the U.S. around 1998. She has been involved in global women’s ministry (including work in dozens of countries) and other initiatives focused on healing, reconciliation, and empowerment. The organization began as She Leads Michigan in 2019 and expanded nationally (with formal nonprofit status around 2023). Doyle serves as founder and executive director/president. The organization is based in Blissfield, Michigan (EIN 88-4257500).⁠

Activities and Structure:
Honoree Network / Christian Women of Distinction: Peer-nominated recognition of accomplished Christian women in areas including business/industry, health/wellness, education, government/law/military/first responders, nonprofits/ministry, family life/welfare, and media/sports/entertainment. Honorees often receive state or congressional recognition (e.g., entries in the Congressional Record). Past honorees have included figures such as Joni Eareckson Tada, Terry Meeuwsen, and others in public life and ministry.⁠Sheleadsamerica
Annual galas (often at the Museum of the Bible in Washington, D.C.) and state-level events (teas, brunches).

State chapters in multiple states (examples include Michigan, Kentucky, California, Florida, Louisiana, Indiana).

Prayer, collaboration, resources, and networking. It has expanded internationally with efforts such as She Leads UK and She Leads the Nations (including a 2026 Capitol Hill launch involving leaders from many countries).

Other activities have included trips (e.g., to Israel) and related programming.⁠Sheleadsthenations
It positions itself as a “safe platform” for faith-focused women to exchange ideas, support one another, and collaborate on biblical solutions, with an emphasis on honor, trust, and affirmation through recognition.⁠

Official site: https://t.co/K7dW7Ztiyr. It accepts donations as a registered 501(c)(3).

The Relay Race of American Genius: Historical Precision, Shared Credit, and Fifteen Verified Black American Pioneers

Presented by DIOGENES REIPUBLICAE AMERICANAE

Page 2 of 3

1Dr. George Washington Carver 

(circa 1864 to 1943 | Missouri)
Reducing Dr. George Washington Carver to the viral myth that he invented peanut butter, a food paste made by the ancient Aztecs and patented by Marcellus Gilmore Edson in 1884, obscures one of the deepest scientific intellectuals and transformative public figures in American history. 

Born into slavery in Missouri at the close of the Civil War, Carver was far more than a laboratory tinkerer; he was a visionary ecologist, economist, and philosopher of sustainable agriculture who diagnosed the structural collapse of the Southern farm economy decades before the Dust Bowl. Seeing that generations of single crop cotton farming and the boll weevil epidemic had exhausted the soil and trapped rural farmers, both Black and white, in perpetual debt, Carver championed a closed loop philosophy of regenerative agriculture and chemurgy, teaching that nature creates no waste, only unutilized resources. 

Through systematic crop rotation with nitrogen fixing legumes such as peanuts, cowpeas, and sweet potatoes, he showed farmers how to rebuild depleted topsoil naturally without expensive synthetic fertilizers. To ensure those soil restoring crops commanded real market value, Carver engineered more than 300 industrial and commercial applications from peanuts and over 100 from sweet potatoes, including synthetic dyes, wood stains, paints, plastics, industrial adhesives, flours, and medicinal oils, securing three U.S. patents (U.S. Patent No. 1,522,176 and No. 1,541,478 in 1925, and No. 1,632,365 in 1927) while deliberately leaving his agricultural discoveries unpatented so poor farmers could use them freely. 

His scientific mastery so tangibly rescued the Southern economy that during the height of rigid Jim Crow segregation, even though he still encountered prejudice when traveling unannounced, white Southern agricultural boards, chambers of commerce, and business leaders repeatedly suspended whites only hotel and dining barriers to host him as an honored guest, and in 1921 Congress extended his scheduled five minute tariff testimony to nearly two hours. Refusing lucrative offers from Thomas Edison and Henry Ford to remain at Tuskegee, Carver laid the intellectual foundation for modern green chemistry.

2Norbert Rillieux (1806 to 1894 | Louisiana)

For centuries, sugar refining across the Atlantic world relied on the "Jamaica Train," an inefficient, fuel guzzling assembly line in which enslaved workers stood over open fires ladling boiling cane juice from one open copper kettle to the next. Because boiling syrup at atmospheric pressure required extreme heat, vast quantities of sugar scorched into dark molasses, wood consumption stripped entire forests, and workers suffered constant, fatal burns. 

Trained in mechanical engineering at the Ecole Centrale in Paris, where he taught applied mechanics and published foundational papers on steam power, Norbert Rillieux returned to Louisiana and revolutionized both global sugar production and industrial chemical engineering by applying fundamental thermodynamics to solve every flaw in that process simultaneously. Under U.S. Patent No. 3,237 (issued August 26, 1843, and expanded under U.S. Patent No. 4,879 on December 10, 1846), Rillieux invented the multiple effect vacuum evaporator. His design rested on two interlocking laws of physics: reducing atmospheric pressure inside a sealed vessel lowers the boiling point of a liquid, and the latent heat contained in the steam rising from the first boiling chamber can be captured and routed through internal coils to boil the juice in a second and third chamber at progressively lower pressures. 

By enclosing cane juice inside a series of partial vacuum chambers, Rillieux eliminated open fire boiling, cut fuel consumption by up to 80 percent, produced vastly purer white sugar crystals, and ended manual ladling. Today, Rillieux's thermodynamic architecture remains an indispensable cornerstone of chemical engineering worldwide, powering condensed milk manufacturing, gelatin processing, paper mill liquor recovery, and industrial seawater desalination.

3Lewis Howard Latimer (1848 to 1928 | Massachusetts)

Lewis Howard Latimer never claimed to have invented the incandescent light bulb, which was pioneered by British chemist Joseph Swan and commercialized as a lighting system by Thomas Edison in 1879. However, early incandescent bulbs suffered from a fatal manufacturing defect: their fragile carbonized paper and bamboo filaments warped, cracked, and burned out within days, making electric lighting too unreliable and expensive for ordinary homes and city streets. 

A Union Navy Civil War veteran who taught himself mechanical drafting after the war, Latimer first executed the official technical patent drawings for Alexander Graham Bell's telephone application in February 1876, helping Bell file his specifications hours ahead of rival Elisha Gray. Working under Hiram Maxim at the U.S. Electric Lighting Company, Latimer then invented and patented the cardboard envelope carbonization process (U.S. Patent No. 252,386, issued January 17, 1882, alongside U.S. Patent No. 247,097 in 1881). 

By encasing raw carbon filaments inside protective cardboard envelopes during high temperature furnace firing, Latimer prevented twisting and structural fracture, yielding a uniform, durable carbon filament that dramatically extended bulb life and slashed manufacturing costs. Recruited directly by Edison in 1884 as the only Black member of the elite Edison Pioneers, Latimer supervised the installation of public electric street lighting in New York, Philadelphia, Montreal, and London, authored the first comprehensive engineering textbook on incandescent lighting in 1890, and served as Edison's chief expert witness in federal patent infringement trials.

4Granville Tailer Woods (1856 to 1910 | Ohio)

Telegraphy and electric streetcars were already operating in American cities during the 1880s, yet both industries faced severe safety and efficiency bottlenecks: moving trains could not communicate with station dispatchers or other trains on the same track, leading to devastating head on collisions, and overhead trolley wires suffered from constant sparking and power loss. 

A self educated mechanical and electrical engineer who mastered his craft in machine shops, railroad cabs, and night study, Granville Tailer Woods registered nearly sixty U.S. patents that solved these critical engineering problems. His Synchronous Multiplex Railway Telegraph (U.S. Patent No. 373,915, issued November 29, 1887) used electromagnetic induction between stationary trackside telegraph wires and induction coils mounted on moving trains so engineers and dispatchers could transmit voice and Morse code messages in real time while traveling at full speed, warning crews of obstructions or oncoming trains ahead. In parallel, Woods invented the grooved streetcar "troller" wheel, giving rise to the word "trolley," and patented foundational designs for the third rail electric power distribution system (U.S. Patent No. 687,098, 1901) still utilized by modern subway systems in New York, Chicago, and London, alongside major improvements to Westinghouse automatic air brakes. Woods's laboratory notebooks and patent filings were so airtight that when Thomas Edison's legal team challenged him twice in federal patent interference proceedings over induction telegraphy, Woods defeated Edison both times, prompting Edison to offer Woods a senior engineering position that Woods declined to remain independent.

5Garrett Augustus Morgan (1877 to 1963 | Kentucky)

Honest scholarship requires refusing to repeat the viral myth that Garrett Augustus Morgan invented the very first traffic light, as manual semaphore signals existed in London in 1868 and two way electric "stop/go" lights appeared between 1912 and 1914. Refusing to overclaim that credit keeps Morgan's two genuine, federally patented life saving inventions completely unassailable. On October 13, 1914, Morgan received U.S. Patent No. 1,113,675 for his Safety Hood and Smoke Protector. Recognizing from basic physics that smoke and toxic gases rise toward the ceiling while cooler, cleaner air remains near the floor, Morgan designed a canvas hood fitted with two long intake tubes dangling to the ground and lined with moistened sponges that cooled and filtered incoming air, paired with a one way exhaust valve. 

On July 25, 1916, when a natural gas explosion trapped workers 250 feet beneath Lake Erie inside a smoke filled waterworks tunnel, rescue crews failed until Morgan and his brother Frank donned Safety Hoods, entered the toxic tunnel, and carried survivors out alive; the U.S. Army subsequently refined his hood into World War I combat gas masks, and municipal fire departments adopted it nationwide. Seven years later, on November 20, 1923, Morgan patented the three position traffic signal (U.S. Patent No. 1,475,024), solving the fatal flaw of abrupt two way signals by introducing a mandatory intermediate all directional caution phase to clear intersections safely before cross traffic moved, a patent General Electric purchased for $40,000.

6Frederick McKinley Jones (1893 to 1961 )

Honest scholarship never claims that Frederick McKinley Jones  invented stationary building air conditioning, which Willis Carrier pioneered in 1902, or the first mechanical ice making machines developed in the mid nineteenth century by pioneers such as James Harrison and Ferdinand Carre. Saying he invented stationary cooling hands critics an immediate opening. 

Instead, what Jones actually invented was the shock resistant, self contained, automatic mobile refrigeration unit, solving the brutal engineering problem that kept mechanical cooling off the world's highways, railroads, and oceans for decades. Before the late 1930s, haulers transported perishable meat, dairy, and produce by packing trailers with massive blocks of harvested lake ice and salt; on rough roads or long ocean voyages, that ice melted, consumed up to twenty percent of cargo space, corroded metal hulls, and failed whenever temperatures spiked, while existing stationary compressors shook apart and ruptured refrigerant lines under road vibration. 

Self taught in mechanical and electrical engineering through trade journals and hands on experimentation, Jones solved every bottleneck simultaneously. Beginning with his foundational vehicle refrigeration patents (U.S. Patent No. 2,336,735 on December 14, 1943, and U.S. Patent No. 2,475,841 on July 12, 1949, alongside his 1940 patent work) and co founding the U.S. Thermo Control Company, later renamed Thermo King, Jones engineered a ruggedized, vibration dampened cooling unit powered by an independent small gasoline engine and automatic thermostat mounted externally on the nose of trailers, railcars, and ships, keeping cargo frozen even when the truck's main engine was turned off. During World War II, the U.S. military deployed Jones's portable units across the European and Pacific theaters to preserve whole blood, penicillin, vaccines, and fresh rations on front lines worldwide. 

That breakthrough directly enabled modern intermodal refrigerated shipping containers ("reefers"), nationwide supermarket and frozen food distribution, and the temperature controlled medical cold chain used today for insulin and vaccines. Holding over sixty patents (forty in refrigeration alone), Jones became the first Black member of the American Society of Refrigeration Engineers in 1944 and was posthumously awarded the National Medal of Technology in 1991.

7Dr. Percy Lavon Julian (1899 to 1975 | Alabama)

Naturally occurring human hormones, glaucoma alkaloids, and chemical fire extinguishers already existed prior to the twentieth century, yet obtaining medicinal steroids required harvesting microscopic quantities from thousands of slaughtered animal glands at astronomical expense, making treatment impossible for ordinary patients. Born in segregated Montgomery without access to a public high school and earning his Ph.D. in organic chemistry at the University of Vienna in 1931, Dr. Percy Lavon Julian registered more than 130 U.S. chemical patents that transformed pharmaceutical manufacturing and wartime survival. 

Working with colleague Josef Pikl at DePauw University in 1935, Julian achieved the first total chemical synthesis of physostigmine for glaucoma, proving in peer reviewed chemistry that Oxford University's preeminent chemist and future Nobel laureate Sir Robert Robinson had published an incorrect synthesis, a feat later designated a National Historic Chemical Landmark. Hired in 1936 as Director of Research for the Soya Products Division at the Glidden Company in Chicago, Julian unlocked the industrial scale synthesis of progesterone, testosterone, and cortisone from soybean plant sterols (U.S. Patent No. 2,752,339), collapsing the cost of steroid therapies from hundreds of dollars per drop to pennies per gram and relieving rheumatoid arthritis for millions. In parallel, his patented process for isolating purified alpha protein from soybeans, originally created to replace milk casein in paper coatings, was recognized by fire protection engineers at National Foam System, Inc., who formulated it into Aer O Foam ("bean soup"), extinguishing burning aviation fuel aboard U.S. Navy aircraft carriers in World War II and saving thousands of sailors and firefighters.

BIG TIGGER'S WIFE WAS ARRESTED SEVEN YEARS AFTER HER DAUGHTER VANISHED. BUT SHE IS STILL MISSING.

THE DISAPPEARANCE OF AILEA BROWN  
Reisterstown, Maryland — May 25, 2019

Ailea Brown was only 10 years old when she disappeared from Reisterstown, Maryland, during a bitter custody dispute between her parents.

Seven years later, her biological mother has been arrested on kidnapping-related charges, but Ailea has still not been found.

And her father is still waiting to learn where his daughter is.

On May 25, 2019, around 1:00 a.m., Ailea was last seen in the 300 block of Erin Russell Court.

Her father, Durrell Williams, had been awarded full legal custody, and Ailea disappeared shortly before she was scheduled to return to his care.

Investigators suspected a parental abduction rather than a random kidnapping. Neighbors also reported seeing a white SUV near the residence around the time she vanished.

Durrell has maintained for years that Ailea's mother, Alicia Denise Brown, knows where their daughter is.

“Her mom knows exactly where she is. The only people that do not know where this child is are the police and myself.”

The family's custody history included a January 2014 incident in which authorities arrested Alicia after she reportedly left then-4-year-old Ailea inside a freezing vehicle for approximately eight hours while visiting Maryland Live! Casino.

Then, on July 6, 2026, investigators made a significant breakthrough.

Georgia authorities stopped Alicia Brown, 37, along Interstate 85 in Hart County and arrested her on outstanding Maryland kidnapping-related warrants.

Alicia, who is also the estranged wife of Atlanta radio personality Darian “Big Tigger” Morgan, was traveling with two young children.

Both children were safely recovered.

Neither was Ailea.

Alicia also faced a felony interference-with-child-custody charge in Fulton County, Georgia.

Following her arrest, she was extradited to Maryland to face child abduction charges.

She was initially released on home detention, but prosecutors later accused her of making false statements in a police complaint involving custody of another child. Her bond was revoked, and additional perjury charges followed.

During a November 2026 court appearance, Alicia's trial was postponed until February 2027. She was ordered to remain jailed without bond.

According to Ailea's father, prosecutors offered Alicia a plea agreement involving four years in prison, with ten additional years suspended, if she disclosed Ailea's location. He said she declined the offer.

That reported plea proposal has not been independently confirmed through court records.

Alicia has not been convicted of the pending charges.

Ailea was 10 when she disappeared. She is now 17 years old.

At the time, she stood approximately 4'8" tall, weighed 85 pounds, and had brown hair, brown eyes, and a medium complexion. Her appearance may have changed considerably.

Seven years have passed. Her mother is in custody. But the question that matters most remains unanswered: WHERE IS AILEA BROWN?

Anyone with information is urged to contact the Baltimore County Police Department at 410-887-2222 or the National Center for Missing & Exploited Children at 1-800-THE-LOST (1-800-843-5678).
