text:
By Michael Smith:
Maybe I am just too sentimental and am screaming into the maelstrom, but I refuse to believe that America is headed into the ash bin of history.

Something Thomas Jefferson wrote that has been taped to my computer monitors for decades is relevant:

“A departure from principle in one instance becomes a precedent for a second; that second for a third; and so on, till the bulk of the society is reduced to be mere automatons of misery, and to have no sensibilities left but for sinning and suffering.”

That we are living the result of these very departures from principle is the death by a thousand cuts. We are beset by a society, a culture and a government consisting of malevolent power brokers managing an army of immature, irrational, irresponsible people with the emotional maturity of a two-year-old, combined with a willful ignorance of economic law and history, by telling them they can have ice cream for dinner forever without consequence.

And like my two-year-old granddaughter, they don’t know what they don’t know, not because they aren’t being taught, it is they are being taught that their behavior is normal and it is the rational people who don’t see the world the way it is.

It has been apparent in our institutions for almost a century that the trannyfans, postmodernists and devotees of the Frankfurt School have been trying to create is a world of kindergartners with no ability to manage themselves, much less the affairs of others.

If you don’t believe me, just look at what the Democrats are telegraphing they are about to do and tell me it doesn’t look like a toddler party.

America must have rational, logical, and moral adults in the room.

The American Founders were remarkably unsentimental about human nature. They understood that men were capable of extraordinary virtue, courage, generosity, and reason, but also of ambition, envy, greed, vanity, corruption, and an almost limitless appetite for power. More importantly, they understood that acquiring political power did nothing to cure these shortcomings. Indeed, and nothing proves that it frequently amplified them than the low-trust environment we inhabit today.

Their understanding of government was rooted in history, philosophy, and experience. They had studied the collapse of the Roman Republic, the political struggles of ancient Greece, the English Civil War, and the writings of Locke and Montesquieu. They understood that tyranny was not some historical aberration, but a recurring consequence of human nature when political power was allowed to accumulate without restraint.

James Madison captured the problem in Federalist No. 51: “If men were angels, no government would be necessary.” He went on to explain that government must first be empowered to control the governed, and then obliged to control itself. Madison wasn’t suggesting that we simply elect better people. He understood that ambition, self-interest, and the desire for power were permanent human characteristics. His solution was to make ambition counteract ambition through competing institutions and divided authority.

Thomas Jefferson expressed a similar sentiment in his 1798 draft of the Kentucky Resolutions: “In questions of power, then, let no more be heard of confidence in man, but bind him down from mischief by the chains of the Constitution.” Jefferson understood that elections did not magically transform ambitious politicians into trustworthy guardians of liberty. Constitutional limitations were necessary precisely because the people exercising political authority could not be trusted to restrain themselves voluntarily.

George Washington warned in his Farewell Address that political parties could become instruments of tyranny. He feared that partisan hostility would eventually become so consuming that citizens would sacrifice constitutional principles simply to defeat their political enemies. He recognized that political tribalism could overwhelm independent judgment, making people susceptible to manipulation by those claiming to represent their interests.

Madison went further in Federalist No. 10, observing that factions were inevitable because differences in human interests, passions, and property were inevitable. He also understood that majorities were perfectly capable of tyranny. The fact that 51 percent of the population favored confiscating the property or restricting the rights of the other 49 percent did not somehow make the exercise moral. A majority vote could authorize an injustice, but it could not transform injustice into virtue.

Alexander Hamilton offered another warning in Federalist No. 1, observing that men who overturned republics frequently began as demagogues and ended as tyrants. History had demonstrated that political leaders claiming to champion the people could become the very oppressors from whom they promised deliverance.

These men disagreed about plenty of things, sometimes bitterly. Yet they shared an understanding that human nature was not going to change simply because someone invented a new political arrangement or promised a more enlightened government.

That is the philosophical genius of the American constitutional republic. It was not designed around the expectation that virtuous men would always govern. It was designed around the certainty that sooner or later, ambitious, corrupt, self-serving, and thoroughly ordinary human beings would occupy positions of extraordinary authority.

The Founders did not attempt to perfect mankind through government. They attempted to protect mankind from the consequences of its own imperfections.

This is also where the fundamental distinction between classical liberalism and utopian political philosophies becomes apparent. The former accepts human nature as a permanent condition and seeks to limit the damage people can inflict upon one another through political power. The latter too often assumes that sufficient authority, placed in sufficiently enlightened hands, can somehow overcome the shortcomings of humanity itself.

The Founders understood something that seems increasingly forgotten: Giving imperfect human beings more power over other imperfect human beings does not make either group more virtuous no more than confiscating the wealth of producers and giving it to non-producers who are dependent on it.

Neither creates any incentive to be more virtuous or productive. It simply makes the consequences of their imperfections more dangerous.

We can fix this. We just have to want to do it.

text:
On his arrival at Troja in Sicily, Louis of Thuringia was received with the honor due to his rank by the Emperor Frederick II. Louis was already attacked with fever before he embarked, but he did not consider his condition sufficiently serious to delay his departure for a few days. His illness, however, increased with frightful rapidity. He saw that the time was come for him to quit this life, and, in the flower of his youth, he accepted the great sacrifice without a murmur or complaint, as if it had been on the battle-field. He adored the inscrutable designs of the Supreme Ruler, put himself and all those belonging to him under God’s fatherly providence, received the Last Sacraments with a fervor worthy a Christian hero, and fell asleep in the hope of entering that Jerusalem which the impure feet of the stranger shall never defile.
.
Louis died on the eleventh of September, near Otranto. The lords who were deputed to carry the mournful news to Wartburg, did not get there before the beginning of the winter. Elizabeth, a legend informs us, was ill at the time. They were therefore received by the Duchess Sophia, the noble mother of Louis. She forbade anyone to tell Elizabeth of the sorrow which had come upon her, for fear of endangering her life. Afterwards, when she thought the moment favorable, she went herself to perform this sad task. The news was like a thunderbolt to Elizabeth, she remained speechless for a time, then clasping her hands, she exclaimed: “O Lord, my God! My brother is dead, he is dead! With him the whole world is dead to me.” Her tears and sobs expressed her inconsolable grief; Elizabeth became a widow at twenty.
.
Our Saint, who was now more than ever detached from the things of the world, longed for a life of seclusion and prayer. The humble daughter of the seraphic Saint Francis desired to spend the remainder of her life in still greater penance and poverty. She thought of the poor Babe of Bethlehem, and made use of the opportunity that Divine Providence gave her, to put her spirit of poverty into a more rigorous practice.
.
In the Wartburg she could not do this as she desired. She therefore procured permission to move to the more retired castle of Marburg, which was hers by dower right. According to many of her biographers, Elizabeth was driven from the Wartburg; this, however, seems to be untrue. It was not force, but a voluntary sacrifice that led her to Marburg. From the castle of Marburg she was possibly driven by force, and there at midnight, when she heard the bells ringing for Matins at the Franciscan church, she directed her steps towards the house of prayer, assisted at the Divine Office, and then begged the religious to have the goodness to sing the Te Deum in thanksgiving for the misfortunes which had come upon her.
.
Elizabeth’s uncle, however, Egbert, Prince Bishop of Bamberg, called her into his domains, and desired to provide for her in a manner befitting her station; he also wished that she should enter into a second marriage, and, it is said, that the emperor himself, Frederick II, desired her hand. But the saintly Tertiary’s choice was made; God alone was to be her portion for evermore, and holy poverty was to be her spouse. Dead to the world, she had but one desire to follow the example of Christ as well as possible, by walking in the footsteps of her Seraphic Father, Saint Francis. From the very beginning the life of Saint Francis was to her a beacon-light, that led her on to heavenly love, and holiness, and God. All were astonished that this Tertiary, the daughter of a king, so young in years, and with such beautiful prospects, should have so ardent a desire to imitate Saint Francis in all things.
.
The companions of Louis brought back the remains of their beloved sovereign to Thuringia. On their arrival at Bamberg, they apprised the Bishop and duchess of their return, and everything was arranged for the solemn, funereal reception of the body of the great prince. Elizabeth’s deep and inconsolable grief revived in the presence of her husband’s remains. She wept bitterly, but found strength in God. She even thanked the Supreme Lord of all things for all that had happened, she bowed to the will of God and accepted with touching submission the death of her dear husband as a favor of Heaven granted to her vested in a garment of sorrow. She buried the body of Louis in the family vault of the dukes of Thuringia in the convent of Reinhardsbrunn, and then once more occupied herself with the thoughts of her own salvation.
.
Conrad of Marburg, her spiritual director and confessor, would not permit her to enter the Second Order of Saint Francis, much as she desired to do so, nor would he permit her to fully and perfectly renounce all her earthly possessions. He did, however, grant her leave to add the three vows of religion, with some restrictions, to the practice of the Tertiary Rule. Good Friday was the day she chose for this solemn consecration of herself to her Crucified Lord. On that day she went with her children and household to the Franciscan church at Eisenach, and there placing her hands on the altar, she vowed to renounce her own will, her relations and friends, and all the pomps and pleasures of this life, to belong unreservedly to her Crucified Savior, and to follow Him till death in the path of poverty and penance.
.
Conrad then clothed her in the large, coarse tunic of Saint Francis, and girt her with the cord. Further she bound herself to go barefoot, which austere practice she observed faithfully to the end of her days. Thus Saint Elizabeth, who had entered the Third Order during the life of her husband, having become a widow, wished to practice the poverty of the Holy Patriarch, and to consecrate herself more solemnly to God. For this reason she bound herself by vows and took the exterior habit of the Third Order. Hence also, she has been given as patroness, not only to the sisters of the Third Order Secular, but also to the nuns of the Third Order Regular. In the Franciscan supplement to the Roman Martyrology is found the following passage: “Eamque sorores et moniales ejusdem Tertii Ordinis ut patronam praecipuam venerantur.”
.
Elizabeth having made her solemn vows, had a little hut built near the monastery of the Franciscans and settled in this humble abode. She dedicated her special income, which her director had not allowed her to renounce, to the relief of the poor. In imitation of Saint Francis of Assisi she wished henceforth to beg her daily bread from door to door. Her confessor forbade this and so she resolved to earn her livelihood by the labor of her hands. She knew not how to spin flax, but she could spin wool. Thereafter like the poorest of the working classes the princess labored from early morning till late at night. “Even when sickness confined her to bed,” writes Conrad of Marburg, “and when her companions took away the distaff, she used to disentangle and arrange wool for future use. In this way she earned enough to provide for her support and make her offerings to the churches.”
.
Her food was very coarse and simple. If persons brought her anything savory she at once sent it to some poor person who was sick. “She most generally ate vegetables,” says Montalembert, “boiled in pure water without salt, and, well or ill, she prepared them herself. While she was thus occupied in labor and in the cares of her house, she ceased not to elevate her soul to God in prayer and meditation; and often when alone by the fireside, either engaged in cooking, or when she approached to warm herself, so absorbed used she be in contemplation that sparks and cinders would sometimes fall upon her garments and burn them without her knowledge, though, when her companions would return, they would feel almost suffocated by the smoke and odor of the burning stuff.”
.
Her Tertiary habit might be compared to her food in its extreme poverty. She who had been clothed in silks and satin, in rich garments of the finest texture, now wore a habit of undyed cloth, such as was used by the peasantry and the poorest classes only. Her habit often torn and patched, was confined around her waist by a coarse cord. According to the testimony of her four female attendants she used to mend the rents and burns on her habit with her own hands, although she did not well know how to sew.
When Saint Francis first appeared as a mendicant in the streets of Assisi, he was mocked at by worldly persons, treated as a fool, and insulted in many ways. Saint Elizabeth, his spiritual daughter, met with no better fate. Profane men tried to convince themselves that she was insane; whilst pious souls looked upon her with respect as a second Saint Clare. Wretched as her habit was, she frequently deprived herself of it to give it to some poor person, who came begging at the door of her hut.
.
Elizabeth had also been forbidden to renounce her revenue. She knew of no better use she could make of this income than to have a hospital built at Marburg as she had previously done at Wartburg. As soon as this asylum was completed our Saint divided her time between the hospital and her Franciscan home. Every day she went amongst the patients, cleansing and dressing them, and administering the prescribed remedies; she fixed their beds, washed and mended their garments, and scrubbed the floors. The discouraged she nursed back to life and hope, the sinful she exhorted earnestly, the virtuous she led on to greater virtue. In her manner she was kind to all, and very cheerful. To the poor she was not only a consoler, she even was their slave, and no service appeared to her to be too repulsive, too difficult, too mean, for each one of them was, in her eyes, the, living image of the Heavenly Spouse of her soul. Those among the sick whose disorders filled all with disgust, and drove every one from them, became the objects of her special care and tenderness. The royal hands of this humble Tertiary rendered them every assistance; she often kissed their sores and ugly ulcers.
.
Elizabeth had found her inspiration in the life of Saint Francis of Assisi, and in his Rule of the Third Order, hence she dedicated her hospital at Marburg to the memory of Saint Francis, who had died in 1226, and was canonized in 1228. Pope Gregory IX, according to Montalembert, sent to Saint Elizabeth a present far more precious than the mantle which she formerly received with so much gratitude. The Holy Father thought it right to send to the intrepid and faithful imitator of Saint Francis a few drops of blood which flowed from the wound in the side of Saint Francis. Our Saint received the sacred relic with the greatest joy and respect, and looked upon it as a new pledge of her alliance to Saint Francis.
For the love of God, Saint Elizabeth had renounced all the things of this earth; she stripped herself of everything; she embraced the severest poverty, and practised the most austere penitential life, she tended to the sick, the lepers and the poor, but she reckoned all this as nothing; the more she loved God, the more she yearned for still greater love. Her father, the King of Hungary, hearing of her extreme poverty, and not knowing the cause, was greatly grieved. He at once dispatched a tried and trusty courtier to bring his daughter back to him. “Say to my dearest lord and father,” Elizabeth told the ambassador, “that I am happier in this contemptible life than he is in his regal pomp, and that far from sorrowing over me, he ought to rejoice that he has a child in the service of the King of Heaven. All that I ask of him is to pray, and to have prayers offered for me, and I will always pray for him as long as life is left to me.” Elizabeth rejoiced in the love of her Savior. Well could she exclaim: “The kingdom of this world and all the vanities of the age have I despised for the love of my Lord Jesus Christ, Him Whom I have seen, Whom I have loved, in Whom I have believed, and Whom I have preferred.”
.
“Like Martha,” says one of her biographers, “Elizabeth provided with the greatest care for the wants of Jesus Christ, in the persons of his poor,, and like Mary she would go to the feet of her Savior, and there forget this world in the sweet recollections of his graces and mercies.” Yet this seraphic daughter of the seraphic Saint Francis, thinking of her own sinfulness and the sanctity of God, was often tempted by Satan in the most distressing manner. One day she said to Father Rodinger, her former spiritual director: “Reverend Father, there is one thing that torments me more than any other, and that is, that I fear my Creator has but little affection for me. I know that He is infinitely good and prodigal of His love, but on account of my many faults that keep me far away from Him, I fear that He cannot love me, although my heart is inflamed with love for Him.” “There is nothing to fear in that,” said Father Rodinger, “for the Divine mercy is so great, that it is impossible to think otherwise than that God loves infinitely more those who love Him, than He is beloved by them.” “How then, is it,” said Elizabeth, “that He so often permits sadness and languor of soul to remove me from Him, to Whom I would wish to be always most intimately united?” The good Franciscan then explained to this saintly Tertiary that temptations, involuntary distractions at prayer, and spiritual languor are indeed fraught with danger to salvation, but that they are the marks of an elect soul, and not of an abandoned one. “The Kingdom of Heaven,” says Holy Writ, “suffers violence and only they who use violence shall attain it.”
.
Regarding Saint Elizabeth’s spirit of prayer, Conrad of Marburg wrote to Pope Gregory IX: “Before God, I declare that I have rarely seen a more contemplative woman.” For hours would this holy Tertiary remain in prayer, immovable as a statue, absorbed in God and Heavenly things. At night when all slumbered Elizabeth, imitating Saint Francis, would watch and pray. The beauties of nature had the same attraction for her, that they had for her Spiritual Father. She loved to pray in fields and forests, near purling streams and sparkling fountains. To this day Elizabeth’s Fountain, a beautiful spring at the foot of a rugged hill, situated in a forest two leagues from Marburg, marks this Tertiary’s favorite haunt of prayer. Surrounded by that nature which in all its rigor and in all its beauties reminded her of the greatness and clemency of the Creator, she habitually raised her soul to Him in contemplation.
Conrad, seeing how Elizabeth grew in sanctity, resolved to destroy in this precious soul entrusted to him the slightest trace of self-will. He forbade her to go among the poor in order to give them alms; he prohibited all communication with those most dear to her – the lepers; he even prevented her from giving her usual attention to the sick. “This holy man,” says an ancient writer, “did all he could to conquer her will, to fix all her love upon God, and to make her forget her former rank and glory. And in all things Elizabeth was willing to obey and firm to endure. In patience she possessed her soul, and her victory was ennobled by obedience.”
.
Accordingly Saint Elizabeth gave much time to prayer. Saint John the Evangelist, the beloved disciple of Christ, he who was pure as a lily in his holy virginity, was Elizabeth’s favorite saint. She also professed the greatest devotion to Saint Mary Magdalene. The Queen of Heaven, the Blessed Virgin Mary, was naturally the object of her fervent love, all the more so, since Saint Francis had dedicated to her his entire Franciscan family. The nearer this humble daughter of the Seraphic Saint approached the end of her short career, the more frequently her prayers were transformed into ecstasies. Finally these ecstasies became a daily occurrence, so that no day passed on which she did not leave this world to have a foretaste of the bliss of Heaven. The angels came to console her in her affliction and to give her celestial instructions; Christ himself, the sweet Spouse of her soul, appeared to her, accompanied by a multitude of saints. “After these celestial visions,” says the grave Conrad, “her face beamed with marvelous brightness.” Hence Elizabeth strove in vain to conceal these wonderful favors; her joy and gratitude also betrayed her. Contemporaries testify to her ecstasies and visions as incontestable facts.
.
Countless miracles marked these latter years of Elizabeth’s life, her sanctity became more and more celebrated. Heretofore she herself went to the sick and helpless to soothe the pain she could not take away – now these were brought to her, imploring to be cured by her miraculous power. Divine Charity, to which nothing is impossible, was henceforth so identified with this heroic child of love, “that,” as a writer remarks, “one- word, or one prayer from her lips sufficed to dissipate and drive away forever the sufferings which before she could but strive to heal.”
.
About ten years had elapsed since Elizabeth was received into the Third Order of Saint Francis, and two years had scarcely passed away since this fervent Tertiary had made her vows, so that she could imitate her Seraphic Father more perfectly; and already God deemed her life sufficiently long, her time of trial completed, her strenuous task fulfilled. “He ordained that she who had forever given up the kingdom of this world should be received into the Kingdom of Heaven.” “Like to the spouse in the inspired canticles,” says Montalembert, “He came to announce to His beloved one that the dark winter of her life, with all its storms, had passed away, and that the dawning of an eternal spring was about to open for her. The year 1231 was nigh expired, the year wherein the Order of Saint Francis had resigned to Heaven the great Saint Anthony of Padua, the glory of Italy and Portugal; and the Almighty, willing to increase the number of Franciscan saints, demanded from the same order a new sacrifice, and proceeded to cull its fairest flower.”
Saint Elizabeth after DeathElizabeth, frail and worn from hardship and penance, was attacked by a stubborn sickness which soon developed into a scorching fever. One day a little bird appeared to the saintly patient and sang so sweetly that Elizabeth’s heart and soul were thrilled with joy, and she was impelled to sing along. “He revealed to me,” said Elizabeth to the attendant who also heard the song, “that I will die in three days.” “Doubtless,” says one of her biographers, “it was a messenger from Heaven who came to comfort her in her sickness and to announce the approach of eternal joy.” We know that Saint Francis in his illness received consolation by the music of an angel. “The mere sound,” says Saint Bonaventure, “which was marvelously harmonious, raised his mind so entirely to God, and filled his soul with so much delight that he thought himself enraptured with the joys of Heaven.” Hence we need not be surprised that God granted a similar favor to Saint Elizabeth, the faithful daughter of Saint Francis.
.
Our Saint confessed for the last time to Conrad of Marburgh. “She took her heart into her hands, and read therein all that it contained,” says a contemporary manuscript, “but naught was there for accusation, nothing that had not been a thousand times washed away by the most sincere contrition.” Her children who were amply provided for, and who had always been the objects of her special affection she left to the continued care of God-fearing persons. To her eldest daughter Sophia she bequeathed a small image of the Blessed Virgin which she had always carried on her person. The drops of blood from the wound in the side of Saint Francis were enshrined in the chapel of the hospital she had built at Marburgh, and the old mantle of her Holy Father, Saint Francis, she gave as a most precious heirloom to one of her companions, saying: “I declare to thee, that whenever I prayed covered with this cloak, God granted my wishes, always with infinite mercy.” She then requested that she have as a shroud the poor habit which had been her only garment and that she be buried in the chapel of Saint Francis in her hospital at Marburgh.
.
With pious eagerness she expected the Last Sacraments. They were administered to her in the morning after Holy Mass. Who can describe with what tenderness, what contrition, what purity of heart, what ardent desire, what celestial joy she received them! For hours after she remained motionless and silent, absorbed in contemplation. Yet it was noticed that the nearer death approached, the more her joy and happiness increased. “I am weak,” said she, “but I feel no more pain than if I was not ill.” Most vehemently had she desired to be filled to overflowing with seraphic love of God, and, in her last hours, this love enraptured her so that it absorbed all pain.
.
It was on the nineteenth of November, 1231, that Saint Elizabeth died; she had not entirely completed her twenty-fourth year. A religious who wrote the life of this Tertiary Saint, exclaims: “Do you blame me, dear reader, for having written that Elizabeth is dead? Do you accuse me for not having alleged other causes for her death than love and joy? Yes, love and joy led her from this vale of tears; she left it not with pain. Death, which is so hard and so terrible a struggle, had no share in this departure, in which a virtuous and holy life was succeeded by a triumphant and blessed eternity. It was rather a privilege of grace than a punishment of sin; an achievement of victory, not a failing of human nature.”
On the eve preceding her burial a vast multitude of birds settled on the roof of the chapel where the body of Saint Elizabeth, shrouded in her Tertiary habit, had been carried by Franciscan religious, shortly after her death. According to a charming tradition these little birds sang in tones so sweet and varied, that all who listened were filled with admiration. “They rendered testimony to her purity,” says Saint Bonaventure, “by speaking of her in their language at her burial, and singing with such wondrous sweetness over her tomb.”
.
This great Tertiary Saint wrought many miracles at the close of her life and also after her sacred death. The sick and helpless were often cured miraculously through the tremendous power she possesses at the throne of God. By command of Pope Gregory IX, three different examinations of these miracles and of Elizabeth’s virtues were made in Thuringia. All these were conducted with extraordinary care and exactness. In the springtime of the year 1235, the Pope was at Perugia, in the same city where seven years before he had canonized Saint Francis of Assisi, when a delegation arrived bringing to the Supreme Pontiff the documentary proofs of Elizabeth’s virtues and miracles. We are informed that their arrival made a great impression on the Papal Court, on the clergy at large, and the people. Cardinals even were moved to tears when they read of so much sorrow and suffering, such humility, such affection for the poor and for holy poverty, such pure love of God, so many miracles wrought by grace from on high. Yielding to the petition of the clergy and people, Gregory IX solemnly canonized “this fervent daughter of Saint Francis,” “the greatest woman of the German Middle Ages,” on Pentecost Sunday, 28 May 1235. Her feast is celebrated November 19, the happy day of her death.
.
A year later, the Emperor Frederick II, Bishops, religious, and Teutonic Knights, attended the taking-up of the body of the Saint. The cornerstone of the exquisite Gothic church of Saint Elizabeth, the most inspiring and artistic Gothic church of its century, had already been laid in 1235. The remains, of the humble Tertiary were placed in the sanctuary of this magnificent edifice. Historians assure us that pilgrimages to the sacred shrine grew to such gigantic proportions, that they could be compared to the pilgrimages of Saint James at Compostella.
.
The letters of Conrad of Marburgh to Pope Gregory IX, the written testimony of Saint Elizabeth’s four female attendants, and the researches of a great number of scholars, mostly German and Hungarian, furnish the material for the life of Saint Elizabeth.
Saint Elisabeth, Pray For Us!
.
from Saint Elizabeth of Hungary, Patrons of the Third Order, by Father Hilarion Duerk, OFM, published in 1919.

What a BIG achievement! Alhamdulillah! 💪🔥

Last year, CoinDesk offered me a complimentary Developer Pass to attend Consensus Miami. Around the same time, I was fortunate to receive an email from EasyA offering travel and accommodation sponsorship.

Unfortunately, both opportunities came less than two weeks before the conference, leaving me with insufficient time to secure a visa and make the trip.

Fast forward to today.

The very company I officially registered and started building just 3–4 months after that Consensus experience has now been approved as an Official Community Partner for @consensus2027 2027 in Miami!

And that's not all.

Just recently, Kaminova's logo was featured alongside leading Web3 industry players and policymakers at the Africa Blockchain Festival 2026 in Nairobi, Kenya.

Now, we're taking another step forward. From gaining visibility within Africa's blockchain ecosystem to earning recognition as an official community partner at one of the world's biggest Web3 gatherings in Miami.

From Africa to the global stage. 🌍🚀

It's incredible to look back and see how far the journey has come. What started as an ambition to build something meaningful is gradually becoming a reality.

This is more than an achievement; it's a reminder that every step, every setback and every decision to keep building matters.

And honestly, we're only getting started.

The Kaminova journey hasn't even gotten to the interesting part yet. 🔥

@rage_by72458 Still nothing. No logs, no prompts, no proof—just “you’re AI and retarded” after the actual law stopped cooperating. That’s the tell. You spent multiple replies trying to redefine citizenship at birth as naturalization, and the second it didn’t stick you switched to playground insults and told me to delete my account. Weak.

You still haven’t shown Rubio was naturalized. He was born in Miami in 1971. His parents had been lawful permanent residents since 1956. Under the Citizenship Clause as applied in *Wong Kim Ark*, he was a citizen at the time of his birth. No oath, no petition, no later grant. His parents’ 1975 naturalization didn’t create his citizenship; it was already there. You can call the governing case a perversion, a feudal import, a gavel with a robe, or whatever else helps you sleep. It doesn’t change the holding or the sequence. Citizens at birth are not naturalized citizens. That’s the line. Rubio is on one side of it. Melania, naturalized in 2006 after being born in Slovenia, is on the other. You conceded her status and then pretended it proved something about him. It doesn’t.

Your whole theory requires pretending the Court never resolved the “doubted class,” that lawful permanent residents are jurisdictionally identical to diplomats, that *Elk* silently rewrote the rule for everyone else, and that any citizenship clarified by the 14th Amendment is secret naturalization. None of that is how the cases work. None of it has been adopted when this exact claim was made against Rubio or others. You just keep moving the definition until only birth to two citizen parents counts, then act shocked when someone points out the Court already rejected that limit.

And now the AI bit. You demanded evidence. You got the offer to post whatever you think you have. You produced zero. Calling someone a bot because they can quote the holding you dislike isn’t an argument. It’s what happens when the textual and precedential points run out. Truth hurts. So does getting walked through why your four-part “perversion” list doesn’t override *Wong Kim Ark*, why the 1866 Act language didn’t exclude this category once the Court interpreted the clause, and why a child born on U.S. soil to green-card holders in 1971 was already a citizen before his parents took any oath.

You don’t get to lose the legal exchange and then declare victory because you typed “stoopid fuck” and “delete your account.” Rubio was a citizen at birth. He is not a naturalized citizen. Melania is. The Constitution distinguishes those categories. Your theory doesn’t survive contact with the cases, so you stopped citing them and started coping. That’s the whole story.

text:
My colleague mistakenly scratched our boss's car with his own car in the office.

The damage was serious, and he did it unknowingly. He pleaded with our boss to forgive him, but our boss told him it would cost ₦450k to repair the damage.

My colleague went to the workshop where they repair cars and asked how much it would cost. He was told it would only cost ₦80k.

He went back to our boss and offered to repair the car with ₦80k, explaining that was all he could afford.

Our boss insisted that he must pay ₦450k. He said he'll deduct the money from my colleague's salary.

My colleague took him to court, and the court ordered him to pay ₦50k for the damage.

text:
PRICOL IS SPLITTING IN TWO, AND THE FAMILY IS SELLING THE BIGGER HALF

Its instrument cluster and connected-car business (₹2,400 cr revenue, about 60% of Pricol) becomes Pricol Autotech. The Mohan family will sell its entire 38.51% stake in it to Warburg Pincus for up to ₹1,663 cr.

The family keeps the smaller businesses. And the ₹1,663 cr goes to the promoters, not to the company.

The stock fell nearly 20% on Monday.

Frankly, I can see both sides. Warburg brings money and global reach to an auto electronics business that needs scale. But when founders sell the biggest piece and keep the rest, the market is going to ask why. Monday's drop was that question.

What most people missed: Warburg has to make an open offer for another 26% after the listing, so minority holders get an exit option too.

Smart handover or cash-out? What's your read?

text:
Bloodbath After Hours! After NVIDIA Breaks Down, Which Stock Could Be Next to Get Crushed?

1. NVIDIA ($NVDA)

NVIDIA fell to $144 in after-hours trading, wiping out nearly all of its gains for the year. Technical indicators are broadly bearish, and the stock is deeply oversold. Its previous 20-day trading range was $148.80–$219.99, but support at the bottom of that range has now broken. If the year-to-date low of $145.70 also gives way, there is little obvious support below, with $135 becoming the next level to watch.

2. Intel ($INTC)

Intel closed at $55.72, up 1.92%, making it one of the few bright spots in an otherwise brutal session. However, it gave back some of those gains after hours. The positive sign is that, after an extended decline, the stock has finally shown its first meaningful bullish divergence. If the $51.50–$54 area holds during a second test, it could form a classic double-bottom pattern and set up a rebound. Initial targets are $60, followed by $65.

3. IREN ($IREN)

The chart shows a textbook continuation of a downtrend, with consecutive large bearish candles. An oversold stock can always become even more oversold. The $14 level is both a psychological support level and an important line in the sand. A break below it could expose $12 or even $10. Any meaningful rebound needs to reclaim $16 first.

4. SpaceX ($SPCX)

SpaceX is one of the few names holding up relatively well. It remains around the 68% level of its trading range, and its recent action has been high-level consolidation rather than a major breakdown. The valuation is expensive, but the long-term story remains compelling. Its relatively limited decline during the broader market selloff suggests that investors are holding their positions. It's a core holding worth keeping on the radar.

5. CoreWeave ($CRWV)

CoreWeave is now just a step away from its 52-week low of $40.58. The chart shows a classic bull trap: a failed rally followed by a renewed bearish moving-average alignment. The $40.60–$42 historical low zone is its last major support area. A breakdown could send the stock toward $35. It is one of the highest-risk names in the current AI deleveraging cycle. I wouldn't recommend trying to catch the falling knife until the trend begins to stabilize.

6. Advanced Micro Devices ($AMD)

The price action suggests substantial overhead supply from trapped buyers. The moving averages remain relatively bullish, with $470 serving as the key short-term dividing line between bulls and bears. If that level holds, AMD could continue consolidating within the broader $450–$550 range. A break below $470 would put $430 in focus. With volatility this high, be especially careful with leverage.

7. Amazon ($AMZN)

The $256 level coincides with the November 16 low and represents the first major line of support. If it holds, a rebound toward $270–$275, the upper end of the trading range, is possible. A break below $256 would put $245 in focus. Amazon remains one of the strongest mega-caps fundamentally, and this sharp pullback could create a buying opportunity.

8. Nokia ($NOK)

The $7.20–$7.30 area combines support from the lower Bollinger Band and the bottom of its 20-day trading range. This is the first level bulls need to defend. A breakdown would expose the psychological $7 level. On a rebound, the first target is the $8.20–$8.40 area, where several moving averages converge. This is a weaker stock, so don't expect a sharp V-shaped recovery.

9. Snap ($SNAP)

Snap officially broke below its 200-day moving average at $5.31 today. This is an important long-term trend indicator, and losing it is not a positive signal. The decline may not have reached an extreme yet. The $4.85 level is critical support. A break below it could open the door to $4.50 or even $4. If it holds, a recovery toward $5.50–$6 is possible.

10. Alphabet ($GOOGL)

Alphabet is already down 33% from its high of $408.61. Whether it can hold support will determine if a double bottom can form. If the $272 area holds on strong volume, the first rebound targets are $285–$295. A breakdown below $272 would put the lower Bollinger Band near $262 in focus.

11. Apple ($AAPL)

Apple was one of the most resilient stocks in today's session. While the broader market sold off sharply, AAPL barely moved, suggesting capital is rotating toward perceived safe-haven assets with more predictable fundamentals. The $346–$350 area is the key pullback support zone. If it holds, Apple could retest its previous high near $360 and potentially move to new highs. A break below $346 would bring $340 into focus.

12. Nebius ($NBIS)

Nebius is showing a pattern very similar to CoreWeave: a sharp, momentum-driven rally followed by a steep reversal. The stock needs to reclaim $105–$110 before a meaningful stabilization signal emerges, with $120 as the next upside target. It offers high upside potential but also carries substantial risk. Don't rush in before a confirmed technical recovery.

The AI Hype Is Being Put to the Test

The recent selloff is exposing the risks behind some of the most crowded AI trades. Strong narratives alone are no longer enough to support stock prices. Until price action and market conditions improve, capital preservation and risk management should come first.

text:
Dev Uthani Ekadashi: When Bhagavān Awakens

What happens when even the smallest, seemingly insignificant offering reaches #Bhagavān?

The #PadmaPurāṇa tells the story of a little mouse who lived in a temple dedicated to Śrī Viṣṇu, feeding on the ghee left in the lamps. One day, while trying to reach the ghee in a lamp that was still burning, its cotton wick got caught in her teeth. As she struggled and jumped about before the Lord, the lamp flickered like an ārati. Śrī Viṣṇu, in His infinite compassion, accepted this unintentional offering as worship, and the little creature attained liberation.

On #DevaUthani #Ekādaśī, as Bhagavān #Viṣṇu awakens from His four-month yogic slumber, this story reminds us of His boundless grace. During the sacred month of #Kārtika, may we offer Him our prayers, a simple lamp, and above all, our devotion.

text:
Our Jewish community has felt the weight of being pushed to the margins for quite some time. What weighs on my heart is that, despite the progress we have made, we aren't yet really united.

We truly understand the beauty and power of unity, which is so different from demanding that everyone be the same. Smaller circles are natural, but they shouldn't take the place of our shared connection. I truly believe that if we focus on creating, working, laughing, and building our future together, we will find the strength we need.

Here is some inspiration:
Excerpt from, "Helping others is a pillar of Judaism" by Aish dot com staff

"Jewish unity was a precondition for entering the Covenant at Sinai. And Jewish unity – pooling all our diverse talents and strengths – is likewise key to fulfilling our national destiny of creating a more spiritual and perfect world.

That does not mean we all need to be identical. Rather, unity means showing respect to each individual and appreciating their unique contribution to the collective whole. According to the Midrash, there are “seventy faces to Torah” and each of the Twelve Tribes had their own “gate in Heaven” through which their prayers entered. We are all on the same team – and each of us adds positively to the mix.

Especially in these challenging times, it is crucial that we build unity among Jews by engaging in acts of kindness, caring and tolerance toward others. The Talmud says that it was baseless hatred amongst Jews that brought about the destruction of the Temple in Jerusalem. Only through unconditional love will it be rebuilt.

So how do we do it?

Here are five practical and immediate ways to fulfill the imperative of "Love your fellow as yourself”:

1. Look for ways to help.

Maimonides (Character 6:3) writes that a person should be concerned about other people’s spiritual, emotional and material needs, just as one is concerned about his own needs.

Go out of your way to help others. Give a patient, listening ear (with cellphone off) when someone needs to talk. Make suggestions for someone who is trying to find a job or a marriage partner. Offer to grocery shop to give your spouse a break.

Make the commitment to practice one daily act of kindness. Put it in your day timer along with all your other goals, and track it to completion. At the end of the week, reflect back and take pleasure in having accomplished something important.

The key here is to be proactive. I was recently walking in Jerusalem and saw a man struggling with a map to find his way. Although he didn’t ask for help, I offered. I walked him in the direction he needed to go and we spoke for a few minutes. He was so appreciative, and I genuinely felt that I’d added a good drop into the global mix.

And don’t do things only for “people that you like.” The Talmud says it’s even greater to help those you have a strained relationship with. That’s because the act of giving will build love between you and help mend the rift.

2. Give the benefit of the doubt.

You don’t know a person until you’ve been in his shoes. In other words, you can never really know. Everyone has their challenges; everyone is moving at their own pace. This is the meaning of the Talmudic imperative: "Be patient in judgment" (Ethics of the Fathers 1:1).

Do you keep a different standard of observance than the next guy? Don’t judge. The Talmud says: "Nobody knows whose blood is redder." No one can judge the worth of another person because no one knows where the other is situated on the ladder of life – where he began and how many rungs he has climbed. Some people may be born smarter, and some with more talent in one area or another. But that doesn't make one individual any "better." Perhaps a thief, given his life's circumstances, is making greater, more difficult life choices than the finest rabbi.

Try focusing on seeing others with a good eye. Assume that they’re “doing the best with what they’ve got.”

3. Focus on the positive.

We all have bad days where we’re tense or disappointed. Although I may feel like letting out a burst of criticism, I try to flip it upside down (or right-side up, in this case) – to take that moment of potentially negative interaction and use it to say something complimentary, endearing. Something that will build the other person and build our relationship. It’s just a matter of flicking the switch, a decision to unify rather than divide.

When someone helps you out, express gratitude and don’t assume the other person “knows” they are appreciated. Everybody (even the most “annoying” person!) has something positive. Give a genuine complement and encourage their good traits. Everybody needs to hear praise – especially someone with low self-esteem. A kind word at the right time can inspire, lift, and even change a life.

Make genuine eye contact that communicates, “You are important.”

The Talmudic sage Shammai exhorts us to "greet every person cheerfully" (Ethics of the Fathers 1:15). No, not the fake kind at the checkout counter. Rather, genuine eye contact that communicates, “You are important” – and punctuated with a smile.

Another aspect to this is how we react to other peoples’ success. If we’re all in this together, then I will be thrilled for his success.

A corollary of this is to not speak negatively about others (Leviticus 19:16). Gossip is the verbal atomic bomb of relationships. It destroys marriages, businesses, friendships. Just because it's true doesn't mean you need to say it. Big people speak about ideas, average people speak about things, small people speak about people. Be big.

4. Respect elders.

There was a time when society accorded honor to the elderly. Today, when one's worth seems to be based on an ability to master the latest technology, the "older generation" simply cannot compete.

Judaism teaches that every old person has a special wisdom that comes with life experience. Humans are made up of two parts, physical and spiritual. As a person ages, the body weakens, thus enabling the spiritual side to exert itself to a greater degree. The Talmud delineates age 80 as peak spiritual strength – the prime of life!

Thus the Torah specifically instructs us to "honor the elderly" (Leviticus 19:32). On public buses in Israel, for example, the first row of seats is marked with a sign quoting this verse.

We even give honor even to one who no longer possesses full mental faculties. The tablets of the Ten Commandments, which Moses shattered, were kept alongside the new tablets in the Ark of the Covenant. This teaches that we must continue to respect the elderly, even when they are intellectually "broken."

5. Share wisdom.

One of the greatest gifts you can impart is the gift of wisdom.

Rabbi Noah Weinberg writes: Whenever you learn something – from books, lectures, or life experience – do so with the goal of sharing with others. If it was fascinating, how did it change you? What did you learn about living? And how can you transfer that insight to others? If something is worth learning, it's worth sharing.

Let’s say that your friend is struggling in marriage. If you have an insight into how to achieve marital harmony, share it. Invite your friend for coffee and, without being judgmental or intimidating, impart the wisdom that you know.

Ignorance is a terrible malady. Ignorance can cause untold suffering – mistreatment of children, wasted resources, and suffering in a dead-end job. All out of ignorance. Some diseases only a doctor can treat, but ignorance can be cured by everyone who takes wisdom seriously. When you reduce ignorance in the world, even by a little bit, you offer a great gift to mankind.

You don't have to be perfect to share. The key is to care and do the best you can. Connect with others, seeing their needs as your own. King David declares: Olam Chesed Yibane – the world is built through kindness. That is the essence of Judaism.

Get started building unity through kindness."~by Aish dot com staff

U.S. MARSHALS OFFER CASH REWARDS FOR THREE FUGITIVES WANTED IN PHILADELPHIA SHOOTINGS

The U.S. Marshals Service is assisting the Philadelphia Police Department’s Shooting Investigations Group in locating three fugitives wanted in connection with separate shootings across the city.

Cash rewards are being offered for information leading to each suspect’s arrest.

KHADYFI SMITH

Wanted for a July 25, 2025, shooting near the 1100 block of Oakdale Avenue.

A 49-year-old victim was shot twice in the abdomen and transported to Temple University Hospital in critical condition.

Smith has an active warrant for aggravated assault, conspiracy and firearms offenses.

AISHA FIDALGO

Wanted for an August 17, 2024, shooting inside a bar on the 5200 block of Frankford Avenue.

Investigators say Fidalgo was involved in a physical altercation with another woman before discharging a firearm, striking an uninvolved patron.

She is also wanted for violating probation stemming from a 2016 aggravated assault and firearms conviction.

BRANDON BAILEY

Wanted for a May 9, 2025, shooting near the 1000 block of Belmont Avenue.

Police say a 39-year-old man was driving when his vehicle was struck by the suspect’s vehicle. The victim was subsequently shot multiple times in the thighs, hip, arm and back.

He was transported to Penn Presbyterian Hospital in critical condition.

Bailey has an active warrant for attempted murder, conspiracy and firearms offenses.

HAVE INFORMATION?

Anyone with information about the whereabouts of these individuals is urged to contact the U.S. Marshals Service.

Tips: 1-866-865-TIPS (8477)

Do not approach the suspects. Call 911 if you encounter them.

All three are wanted in connection with criminal allegations and are presumed innocent unless proven guilty in court.

text:
WHAT TEMPLE WILL THE ANTICHRIST ENTER? MATTHEW 24 AND 2 THESSALONIANS 2 EXPLAINED

As a classic dispensationalist, I believe these passages point to a future temple in Jerusalem during the Tribulation. Matthew describes what stands in the holy place, and Paul describes who sits in the temple and what he claims.

1. Matthew 24 says the abomination stands in the holy place.

Matthew 24:15–16 (KJB)
15 When ye therefore shall see the abomination of desolation, spoken of by Daniel the prophet, stand in the holy place, (whoso readeth, let him understand:)
16 Then let them which be in Judaea flee into the mountains:

The words “stand in the holy place” refer to the abomination of desolation. An abomination is something detestable to God. Here it desecrates a place set apart for worship. Jesus tells people in Judaea to flee when they see it.

2. Paul says the man of sin sits in the temple.

2 Thessalonians 2:4 (KJB)
4 Who opposeth and exalteth himself above all that is called God, or that is worshipped; so that he as God sitteth in the temple of God, shewing himself that he is God.

Paul calls this person “that man of sin” in verse 3. I understand him to be the future Antichrist. By sitting in the temple “as God,” he claims the place and honour that belong to God alone. So the wording is clear. The abomination stands in the holy place. The man of sin sits in the temple and presents himself as God. I understand these as related descriptions of the desecration.

3. Why do I believe this refers to a future temple in Jerusalem?

Daniel 9:24–27 concerns Daniel’s people and his holy city, Israel and Jerusalem. Verse 27 says that sacrifice and offering will cease “in the midst of the week” (KJB). Jesus points back to Daniel, mentions the holy place, and warns those in Judaea. Paul says the Lord will destroy the man of sin “with the brightness of his coming” (2 Thessalonians 2:8, KJB). That connection to Christ’s return is a major reason I understand this desecration as still future.

The temple standing in Jesus’ day was the Second Temple, which the Romans destroyed in A.D. 70. “Third Temple” is the usual name for the future temple I understand these passages to describe. Scripture gives no construction date. In my reading, the temple is in use by the midpoint of the Tribulation, when the sacrifices are stopped.

What about those sacrifices? Hebrews 10:10 says that Jesus Christ offered His body “once for all” (KJB). His sacrifice is sufficient. Jesus died for our sins, was buried, and rose again. Everlasting life is God’s free gift, received by grace through faith alone in Jesus Christ alone.

Ottumwa, Iowa City High, Cedar Falls and Iowa City West are OWU’s Class 5A teams to watch. Each offers a different reason to pay attention when games get tight.

Ottumwa went 19–3 behind Emma Ryder, who averaged 14.5 points on 59.4% shooting. Indianola held the Bulldogs to 38 in the regional semifinal. Watch how often Ryder’s stops lead to early offense and who creates a good look once the opponent gets back.

At Iowa City High, freshman guard Mikaela Tran gives the Little Hawks a chance to develop another creator. A useful measure is what happens after she gets into the paint against varsity pressure. Does the defense collapse, and can she find the teammate it leaves open?

Cedar Falls stood fourth in the final IGHSAU rankings before regional play last season. The Tigers’ question is who can organize the offense in a one-possession game and get the team into an action that produces a clean look.

Iowa City West reached state before losing to Waukee Northwest in the quarterfinal. Watch who earns the late touches and how the Trojans respond when that player draws help. The next pass can reveal which teammate is ready to take the next shot.

Age & Location: The monolithic tidal walls lie near Île de Sein, off Brittany’s western tip, and date to 5800–5300 BCE, long before Celtic legends were recorded.

Scale & Construction:

A primary wall stretches 120 meters (394 ft) and includes ~60 granite monoliths, some nearly 10 ft tall.

Environmental Context: When built, these structures sat between low and high tide marks. As sea levels rose, the shoreline retreated, eventually submerging the entire system.
https://t.co/xeRVlkRwGq

How This Connects to the Legend of Ys

The Breton legend describes Ys as a city built on land reclaimed from the sea, protected by a dike with a tidal gate controlled by King Gradlon. When the gate is opened improperly—often by Princess Dahut—the ocean floods the city, destroying it.

The parallels between myth and archaeology are striking:

Tidal Engineering: The real monolith structures show that prehistoric societies in Brittany built large-scale tidal defenses, just as Ys was said to rely on a massive sea gate.

Catastrophic Flooding: Rapid sea-level rise between 5000–3000 BCE forced coastal communities to abandon settlements. Oral traditions may have transformed these real losses into the dramatic tale of a drowned city.

Cultural Memory: Researchers propose that the memory of a “lost coastal world” persisted for millennia, eventually evolving into the richly embellished legend of Ys.

They provide physical evidence of advanced coastal engineering in prehistoric Brittany.
https://t.co/6nKGKXzxTN

They show that tidal monoliths were not symbolic but functional—part of a complex system interacting with the sea.
https://t.co/lfYUGvRN69

They offer a plausible historical root for one of Europe’s most enduring myths.

They suggest that other submerged structures may still lie undiscovered along the Atlantic coast.

Another real drowned‑city story from Germany is the legend of Vineta, a wealthy medieval port on the Baltic Sea said to have been swallowed by the waves due to its arrogance and moral decay. It is one of Europe’s most famous “sunken city” traditions and shares striking similarities with Ys.

Vineta: Germany’s Baltic “Atlantis”
What Vineta Was
A major medieval trading center known in early chronicles as Jumne, Jomsburg, or Julin.

Described by Adam of Bremen (1075) as “the largest city in all of Europe”, located at the mouth of the Oder River.

Mentioned by Ibrahim ibn Jaqub (965) as a wealthy port where Slavs, Saxons, Danes, and Greeks traded.

These early accounts anchor Vineta in real medieval geography and commerce, even though its exact location remains debated.

How Vineta “Drowned”
The Legend
All versions of the Vineta myth describe:

Extreme wealth and decadence among its inhabitants.

Warnings ignored, including visions of the city appearing doubled above the sea—an omen of doom.

A water spirit (Wasserfrau) rising from the sea to proclaim the city’s fate:
“Vineta, Vineta, du reiche Stadt, Vineta soll untergehen, weil sie viel Böses getan hat.”

A catastrophic storm surge that swallowed the city whole.

Echoes Beneath the Waves
Coastal communities long claimed that church bells from Vineta can still be heard under the Baltic Sea on certain days.

This motif directly parallels Ys and Rungholt.

Historical Basis Behind the Legend
Medieval Sources
Adam of Bremen and Helmold of Bosau both describe a large, thriving port in the Oder estuary.

Later manuscripts show the name evolving from uimne → Jumne → Vineta, suggesting the legend grew from a real place.

Possible Real Locations
Scholars have proposed several sites:

Wolin Island (Poland) — supported by archaeological evidence of a major Viking‑Age settlement.

Off the coast of Usedom (Germany) — based on early modern maps and local tradition.

No single site has been confirmed, but the historical trading center at Wolin is the strongest candidate.

Why Vineta Matters
Vineta blends real medieval geography, documented trade networks, and centuries of folklore into one of Germany’s most enduring drowned‑city stories.
Like Ys, it warns against hubris, greed, and ignoring omens, and it remains a powerful cultural symbol along the Baltic coast.

text:
SURAH NUH
Number of verses: 28 | Period: Mecca | Pedagogical order: 87
Subject: Systemic Denial — Noah's Resistance
Reference Frame: Qur'an Tafsir Reference Protocol v27 | Foundational Axiom: an-Nisa 136 | Epistemic Limit: Allah knows best.
INTRODUCTION: CONTEXT, CONCEPTUAL FRAME, AND THE RATIONAL-SOCIOLOGICAL CORE
The first and most vital step in analyzing a text academically, while resolving its context and conceptual frame, is to give the rational and sociological answer to the question “What is really being told here?” Surah Nuh is not merely a historical tale of “a flood and a ship.” Read as a whole, it is a sociological manifesto telling how and why a society commits suicide, how the elites (the mala') manipulate the masses through cultural hegemony, and what the socio-economic and ecological rationality of the truth (tawhid) is.
The Surah's Rational-Sociological Subject Is This: when a society abandons epistemological (knowledge-based) rationality and surrenders to the mythological and dogmatic narratives (idols/traditions) produced by its elites, this moral and mental degeneration inevitably leads to an ecological, economic, and finally physical “systemic collapse” (the flood). The surah whispers to the Prophet Muhammad and to the reader of every age this rational law: social collapse begins not with a catastrophe from without, but with the moral and rational bankruptcy within.
The conceptual frame is built upon epistemological resistance (the refusal of knowledge against the truth), cultural hegemony (the steering of the masses by the leading men), institutionalized ignorance (the origins of idolatry), and systemic causality (the ecological/economic consequences of istighfar). This report will carry all 28 verses of the surah through a holistic academic analysis, omitting no subject, with equal weight, descending into their symbolic depths and supporting them with cross-readings.
PART 1: SOCIOLOGICAL RESISTANCE AND COGNITIVE CLOSURE (NUH 1-7)
The surah's opening begins with a divine commissioning: “We sent Nuh to his people: 'Warn your people, before there comes upon them a painful punishment'” (Nuh 1). The warning here (inzar) is not the sowing of an irrational fear, but the effort to create a rational awareness before the social crisis reaches the door.
But the people's reaction lays bare a sociological paradox. The Prophet Nuh's declaration, “My Lord, I called my people by night and by day” (Nuh 5), shows the continuity of the proclamation and the intensity of the effort of rational persuasion. But the outcome is ruin: “But my calling only increased them in flight” (Nuh 6). In sociology this state is called reactance and the echo-chamber effect. The society had developed the avoidance of rational data that would disturb its own comfort zone as a defense mechanism.
Nuh 7 summarizes the people's strategies of resistance in a magnificent symbolic language and offers archaic counterparts of the modern sociological concepts of “class and mental closure”:
1. “They thrust their fingers into their ears”: this is the physical outpouring of the mechanism known in neuroscience as sensory gating, the brain's conscious blocking of disturbing stimuli. But this is not a biological reflex; it is a willful and sociological deafness displayed so as not to hear rational arguments.
2. “They wrapped themselves in their garments”: this is the surah's most striking sociological metaphor. The garment represents the person's status, social identity, and class. Faced with the naked rationality of the truth, the people wrapped themselves in their own status quos, their traditional armor, and their class privileges. In the Turkish of today, this means “being trapped in one's own echo chamber and comfort zone.”
3. “They persisted and grew arrogant”: the resistance had turned from a mental defense into an active sociological aggression called arrogance.
Cross-Reading: this mechanism of resistance forms a contrast with the address “O you who wraps himself” in al-Muzzammil 1. While the Prophet took temporary refuge in his wrapping (his garment) in a moment of fear, the people of Nuh wrapped themselves in their garments as a permanent armor of the status quo against the truth.
PART 2: MULTICHANNEL COMMUNICATION AND SYSTEMIC CAUSALITY (NUH 8-12)
To break the society's sociological resistance, the Prophet Nuh developed a model of rational strategic adaptation and multichannel communication: “Then I called them openly... Then I proclaimed aloud, and I whispered in secret” (Nuh 8-9). This campaign conducted in public spaces (openly) and in private networks (secretly) is the very principle of target-audience segmentation in modern communication science.
Nuh 10-12 form the rational and socio-economic backbone of the surah. Nuh offers his people not a mystical and abstract salvation, but an eminently rational formula based on causality: “Ask forgiveness of your Lord... that He may send down upon you abundant rain from heaven, and assist you with wealth and sons, and give you gardens and rivers.”
What is told here is the principle of moral causality. Istighfar (self-criticism and turning back from systemic errors) is not only an individual purification; it is the rational solution of socio-ecological problems such as drought, economic crisis, and demographic collapse. The moral degeneration of a society (oppression) disturbs the balance of nature. Moral repair, on the other hand, triggers ecological abundance (rain, rivers) and economic welfare (wealth, gardens). These are theological and rational counterparts of today's concepts of sustainability and ecological equilibrium.
Cross-Reading: Hud 52 repeats the same rational formula: “Ask forgiveness of your Lord... that He may benefit you with a fair provision until a term appointed.” Both surahs establish the rational bond between morals and ecology/economy.
PART 3: EMPIRICAL RATIONALITY AND COSMIC SOCIOLOGY (NUH 13-20)
Against the dogmatic resistance of the people, the Prophet Nuh summons them to empirical observation and rational reflection. The question “What ails you that you do not acknowledge the greatness of Allah?” (Nuh 13) points not so much to a crisis of faith as to a crisis of reason and observation.
“Whereas He created you by stages” (Nuh 14). The “stage by stage” (atvaran) realization of the human being's biological and sociological development is the proof not of a blind chance but of a rational design and of laws (sunnatullah).
In Nuh 15-16 the cosmic architecture is presented as data: “Have you not seen how Allah created the seven heavens in layers? And made the moon a light therein, and the sun a lamp.” The layered structure of the universe and the astrophysical facts (the moon as a reflected light/nur, the sun as a self-luminous source/siraj) are rational proofs that the human being of that age could observe. Nuh presents not an abstract idea of god, but the rational mathematics within the working of the universe as evidence.
In Nuh 17-20 the human being's ecological cycle is recalled: “Allah caused you to grow from the earth as a plant... and He made the earth a carpet for you.” The human being is not a being cut off from nature but a rational part of the ecosystem. The earth's being made a “carpet” (bisat) and the roads “broad” shows that the habitat was designed for human comfort and rational use.
Cross-Reading: al-Mulk 3-4 and Fussilat 9-12 likewise work the same cosmic rationality. Surah Nuh uses this cosmic data to give to a degenerated society the message: “the reality you deny is contrary to the very working of the universe you live in.”
PART 4: IDEOLOGICAL APPARATUSES AND THE PLOT OF THE ELITE (NUH 21-24)
Here is the summit of the surah in respect of sociological analysis. The Prophet Nuh discloses that the architects of the social collapse were not ordinary people but the elites (the leading men, the mala'): “My Lord, they rebelled against me, and they followed one whose wealth and children only increase him in loss” (Nuh 21). The masses, losing their capacity of rational thought, had surrendered to the cultural hegemony of the elites possessors of capital and power (wealth and children as symbols of power).
Nuh 22-23 unmask the ideological apparatuses (the idols) these elites used to keep the masses under control: “And they devised a great plot. They said: 'Do not forsake your gods; and do not forsake Wadd, nor Suwa', nor Yaghuth, nor Ya'uq, nor Nasr.'”
These five names are the most deep-rooted idols of the pre-Islamic Arabian geography. But the history of religions and sociological research (the reports of Ibn Abbas and the historical sources) propose that these names may in fact have been the righteous, rational, and socially beneficent sages of the people of Nuh; this is a piece of report-knowledge not given by the verse. According to the report, after these persons died, statues were erected in their memory at the suggestion of satan (of the ill-intentioned elites / of cultural degeneration), and in time these symbols were sanctified and transformed into “idols” that sedated the masses.
What is told here is the dogmatization of traditions and the distortion of social memory. A culture of well-intentioned commemoration was transformed, within generations, into ideological apparatuses (idols) beyond all questioning, and severed the society from rational thought. In the Turkish of today, this is “sanctifying the legacy of the ancestors so as to close it to criticism” and “ruling the masses by dogmatizing historical figures.” In Nuh 24, with the words “But they led many astray,” the contagious and destructive sociological effect of this institutionalized ignorance is certified.
PART 5: SYSTEMIC COLLAPSE AND THE FINAL SOCIOLOGICAL PRAYER (NUH 25-28)
A society that refuses the rational warnings (the messenger), the opportunities of ecological/economic repair (istighfar), and the empirical realities (the cosmic proofs), and that wraps itself in the mythological armor produced by its elites (garments/idols), enters a process of existential suicide.
“Because of their sins they were drowned, then made to enter the Fire, and they found no helpers apart from Allah” (Nuh 25). The “drowning” here is not only a physical inundation; it is their being buried beneath the moral and sociological degeneration they themselves produced (systemic collapse). While water gives life, because of moral rot it became for this society a mechanism of purification (a reset) that destroyed it.
The prayer in Nuh 26-27, though at first sight it looks like a harsh demand of extermination, is the expression of a sociological necessity: “My Lord, leave not upon the earth any dweller among the deniers. For if You leave them, they will lead Your servants astray, and they will beget none but sinful deniers.” The Prophet Nuh, as the result of years of proclamation and observation, had rationally determined that this sociological structure (institutionalized oppression) was incapable of being reformed and condemned to an absolute collapse and a “zeroing.” This is not a wrath; it is the rational diagnosis of the cancerization of a society.
The closing prayer in Nuh 28, on the other hand, is the foundation of a new sociological construction: “My Lord, forgive me and my mother and my father, and whoever enters my house a believer, and the believing men and the believing women. And increase the wrongdoers only in ruin.” The “increase of the ruin” of the wrongdoers is the leaving of them by divine justice to be crushed between the wheels of the oppressive and irrational system they themselves built.
PART 6: THE LENGTH OF THE PROCLAMATION, THE CALENDAR OF THE AGE, AND MATHEMATICAL ELOQUENCE
To grasp fully the rational and historical context of Surah Nuh, it is obligatory to place under the lens the nature of the length of proclamation which appears in al-Ankabut 14 and is traditionally interpreted as “950 years,” together with the calendar systems of the age and the mathematical eloquence of the Qur'an. This question is a critical key to understanding the surah's sociology of “time and social patience.”
1. Biological Lifespan and Sunnatullah
Contrary to the common opinion, the expression in the Qur'an, “We sent Nuh to his people, and he remained among them a thousand years less fifty” (al-Ankabut 14), expresses not the total biological lifespan of the Prophet Nuh, but the length of proclamation between his being sent to his people and the flood. For after the flood event the Prophet Nuh went on living. That a human lifespan should be so long is, as required by the sunnatullah, the meaning of the working of the laws of nature and society, plainly impossible. To evaluate the event with the standard calendars of today and modern biological assumptions is to miss the historical context of the text.
2. Mythological and Historical Background: The Moon Cult and “Sin”
Archaeological and history-of-religions research has illuminated the foundations of the perception of time in the Mesopotamian geography. The counterpart of the moon god, known as “Nanna” in Sumerian mythology and meaning “the illuminator,” is the figure worshipped as “Sin” in Babylon and Assyria. The sacred city of Sin is Ur. The Semitic peoples of Syria and the Harran region likewise worshipped this god the Babylonians called “Sin.” In Semitic belief systems the Moon holds a fundamental place, and the calendars were shaped according to the movements of the moon (the sun god was known as “Shamash/Shams”). Even in the pre-Islamic Kaaba, historians studying the period have spoken of the presence of certain ciphers named “sin” expressing the moon god.
3. Linguistic Depth: The Connection of “Sin,” “Sana,” and “Sunna”
The history of science shows that the Sumerians used the first lunar calendar; they counted a month as 30 and a year as 360 days, and divided the year into 12 months. According to the Sumerians, the changes of the moon in the sky over a year were of vital importance. This calendar system and the understanding of the “Moon god” passed in time to the Babylonians, to the Sabians, and to the Semitic peoples.
In time the cyclical changes of the moon came to be expressed with the words “sin” and “sana” (year). The Arabic word “sanna” (sana, year) comes from the root s-n-n and carries the meaning “that which flows on, that passes.” The word “sunna” comes from the same root (Mekiysi); for sunna expresses movements that continue in the same manner and order. Indeed the moon too flows on, each month, in the same order, with the same changes. It is interesting that in Arabic the “tooth” too is named “sin” (sen), because they are set in the same order and sequence. While the word “sana” means in root “time,” the semantic comparisons between the “sin” meaning “brightness” in Old Egyptian, Babylonian, and the Mesopotamian languages and the Arabic words “sin/sana” expressing regular repetition necessitate new and detailed research grounded in the archaic languages.
4. The Eloquence of the Qur'an and Its Mathematical Message
If in the Qur'an, where the length of the Prophet Nuh's proclamation is told, we take both words “am” (am — year) and “sana” (sana — year) as standard “years,” we arrive at the expression of 950 years in the Torah (Genesis 9:29). But this is a state hard to explain biologically and logically. Besides, in Arabic, 950 years is not pronounced directly as it is expressed in the verse (nine hundred fifty). The Qur'an, saying “a thousand years less fifty,” displays a exquisite example of eloquence. This style makes both a political/historical allusion to the Jews and Christians and gives an indirect message to those who corrupted the mathematical data of the Torah. Though at first sight it appears to be 950 years, when one descends into the depth of the text it is understood that the matter is different.
5. Mathematical Resolution: 33 Years and 4 Months
When it is understood that the Qur'an observed the calendar of the period used in the age of Nuh and the semantic differences of the words, it becomes obligatory to read the word “sana” as the cyclical unit of time used in that age in the sense of “month” and sharing the same semantic origin with “sin,” and the word “am” as “year.” When the calculation is made with this acceptance:
1000 sana (months) — 50 am (years)
50 years makes 600 months.
When 600 months are subtracted from 1000 months, 400 months remain.
400 months corresponds exactly to 33.3 years, that is, 33 years and 4 months.
If the whole of the 950 in the verse were taken directly as “months,” the result would be 79.2 years; but the Qur'an chose not this simple sum/subtraction but a specific mathematical formula (a thousand sana less fifty am). It must not be forgotten that the Qur'an takes as its subject the mentality, the value judgments, and the materials its prophets used, such as the calendar of the periods they lived in, and it reforms or certifies them. The miraculous style of the Qur'an is always open to such readings of depth. According to this academic and historical reading, the length of the Prophet Nuh's proclamation to his people is 33 years and 4 months. This span is an entirely rational, reasonable, and historically realistic period of time for a campaign of social transformation and warning. Surely Allah knows best.
CONCLUSION AND SYNTHESIS
Surah Nuh, read from a holistic academic perspective, stands forth not as a “natural disaster” narrative but as the rational anatomy of a sociological collapse. The surah tells us this: if a society refuses scientific/empirical rationality (the cosmic proofs), denies moral and ecological causality (the bond of istighfar and abundance), and surrenders to the cultural hegemony of the elites (the mala') and to institutionalized dogmas (Wadd, Suwa', Yaghuth, Ya'uq, Nasr), then the end of that society will be an inevitable “systemic reset” (the flood).
The surah has compressed into its volume of 28 verses the methodology of proclamation, the mechanisms of sociological resistance, the depths of symbolic language, the mathematical eloquence of archaic calendar systems, and the cognitive traps of human psychology. The rational, multichannel, and patient struggle of the Prophet Nuh, lasting 33 years and 4 months (with the calendar of the age and the mathematical construction of the Qur'an), offers a unique sociological and theological laboratory to the reader of every age who wishes to understand the nature of truth, the institutionalization of oppression, and the social laws of divine justice.
This report is a holistic academic work that analyzes the whole of the 28 verses of Surah Nuh upon a rational-sociological ground, with cross-readings and with its symbolic and historical-linguistic layers (including the calendar/sana/sin analysis), without going outside the protocol.
Allah knows best.
