A. Primary Source: Semantic Analysis, Calendar System, and Mathematical Computation
1. Yakit, Prof. Dr. Ismail, Kur'an-i Hakim Meali; Semantik Analizli, Aciklamali ve Yorumlu (The Noble Qur'an: A Semantic, Annotated, and Interpretive Rendering), Otuken Nesriyat, Istanbul, 2021.
(Note: this is the source work for the semantic rendering of al-Ankabut 14 as “a thousand months less fifty,” for the establishing of the etymological bond of the Arabic roots sana/sin/sunna with the Mesopotamian lunar calendar (the Moon God Sin), and for the mathematical decipherment that the length of Nuh's proclamation was not 950 years but 33 years and 4 months.)
2. Yakit, Prof. Dr. Ismail, his academic seminars and articles on “The Age and Length of Proclamation among the People of Nuh,” and his oral/written glosses on the “Dini Cevaplar” (Religious Answers) platform.
(Note: interdisciplinary studies in which the mathematical tension between the Torah and the Qur'an is set upon a rational ground through the sociological and calendrical mentality of the age (the lunar calendar among the Semitic peoples).)
B. Classical Tafsir, Linguistics, and Islamic Sources
3. The Qur'an (relevant surahs: Nuh, al-Ankabut, Hud, al-Muzzammil, al-Mulk, al-Qamar).
4. Ibn Manzur, Lisanu'l-Arab. (the base lexicon for the etymology of the Arabic root s-n-n; for the philological grounding of the concepts “sana” (year), “sunna,” “sin” (tooth), and regular flow/cycle.)
5. Ibn Kathir, Tefsiru'l-Kur'ani'l-Azim. (the history of the people of Nuh; the reports of the derivation of the idols Wadd, Suwa', Yaghuth, Ya'uq, and Nasr from righteous persons.)
6. Tabari, Camiu'l-Beyan an Te'vili Ayi'l-Kur'an. (early Islamic historiography and the reports on the geography of the flood of Nuh.)
C. Archaeology, Assyriology, and the History of Religions (Mesopotamia and Semitic Mythology)
7. Black, Jeremy & Green, Anthony, Gods, Demons and Symbols of Ancient Mesopotamia: An Illustrated Dictionary, University of Texas Press. (the base archaeological source for the “Nanna” of the Sumerians, the “Sin” (Moon God) of the Babylonians and Assyrians, the “Shamash” (Sun God), and the cult of the city of Ur.)
8. Kramer, Samuel Noah, History Begins at Sumer. (the Sumerian calendar, the moon cult, the 30-day lunar cycles, and the analysis of the Mesopotamian social structure.)
9. The Chicago Assyrian Dictionary (CAD), Oriental Institute of the University of Chicago. (the comparative philology of the time/month concepts of the Semitic languages, Akkadian, and Sumerian.)
10. Eliade, Mircea, The Sacred and the Profane. (moon symbolism, the perception of time, mythological cycles, and the sociology of primitive/social religion.)
D. Sociology, Psychology, and Communication Theory
11. Brehm, Jack W., A Theory of Psychological Reactance, Academic Press. (social resistance, reaction against pressure, and reactance theory, the psychological counterpart of the “wrapping themselves in their garments” metaphor.)
12. Festinger, Leon, A Theory of Cognitive Dissonance, Stanford University Press. (cognitive dissonance, knowing the truth yet refusing it, and the psychological basis of the mechanisms of denial.)
13. Gramsci, Antonio, Selections from the Prison Notebooks. (cultural hegemony; the steering of the masses by the elites (the mala') through ideological apparatuses.)
14. Bourdieu, Pierre, Distinction: A Social Critique of the Judgement of Taste. (class status quo, symbolic capital, and the sociological counterpart of the “garment/wrapping” metaphor.)
E. Hermeneutics, Philology, and Interdisciplinary Readings
15. Izutsu, Toshihiko, God and Man in the Koran. (conceptual analysis, semantic-field theory, and the methodology of the relation of the words of the Qur'an with the mental background of the age.)
16. Noldeke, Theodor, Compendious Syriac Grammar / Studies on the History of the Semitic Languages. (the etymological transitions among the Semitic languages; the etymological comparison of the time-words of Arabic and Hebrew/Aramaic.)

Age & Location: The monolithic tidal walls lie near Île de Sein, off Brittany’s western tip, and date to 5800–5300 BCE, long before Celtic legends were recorded.

Scale & Construction:

A primary wall stretches 120 meters (394 ft) and includes ~60 granite monoliths, some nearly 10 ft tall.
https://t.co/oHicHeJraq

The total mass of the structure is estimated at 3,300 tons, making it the largest underwater stone construction ever found in France.
https://t.co/HYJwmNjvsX

Purpose: Researchers believe the monolith-lined walls served as fish traps or tidal dikes, engineered to withstand powerful Atlantic currents.
https://t.co/ubFfn0AEU9

Environmental Context: When built, these structures sat between low and high tide marks. As sea levels rose, the shoreline retreated, eventually submerging the entire system.
https://t.co/xeRVlkRwGq

How This Connects to the Legend of Ys

The Breton legend describes Ys as a city built on land reclaimed from the sea, protected by a dike with a tidal gate controlled by King Gradlon. When the gate is opened improperly—often by Princess Dahut—the ocean floods the city, destroying it.

The parallels between myth and archaeology are striking:
https://t.co/Dvd5oiBtvD

Cultural Memory: Researchers propose that the memory of a “lost coastal world” persisted for millennia, eventually evolving into the richly embellished legend of Ys.

They provide physical evidence of advanced coastal engineering in prehistoric Brittany.

They show that tidal monoliths were not symbolic but functional—part of a complex system interacting with the sea.
https://t.co/lfYUGvRN69

They offer a plausible historical root for one of Europe’s most enduring myths.

They suggest that other submerged structures may still lie undiscovered along the Atlantic coast.

Germany’s closest real parallel to the legend of Ys is the story of Rungholt, a wealthy medieval town on the North Sea that was swallowed by a catastrophic storm tide in 1362. Like Ys, Rungholt was said to be prosperous, sinful, and ultimately destroyed by the sea—its ruins still believed to lie beneath the waves of the Wadden Sea.

Celtic Countries

🌊 A Real German “Sunken City”: Rungholt

Although the legend of Ys is Breton, Germany has its own drowned‑city tale that mirrors it closely in theme, tone, and fate.

Rungholt (North Frisia, Schleswig‑Holstein)

Location: On the island region of Strand, now part of the Wadden Sea National Park.

Era: Flourished in the Middle Ages as a wealthy trading town.

Destruction: Believed to have been destroyed during the Grote Mandrenke (“Great Drowning of Men”) storm tide in 1362, which devastated large parts of the North Sea coast.

Legend: Rungholt was said to be rich, proud, and morally corrupt. According to folklore, the townspeople mocked the church and ignored warnings of divine punishment. When the storm came, the sea swallowed the entire city.

Aftermath: Fishermen and sailors have long claimed they can still hear bells ringing beneath the water—an echo of Ys’s own mythic cathedral.

Archaeology: Modern researchers have found medieval structures, drainage systems, and artifacts in the tidal flats, supporting the existence of a real settlement beneath the sea.

Rungholt’s blend of wealth, hubris, divine warning, and catastrophic flooding makes it the closest German analogue to Ys’s mythic fall.

Why Rungholt Feels Like Germany’s Ys

Both stories share striking motifs:

A prosperous coastal city whose success leads to arrogance.

Warnings ignored, often framed as moral or spiritual failings.

A catastrophic flood that erases the city almost instantly.

Lingering echoes—bells underwater in Ys, and in Rungholt, stories of sounds or ruins visible at low tide.

Cultural memory that blends history with myth.

Rungholt is not just a legend; it’s a historical place wrapped in folklore, making it even more compelling as a real-world counterpart.

🧭 Other German Flood Legends (Less Similar but Related)

If you want more drowned‑city stories from Germany, here are a few thematic cousins:

Vineta (Baltic Sea): A legendary wealthy city said to have sunk due to greed and decadence.

The Lorelei (Rhine River): Not a city, but a tale of a siren whose song causes shipwrecks—another blend of water, danger, and myth.

Peat bog villages in Lower Saxony: Some settlements were lost to floods, though without the moral legend attached.

Rungholt remains the strongest match to Ys in both narrative and historical depth.

Germany’s closest real parallel to the legend of Ys is the drowned medieval city of Rungholt, whose fall in 1362 blends documented history with mythic elements—divine punishment, moral decay, and a city swallowed overnight by the sea.

Rungholt: The “German Atlantis”

Rungholt was a wealthy North Frisian trading town on the island of Strand, now part of the Wadden Sea. Archaeology shows it may have had up to 500 houses and around 3,000 inhabitants, thriving on agriculture and maritime trade.

The Catastrophe

On 15–16 January 1362, the Grote Mandrenke (“Great Drowning of Men”) storm tide struck the North Sea coast. It destroyed Rungholt and roughly 30 other settlements, killing an estimated 25,000 people. The coastline shifted dramatically, leaving the former land beneath tidal flats.

Archaeological Confirmation

For centuries, Rungholt was treated as half‑legend. But modern surveys—magnetic gradiometry, electromagnetic induction, and seismic mapping—have revealed dikes, drainage systems, wells, sluices, and the foundations of multiple churches, including a large 40×15‑meter parish church. These findings confirm Rungholt’s existence and scale.

The Legends: Moral Decay and Divine Punishment

Rungholt’s folklore mirrors Ys so closely that scholars often call it “Atlantis of the North Sea.”

The Pig and the Priest

One famous tale describes drunken young men forcing a priest to give last rites to a pig. The priest prayed for divine justice, and the storm that followed was seen as God’s answer. This echoes Ys’s theme of hubris and sacrilege leading to destruction.

Bells Beneath the Waves

Sailors and fishermen have long claimed they can hear church bells ringing under the sea near Hallig Südfall. This motif—an underwater city whose bells still toll—directly parallels Ys, where the cathedral bells are said to echo from beneath the ocean.

How Rungholt Connects to Other German Water Legends

Rungholt sits within a broader German tradition of drowned or cursed coastal places:

Niedam – Another settlement near Rungholt, also lost in the 14th century storm tides.

Vineta – A legendary Baltic city said to have sunk due to greed and decadence; often compared to Ys for its moralizing narrative.

The Wadden Sea Halligen – Tiny islands that flood regularly, preserving a cultural memory of living at the edge of the sea.

Why Rungholt Is Germany’s Ys

A real city with archaeological proof, yet wrapped in myth.

A moral legend of arrogance and sacrilege, like Ys.

A sudden, overwhelming flood that erased it overnight.

Lingering supernatural echoes—bells, ghostly ruins, shifting sands.

A cultural symbol of human fragility before the sea.

Rungholt is not just similar to Ys—it is the closest real-world counterpart, where history and legend intertwine so tightly that the boundary between them feels as fluid as the tides that claimed it.

Germany has several real historical stories of cities and villages destroyed by the sea, but the most complete and best‑documented is the true story of Rungholt, a wealthy medieval town swallowed by the North Sea in 1362.

🌊 Rungholt — A Real German City Lost to the Sea

Rungholt was a prosperous trading town in North Frisia, located on the island of Strand (now part of Schleswig‑Holstein). Archaeologists estimate it may have had up to 500 houses and around 3,000 inhabitants, making it one of the larger medieval settlements in the region.

The Disaster: The Grote Mandrenke (1362)

On 15–16 January 1362, a massive storm tide known as the Grote Mandrenke (“Great Drowning of Men”) struck the North Sea coast.

The storm overwhelmed the dikes protecting the reclaimed marshland.

Rungholt and 30–44 other settlements were destroyed.

An estimated 25,000 people died across the region.

The island of Strand itself was torn apart; only fragments like Nordstrand and Hallig Südfall remain today.

1921: First ruins found near Hallig Südfall (wells, trenches, tidal lock).

Historians believe these tales grew as a way to explain the disaster.

🌍 Other Real German “Sunken City” Stories

While Rungholt is the most historically grounded, Germany has other flood legends:

Vineta (Baltic Sea): A legendary wealthy city said to have sunk due to greed.

Niedam: Another settlement destroyed in the same 1362 storm system.

Drowned villages of the Wadden Sea: Many small communities vanished in medieval storm tides.

Another real drowned‑city story from Germany is the legend of Vineta, a wealthy medieval port on the Baltic Sea said to have been swallowed by the waves due to its arrogance and moral decay. It is one of Europe’s most famous “sunken city” traditions and shares striking similarities with Ys.

Vineta: Germany’s Baltic “Atlantis”
What Vineta Was
A major medieval trading center known in early chronicles as Jumne, Jomsburg, or Julin.

Described by Adam of Bremen (1075) as “the largest city in all of Europe”, located at the mouth of the Oder River.

Mentioned by Ibrahim ibn Jaqub (965) as a wealthy port where Slavs, Saxons, Danes, and Greeks traded.

These early accounts anchor Vineta in real medieval geography and commerce, even though its exact location remains debated.

How Vineta “Drowned”
The Legend
All versions of the Vineta myth describe:

Extreme wealth and decadence among its inhabitants.

Warnings ignored, including visions of the city appearing doubled above the sea—an omen of doom.

A water spirit (Wasserfrau) rising from the sea to proclaim the city’s fate:
“Vineta, Vineta, du reiche Stadt, Vineta soll untergehen, weil sie viel Böses getan hat.”

A catastrophic storm surge that swallowed the city whole.

Echoes Beneath the Waves
Coastal communities long claimed that church bells from Vineta can still be heard under the Baltic Sea on certain days.

This motif directly parallels Ys and Rungholt.

Historical Basis Behind the Legend
Medieval Sources
Adam of Bremen and Helmold of Bosau both describe a large, thriving port in the Oder estuary.

Later manuscripts show the name evolving from uimne → Jumne → Vineta, suggesting the legend grew from a real place.

Possible Real Locations
Scholars have proposed several sites:

Wolin Island (Poland) — supported by archaeological evidence of a major Viking‑Age settlement.

Off the coast of Usedom (Germany) — based on early modern maps and local tradition.

No single site has been confirmed, but the historical trading center at Wolin is the strongest candidate.

Why Vineta Matters
Vineta blends real medieval geography, documented trade networks, and centuries of folklore into one of Germany’s most enduring drowned‑city stories.
Like Ys, it warns against hubris, greed, and ignoring omens, and it remains a powerful cultural symbol along the Baltic coast.

Another real drowned‑city story from Germany is the legend of Vineta, a wealthy medieval port on the Baltic Sea said to have been swallowed by the waves due to its arrogance and moral decay. It is one of Europe’s most famous “sunken city” traditions and shares striking similarities with Ys.

Vineta: Germany’s Baltic “Atlantis”
What Vineta Was
A major medieval trading center known in early chronicles as Jumne, Jomsburg, or Julin.

Described by Adam of Bremen (1075) as “the largest city in all of Europe”, located at the mouth of the Oder River.

Mentioned by Ibrahim ibn Jaqub (965) as a wealthy port where Slavs, Saxons, Danes, and Greeks traded.

These early accounts anchor Vineta in real medieval geography and commerce, even though its exact location remains debated.

How Vineta “Drowned”
The Legend
All versions of the Vineta myth describe:

Extreme wealth and decadence among its inhabitants.

Warnings ignored, including visions of the city appearing doubled above the sea—an omen of doom.

A water spirit (Wasserfrau) rising from the sea to proclaim the city’s fate:
“Vineta, Vineta, du reiche Stadt, Vineta soll untergehen, weil sie viel Böses getan hat.”

A catastrophic storm surge that swallowed the city whole.

Echoes Beneath the Waves
Coastal communities long claimed that church bells from Vineta can still be heard under the Baltic Sea on certain days.

This motif directly parallels Ys and Rungholt.

Historical Basis Behind the Legend
Medieval Sources
Adam of Bremen and Helmold of Bosau both describe a large, thriving port in the Oder estuary.

Later manuscripts show the name evolving from uimne → Jumne → Vineta, suggesting the legend grew from a real place.

Possible Real Locations
Scholars have proposed several sites:

Wolin Island (Poland) — supported by archaeological evidence of a major Viking‑Age settlement.

Off the coast of Usedom (Germany) — based on early modern maps and local tradition.

No single site has been confirmed, but the historical trading center at Wolin is the strongest candidate.

Why Vineta Matters
Vineta blends real medieval geography, documented trade networks, and centuries of folklore into one of Germany’s most enduring drowned‑city stories.
Like Ys, it warns against hubris, greed, and ignoring omens, and it remains a powerful cultural symbol along the Baltic coast.

text:
Happy Birthday Evelyn Keyes - the girl with more lovers than Casanova. 

Keyes was an American film actress, whose career began with  promise when she was cast in “Gone With the Wind” as Scarlett O’Hara’s younger sister, Suellen. More prominent roles followed, but Keyes, by her own admission, allowed her unusually active sex life to take precedence over her work. She was also highly intelligent and easily bored. As a result, and due to her perceived lack of knockout beauty, her talent was often overlooked. Keyes was born in Texas in 1916. Aged 18, she travelled to Hollywood and was introduced to Cecil B. DeMille who "signed me to a personal contract without even making a test".  Keyes may have not been Hedy Lamarr, but the effect she had on men should have been bottled. She was cast in “Say It In French” (1938), but had to drop out to have an abortion. She then auditioned for the role of Scarlett in “Gone with the Wind” (1939). Though she failed to get the part, David Selznick was impressed by her ability and cast her as the perpetually dissatisfied Suellen. Her acting was praised, and in 1941, she played an ingenue in “Here Comes Mr. Jordan”. Keyes spent most of the early 1940s in minor dramas and mysteries. She won her breakthrough role opposite Larry Parks in the blockbuster hit “The Jolson Story” (1946), playing the jazz singer’s wife. Studio bosses had not thought her pretty enough, but she countered angrily that talent was just as essential. She sparkled, displaying her prowess as an actress, dancer, and with her hair and neat little figure dolled up, a genuine glamour girl. Keyes then appeared in the screwball comedy, “The Mating of Millie”, with Glenn Ford. By this time she should have been a star, but no one bothered to guide her career. Keyes complained about the lack of good roles offered to her, and when Sam Spiegel bought the story for the film noir “The Prowler”, John Huston, to whom she was then married, thought it would be the perfect vehicle. It was. She shone opposite Van Heflin, as a sexed up housewife who falls for a bent policeman. Similar parts should have followed, but Keyes seemed to lose interest in her work. Her last role in a major film was as Tom Ewell's wife in “The Seven Year Itch” (1955), after which she decided to give up acting. Her personal life was everything her career was not - explosive. Keyes described being sexually harassed by almost everyone she met, and found out she was pregnant by her on-off boyfriend Barton Bainbridge during the filming of “Say It In French,” rushing off to get rid of the baby. She married Bainbridge shortly after. Unfortunately, he was an alcoholic, and threatened Keyes with a gun. They separated, but in 1940, he broke into her car and shot himself. Keyes recalled: "He had written a note. The note said he did it because I had left him. I never left a man again. I made them leave me." She then married and divorced director Charles Vidor, before reeling in the elusive John Huston. They wed in 1946, in a stimulating but turbulent union that lasted four years. In the mid ‘50s, the actress became seriously involved with the intellectual and much-married bandleader Artie Shaw, whose ex wives included Lana Turner and Ava Gardner. Shaw found an equal in Keyes, but they often quarrelled over his arrogance. “Do you think you’re f….. God?” she once asked him, only for Shaw to reply, “Yes.” Still, the marriage lasted from 1957 to 1985. Keyes said of her many affairs: "I always took up with the man of the moment, and there were many moments." Among her other lovers were Mike Todd (who left her for Elizabeth Taylor), Glenn Ford, Sterling Hayden, Dick Powell, Anthony Quinn, David Niven and Kirk Douglas. Keyes added that she regularly fought off Columbia head Harry Cohn. Not bad for a girl who was never considered beautiful. Evelyn Keyes died on July 4, 2008, aged 91.

The US has a major problem with education inequality. Children from low-income families are less likely to receive high-quality education, partly because poorer districts struggle to retain experienced teachers. 

Artificial intelligence could help, by improving the one-on-one tutoring sometimes used to supplement class instruction in these schools. With help from an AI tool, tutors could tap into more experienced teachers’ expertise during virtual tutoring sessions. 

Researchers from Stanford University developed an AI system calledTutor CoPilot on top of OpenAI’s GPT-4 and integrated it into a platform called FEV Tutor, which connects students with tutors virtually. Tutors and students type messages to one another through a chat interface, and a tutor who needs help explaining how and why a student went wrong can press a button to generate suggestions from Tutor CoPilot. 

The researchers created the model by training GPT-4 on a database of 700 real tutoring sessions in which experienced teachers worked on on one with first- to fifth-grade students on math lessons, identifying the students’ errors and then working with them to correct the errors in such a way that they learned to understand the broader concepts being taught. From this, the model generates responses that tutors can customize to help their online students.

“I’m really excited about the future of human-AI collaboration systems,” says Rose Wang, a PhD student at Stanford University who worked on the project, which was published on arXiv and has not yet been peer-reviewed “I think this technology is a huge enabler, but only if it’s designed well.”

The tool isn’t designed to actually teach the students math—instead, it offers tutors helpful advice on how to nudge students toward correct answers while encouraging deeper learning. 

For example, it can suggest that the tutor ask how the student came up with an answer, or propose questions that could point to a different way to solve a problem. 

To test its efficacy, the team examined the interactions of 900 tutors virtually teaching math to 1,787 students between five and 13 years old from historically underserved communities in the US South. Half the tutors had the option to activate Tutor CoPilot, while the other half did not. 

The students whose tutors had access to Tutor CoPilot were 4 percentage points more likely to pass their exit ticket—an assessment of whether a student has mastered a subject—than those whose tutors did not have access to it. (Pass rates were 66% and 62%, respectively.)

The tool works as well as it does because it’s being used to teach relatively basic mathematics, says Simon Frieder, a machine-learning researcher at the University of Oxford, who did not work on the project. “You couldn’t really do a study with much more advanced mathematics at this current point in time,” he says.

The team estimates that the tool could improve student learning at a cost of around $20 per tutor annually to the tutoring provider, which is significantly cheaper than the thousands of dollars it usually takes to train educators in person. 

It has the potential to improve the relationship between novice tutors and their students by training them to approach problems the way experienced teachers do, says Mina Lee, an assistant professor of computer science at the University of Chicago, who was not involved in the project.

“This work demonstrates that the tool actually does work in real settings,” she says. “We want to facilitate human connection, and this really highlights how AI can augment human-to-human interaction.”

As a next step, Wang and her colleagues are interested in exploring how well novice tutors remember the teaching methods imparted by Tutor CoPilot. This could help them gain a sense of how long the effects of these kinds of AI interventions might last. They also plan to try to work out which other school subjects or age groups could benefit from such an approach.

“There’s a lot of substantial ways in which the underlying technology can get better,” Wang says. “But we’re not deploying an AI technology willy-nilly without pre-validating it—we want to be sure we’re able to rigorously evaluate it before we actually send it out into the wild. For me, the worst fear is that we’re wasting the students’ time.”

text:
Central Florida Floods Cut Off My Road. Amazon, Is This How You Treat Flood Victims?

I offered to drive to a safe location to pick up copies of my book, He Feeds Dinosaurs. Amazon promised me a pickup in writing. Then its phone representative told me I had no options.

I live in Geneva, Florida. The water in front of my house and down the road was three feet deep. I contacted Amazon more than a week before the earliest delivery date because I knew a driver couldn’t reach me. I’d ordered 20 paperbacks and paid $396 to enter my book in four categories of the IBPA Book Awards. Thirteen judging copies have to be postmarked by December 15.

Zaki, the Amazon chat representative, first said the box would go to a safe place, “probably nearby pickup location.” I asked him, “But where is that?” He said I’d get an email once the order was out for delivery.

I had a reason to press him. The last time my road flooded, Amazon marked several deliveries undeliverable and returned them. I told him that. The delivery instructions he sent still showed my house. I asked him to show me where Amazon’s written policy said the driver would take my box somewhere else.

Here’s exactly what Zaki wrote.

“Daniel, this is how we works. If there such natural disaster there, we will deliver the item at the nearest pickup location and you will receive an Email confirmation as well”

I believe he was trying to get me off the chat so he could move on. What bothers me most is that the more specific my questions got, the more certain his answer became. “Probably” became “we will deliver.” He never gave me a pickup address or showed me the policy. He left me with every reason to close the chat and wait for an email.

When I spoke to Amazon by phone, the representative told me the books wouldn’t be delivered to my house and there was nothing they could do. That night, Amazon also emailed me that the order couldn’t be canceled.

FedEx and UPS both let customers request pickup holds for eligible packages. FedEx even takes requests the day before delivery. I gave Amazon more than a week’s notice and offered to make the trip myself.

Amazon, was the promise you made me in writing true? If it was, where can I pick up my books? If it wasn’t, why did your representative tell me I could count on it?

text:
Positioning does not determine who the "protagonist" is.

As the host of the APEC summit in Shenzhen—and the chair of this historic, first-ever trilateral closed-door meeting between China, the U.S., and Russia—Xi Jinping’s central seat is a matter of protocol and his role as moderator; it is not proof that he is the "protagonist." 

The arrangement—a round table with Xi in the center and Putin and Trump on either side—is standard practice for a host. 

Determining the true protagonist requires looking at who drives the agenda, who sets the priorities, and what concrete results are achieved, rather than focusing on the composition of a camera shot. 

The "Peace Declaration" issued after the meeting was signed by all three parties, not driven unilaterally by any one side.
The claim that "Trump returned empty-handed" is unfounded.

The absence of an immediate press conference does not mean there were no outcomes. 

After the meeting, Trump boarded Air Force One to return to the U.S., with plans to hold a press conference at the White House the following day. 

He later rated the talks a "12 out of 10," remarked that they were "truly making history," and emphasized that a good rapport had been established among the three leaders. 

The declaration included commitments to: promote UN reform; increase the production and supply of refined petroleum products; ensure that institutions like the International Criminal Court do not abuse their jurisdiction; and reaffirm that "a nuclear war cannot be won and must never be fought," with a pledge to engage in dialogue on reducing nuclear risks. 

According to Putin, the situation in Ukraine was a key topic of discussion, raised at Trump’s initiative. These are not "zero results"—they simply lack the kind of dramatic, short-term breakthroughs that are, in fact, rarely seen at most summits. 

Trump and Xi have met multiple times this year (including in Beijing and at the White House), and the two sides have maintained ongoing engagement on trade, economics, and other issues.

Xi Jinping’s "gains in international standing" are not unique to this event.

While hosting APEC and facilitating this first trilateral meeting certainly amplified his influence, this is part of a long-term diplomatic strategy rather than a sudden, transformative shift. 

Xi has played similar roles on other international stages—such as during his visits to the White House—as the accumulation of international stature is a gradual, long-term process.

Similarly, this is not the first time Putin has "broken out of diplomatic isolation." 

In recent years, Putin has consistently participated in mechanisms like BRICS and the SCO, maintaining frequent interaction with China; his involvement here is not a sudden "return" following a period of total isolation. 

While this trilateral meeting does offer a platform for direct dialogue—including with the United States—and carries symbolic weight, describing it as "breaking out of isolation" likely overstates its novelty.

Overall, the historical significance of this meeting lies primarily in the fact that it was the "first closed-door trilateral summit," as well as in the joint declaration’s shared language regarding nuclear risks, energy stability, and the jurisdiction of certain international institutions. 

It offered no concrete solutions to major conflicts—such as those in Ukraine or Iran—nor did it yield any disruptive strategic breakthroughs; in this regard, the tweet’s assessment is correct. 

However, interpreting the scene—with the host in the center and the absence of an immediate press conference—as evidence that "Xi is the protagonist, Trump a supporting actor, and Putin has returned to the stage" ignores the basic logic of diplomatic protocol and the assessment of substantive outcomes. 

A well-staged photo does not equate to a fundamental shift in the power structure. Ultimately, observing the implementation of the declaration and the subsequent actions of each party will be far more meaningful than analyzing the group photograph.

站位不能决定谁是主角。
习近平作为东道主，在深圳主办APEC并主持这场历史上首次的中美俄三方闭门会晤，按国际惯例坐在中间是礼仪与主持权的体现，并非“主角”的证明。

三方围坐圆桌、习近平居中、普京与特朗普分列两侧，这是标准的东道主安排。真正的主角是谁，要看议程推动力、议题优先权和实际成果，而不是镜头构图。会后发表的《中俄美元首和平宣言》是三方共同签署的，并非单方面主导。

“川普空手而归”缺乏依据。
没有当场开记者会，并不等于没有收获。

特朗普会后直接登上空军一号返美，并计划在第二天中午于白宫举行新闻发布会。他本人事后把这次会谈打到“12分”（满分10分），称“正在真正创造历史”，并强调三方建立了良好关系。

宣言内容包括：推动联合国改革、计划增加精炼石油产品生产和供应、认为国际刑事法院等机构不得滥用管辖权、重申“核战争打不赢也打不得”并承诺就减少核风险展开对话。

乌克兰问题据普京方面称是在特朗普倡议下重点讨论的。这些并非“零成果”，只是短期内没有出现戏剧性突破（这也符合多数峰会的常态）。特朗普今年已与习近平多次会面（包括此前北京与白宫），双边层面也有经贸与其他议题的持续互动。

习近平“收获国际地位”并非这次独有。
作为东道主主办APEC并促成首次三方会谈，确实提升了平台效应，但这是持续外交布局的一部分，而非突然翻盘。习近平此前也在其他国际场合（包括白宫访问等）展现过类似角色，国际地位的累积是长期过程。

普京“打破外交孤立”也不是首次。
普京近年持续出席金砖、上合等机制，与中国保持高频互动，并非完全被孤立后突然重返。此次三方会谈进一步提供了与美国直接对话的平台，确实有象征意义，但说“打破孤立”容易夸大其新奇程度。

总体来看，这场会谈的历史性主要体现在“首次三方闭门会晤”本身，以及联合宣言对核风险、能源稳定和部分国际机构管辖权的共同表述。

它没有解决乌克兰、伊朗等重大冲突的具体方案，也没有产生颠覆性战略成果，这点推文说得对。

但把东道主站中间、没有当场记者会直接解读成“习是主角、川普是配角、普京重返舞台”，确实脱离了实际外交礼仪与成果评估的基本逻辑。画面好看，不等于权力结构就此改写。后续看宣言落实与各方后续行动，比解读合影更有意义。

text:
as he went, and made additional notes as Allyra started arguing,
‘Well, yes I live on Thanata,’ Allyra’s momentum faded, ‘how do you know where I live?’
Cedric pointed to the badge on his coat,
‘I’m a detective, Detective Cedric. Now let us away to the embassy.’

Cedric began to walk at some pace, dragging Allyra along with him. None of the dock workers or fishermen, who were staring, made any attempt to help her. As Allyra’s pace shifted from a walk to a jog, Cedric widened his stride
‘Do try to keep up, woman, I don’t have all day,’ he snapped, ‘I have issues in Neferaten to be dealing with! Soon to be dead veterinarians, soon to be escaped aardvarks and the untimely death of a sheriff that is yet to happen!’

They veered off the quayside, bypassed the town and headed up an old dirt road.
‘I don’t think there is an embassy up here,’ Allyra said, pulling back at the cuff chain. Her tugging made no difference to Cedric who barely noticed,
‘There is indeed an embassy up here. Unlike you, I am not in the habit of lying’
‘What embassy?’
‘The Saparian Nicolassary.’
Allyra yanked on the cuff chain again, but to no avail,
‘This is ridiculous, Nic. Let me go.’

Cedric stopped dead. Turned to her, opened his mouth, and allowed his thick, gnarly, black tongue to lick her cheek. He then vomited an adorable spray of blue and red lumpy blood and brown bile down her leg. His drooling mouth remained open for a short time after, and Allyra who was dumbfounded with desire, caught a glimpse of his canines growing. He licked her again, which was quite disgusting since clumps of his innards clogged about his lips and dripped off of his tongue, then proceeded to march her through an avenue of trees.

At the end of the avenue stood two iron gates attached to stone pillars and on the top of each pillar giant stone carvings of Nicolas were erected. The jackets of each statue were freshly painted yellow and black plaid with a hint of burgundy. The gates, which were broken, hung carelessly on their hinges and only had the adjacent sign, which was painted in blood and housed on the pillars, to talk to. The sign read, ‘Beware all ye who enter here.’
‘That’s very charming,’ Allyra muttered.
Cedric ignored her, and dragged her up the cracked, moss covered path to the doors of an old derelict house. The windows were boarded, the stones crumbled, and a turret that looked quite out of place stood to the north of the building. Above the door was a sign that read, ‘The Nicolassary.’

Nicolas had embassies in every town, port, village, forest, rural district and hamlet throughout the Deep. He even built embassies where construction planning had not yet been granted. Each embassy was managed by a designated Nicolai of the fourth horde, who were all called Theaten, with the exception of the Nicolassary in Sapari. Nicolas only trusted Nicolai to run the Nicolassaries. This measure ensured that no scandal occurred, and it also ensured that no funny business occurred with regards to book-keeping. Entry to any Nicolassary was forbidden without a Nicolai chaperone, of course, no one knew what a Nicolai was which did not matter since no one but the clinically insane wanted to hang around Nicolas’s embassies anyway.

In 1500 P.V. Theaten had proposed building his own embassies for the Kingdom of D’Aten. Nicolas replied that it was quite the fashion to keep one’s embassies within one’s own kingdom, and Theaten, who only cared about appearances, did just that.

Cedric rang the large bell, and both waited ten minutes for a response. Cedric spent this time licking Allyra, which she did not care for, sniffing her, which she did not care for and stroking her hair, which irritated her. She tried pushing him away several times, but it just seemed to encourage him.

Eventually the door opened of its own accord, and a zombified ghoul in a tuxedo stood in the crevice looking bored,
‘Yes?’ Chives growled.
Cedric uncuffed Allyra and shoved her through the door,
‘Chives, she’s all yours.’
Chives did not answer Cedric, as that would mean acknowledging him. Instead, he closed the door and addressed Allyra,
‘The emissary has been expecting you,’ Chives pulled out a pocket watch, ‘and you are quite late.’
‘How can I be late? I didn’t plan on coming here at all.’
Chives shrugged,
‘The master planned on you coming here, and now you are late. I shall show you into the offices. Follow me.’

Allyra followed Chives up the uneven and partially rotted staircase, watching her step all the way, and along a narrow, and even more uneven corridor which had ghastly red and mildew wallpaper dripping from the walls. As they reached the end of the corridor, Chives stopped,
‘I take it you are the future Mrs DeSilva?’
‘I most certainly am not. I am here for one reason and one reason only; your idiot master has been following me around making up stories,’ Allyra replied.
Chives’ eyes widened,
‘Madam, you cannot call his lordship names.’
Allyra just shrugged and waited. Chives eventually opened a side door,
‘Safety officer Felippe is the emissary for Sapari, he likes to be close to the mines because the rock monster keeps him company. I cannot talk to the safety officer, because he is not Nicolas, but you can.’
Allyra pursed her lips,
‘Mmmhmm. Rock monsters. Not Nicolas. Right.’
Chives ignored her tone, and instead did his utmost to help Nicolas’s bride,
‘Tell him your worries and he will try his best to assist.’
‘Is he sane?’ Allyra asked.
‘Madam, he is as sane as myself and the master.’
‘Great.’

Allyra followed Chives into the office only to be met with another man who looked like, you have guessed it, Nicolas! Only this Nicolai was wearing a bright yellow and black plaid safety helmet with a lit candle stuck on the front,
‘Welcome Madam, I am Safety Officer Felippe of the Thanata Felippes, the ones associated with mining of course, not the racket ball crowd. They are quite another brand of Felippe, I am afraid. How can I help you?’
‘You can stop following me please,’ Allyra explained, not unreasonably.
Nicolai-Felippe considered her request, looked through the notes on his desk, then offered a solution,
‘I am the officer on duty, and I can offer you one lecture out of three, we are not a charity you know? Today’s lessons include geology, topography, and the culture and psychology of Fluorotetraferriphlogopite.’
‘What? What?’ Allyra stammered, ‘I don’t want to hear about what metamorphic rocks chat about, or rock therapy, I just want you to leave me alone and stop following me. I’m not marrying you. I’m not dating you. Leave me alone. You’re going to do enough damage to my life…’

Allyra sat in the oversized chair opposite Felippe and Felippe stared at her dumbfounded,
‘I have no idea what you are talking about, woman. Chives do you know what she is talking about?’

Chives did not answer, which made Allyra laugh,
‘Can you not see him?’ She asked.
‘Who, Madam?’
‘Nicolas.’
‘Oh, I see, you want to speak to Nicolas,’ Chives muttered.
Allyra dropped her head into her hands,
‘Yes, I want to speak to Nicolas. For Irkalla’s sake, what is wrong with you people?’
‘Follow me, Mrs DeSilva.’
‘I’m not Mrs DeSilva or Mrs anyone,’ she cried as she rose from her chair.
‘Wait!’ Felippe interjected, mirroring her movement, ‘Before you depart…’
Felippe did not complete his sentence, instead he stalked around the table and stopped close to Allyra’s face. He breathed in deeply through his nose, then released his tongue, allowing it to crawl about her throat and lips. Allyra closed her eyes and waited until the rough damp sensation stopped. When she opened them Felippe had gone.
‘Now you may follow me,’ Chives explained.

Allyra groaned, but followed Chives, nonetheless.
‘This is Nicolas’s office,’ he said signalling to a large door at the opposite end of the corridor, ‘but he does not accept visitors as he is too important.’
Allyra really did not care at this point what Nicolas did or did not accept, or what game he was playing, and pushed the door open, sending Chives flying in the process.

Nicolas was sitting at his desk. He was no longer in his appalling disguise, instead round reading spectacles adorned his nose, and he appeared more refined in his confidence and frame. He was writing quietly. drawing his quill across parchment in one of his great skin-bound books.
‘I am sorry, Sir,’ Chives began, as he tried to grab Allyra’s hand, ‘Mrs DeSilva is being very difficult. She must have had another bad day.’
‘Am I living in an alternate reality or something?’ Allyra asked, her frustration wedged in her throat, ‘I already told you that I’m not Mrs DeSilva.’
Chives placed his hand on hers,
‘And she is confused too!’
Allyra knocked his hand away.
‘Nic!’ She snapped, ‘Stop following me, it’s against the rules. The dressing up or costumes or whatever it is, just stop. Just leave me alone.’

Nicolas placed his quill slowly onto the parchment, slid back in his chair and placed his hands behind his head,
‘Costumes? I have no idea of what you speak. Do you Chives?’ Nicolas asked.
‘No, Sir, not a clue.’
Allyra looked from Nicolas to Chives and back again,
‘So, you are talking to him now?’ She asked Chives.
‘I always talk to the master.’
Allyra tutted and ignored the deranged old ghoul,
‘Can I go now, Nic?’
‘I neither brought you here, Madam, nor stopped you from leaving…’
‘I’m not arguing with you, Nic.’
Nicolas smiled. Not because of the amusing games he was playing, nor because of Allyra’s more amusing reaction, but because he liked her calling him Nic. However, she had also shown some very concerning symptoms.

Nicolas pulled a notebook from his drawer, dipped the quill in the inkpot and started to write, whilst verbalising his thoughts,
‘Does not know that she is engaged, highly aggressive, convinced she is living in a different reality.’ Nicolas looked from Allyra to Chives, ‘Chives, you may leave us.’

Chives nodded and slowly backed out of the door.
‘Come around to my side of the desk,’ Nicolas said softly, whilst smiling. Allyra hesitated, ‘come. I won’t hurt you.’ Allyra walked slowly and cautiously to Nicolas. His hands clasped her hips, and he pulled her onto his lap. Allyra tried to stand again, but he locked his arms about her just tight enough to prevent her escape,
‘I am, as you shall see, a generous lord, and I have made an offer to you which I do not make lightly. I am offering you an exit. An early exit.’
Allyra looked up at Nicolas,
‘You’re offering a prison cell in an asylum.’
‘I am offering you a home, and an eternity with my glorious self. Safe. If you choose this option now it will be easier for you. I promise my offer is sincere.’
Allyra stroked Nicolas’s cheek with the back of her fingers, almost feeling sorry for him,
‘It is still a cage.’
‘Madam, I don’t think you understand the reality of the situation, you will be my wife whether you like it or not. In due course you will come to Corax, I will declare you insane, and no one will be any the wiser. If you are insane, of course, I can do with you as I will. However,’ Nicolas gulped, ‘I want you to choose me freely instead.’
‘Why me?’ Allyra asked.
‘That’s not your business. All you need to know is that my offer is sincere.’

Allyra wriggled within Nicolas’s grip, causing him to become obviously excited. Neither mentioned the issue that sat between them.
‘I will take my chances and decline your kind offer.’
Nicolas sighed,
‘I am saddened to hear that. I am more than saddened, I am deeply wounded. Poor Nicolas.’
‘This is nuts, I only met you a few hours ago. What are you on about?’
Nicolas tightened his grip,
‘Nicolas is sad, but he has not given up. He shall woo you in a more traditional manner.’
‘That’s great. Can I go?’
‘Nicolas is heartbroken,’ Nicolas continued, ‘but he shall prevail. Nicolas always wins.’
Allyra waited for his fake sad face to pass, then spoke again,
‘Nic, can we pick this discussion up again, I have a few people to meet and some business to attend to.’
‘Madam, I would not wish to infringe upon you in anyway, but may I ask, are you meeting a man friend perhaps?’
‘I have a gentleman who has been in my life some five years. He is working in Neferaten today, but I promised to meet him tonight. We have an… Arrangement.’
Nicolas squinted, forcing Allyra to elaborate,
‘We have an open relationship.’
‘Ahhh,’ Nicolas nodded, ‘And what is the gentleman’s name?’
‘Chester, The Cat.’

Nicolas did not seem remotely annoyed by this, in fact the soft smile on his face suggested he was almost pleased. Or gloating,
‘The Pied Piper. Yes. I have heard of him. Very popular with the ladies. Legendary. You must be very special if he has stuck around for five years.’
‘I’m sorry, Nic.’
‘You probably will be. I have already told you the outcome of this matter, it is only the route that will be affected. It seems you wish to take a more difficult pathway.’
Allyra tilted her head,
‘You don’t get told no very often, do you?’

Nicolas stared at Allyra. It was not a comfortable stare, but an icy cold glare. He did not blink. He did not move but sat quite rigidly, and turgidly, beneath her. His grip remained oppressive, then his eyes rolled upwards, and he stayed that way for ten minutes. The whispers growled around Allyra and again she ignored them.

At first, Allyra tried to shift off of his lap, but his arms were quite resolved to keeping her in position. Allyra watched the clock on the wall. Its hands moved rhythmically, then stuttered, and then returned to the original dance. After precisely ten minutes Nicolas’s eyes floated back into position,
‘You were saying?’ He asked as if nothing peculiar had happened.
‘I was saying no.’
Nicolas smirked, then his eyes rolled back into his head again, and this time he held the pose for twenty minutes. Allyra puffed out an exacerbated breath of air and reverted to looking at the clock again. The hands stopped, fidgeted, then moved in reverse. Allyra sighed and waited for the Nicolas show to finish its act.

Eventually, Nicolas returned to insanity and asked again,
‘You were saying Madam?’
Allyra bit her lip,
‘I said nothing.’
‘And an improvement it is!’
Allyra tried to struggle free again, but Nicolas tightened his grip,
‘Why are you doing this, Nic?’ Allyra asked.
‘Doing what?’
‘Following me.’
Nicolas groaned under his breath,
‘Madam, I already told you, I am courting. Perhaps when you return to Corax, Dr Smythe can test your hearing.’
‘I can hardly return to somewhere I have never been.’
Nicolas continued to stare at her. His tongue then escaped from his mouth and scrubbed a nasty long lick around her face,
‘Of course you can return. You cannot not return as it would be detrimental to the science of linguistics.’
‘You have not answered my question, Nic, and don’t keep licking me. I’m not a pot roast.’
‘You may be yet!’ Nicolas exclaimed, his voice vibrant and animated, ‘or a spit roast.’
‘That’s a horrible thing to say.’

Nicolas leaned his head into Allyra’s chest,
‘One last chance. Come home to Corax with me and let us forget all this legal nonsense.’
Allyra could not decide if Nicolas was serious or setting a trap, or both,
‘I have a prior engagement in Sapari.’
‘And where might this engagement be occurring?’
‘The Tavern,’ Allyra frowned, ‘why do you talk like that?’
‘Of what are you speaking?’ Nicolas replied.
‘Never mind.’

Allyra looked over Nicolas’s face, he was not unattractive, but he was certainly not what one would call handsome. His hair was excessively oily, masking the natural streaks of auburn. His face was not much better. He had a nasty blood stain clamped to his lower left lip, and a film of dirt suffocating his skin. His cheeks were nicely angled, and his eyes shone a sympathetic emerald.

Allyra could not help but touch Nicolas’s hair, mostly out of curiosity,
‘Is that lard in your hair?’ She asked.
‘Grade-A thesapien lard, yes indeed,’ Nicolas smiled.
Allyra cast her eye over Nicolas’s suit. The clothes were obviously new but did nothing to hide the noxious airs that floated about him.

As if reading her thoughts, the window sprung open welcoming in a breeze of fresh air. Allyra inhaled with a sense of relief, but once again any relief was short-lived. A swarm of flies had taken it upon themselves to follow the breeze into the building and were instantly attracted to Nicolas’s raw scent. The flies buzzed about his hat with quite a determination to secure his attention. Nicolas did not move. Allyra attempted to waft the flies away with her hand, but the flies were adamant about remaining and stood in protest on the rim of Nicolas’s top hat. Allyra wondered if Nicolas could see properly,
‘Nic, you’re attracting flies.’
Nicolas snorted in a most repulsive and slimy manner,
‘Madam, I am dealing with your enquiry at present, the flies must wait their turn like everyone else.’
‘It’s not very nice, is it?’
Nicolas snorted again, chewed whatever nastiness he had snorted in his mouth, then slid his tongue over Allyra’s lips. She grimaced,
‘Why though?’

Since Allyra had not reacted in the usual horrified manner of the ladies of the Deep and responded to his attentions with the smack of a broom or succumb to some horrific accident, Nicolas decided that she must be more in love with him than he had imagined and decided to gift her with the romantic cherry on the cake. He sucked in a mouthful of air, swallowed it, and tensed his stomach and jaw.
‘What are you doing now?’ Allyra asked, even though something inside her told her not to encourage him. With that Nicolas heaved, then heaved again. Allyra tried to unpick his fingers, but it was too late. A projectile spray of dark red, mushy blood vomited from his mouth and soaked his potential mate. Allyra opened her mouth to protest, and another spray belted her in the face, splattering her teeth and gums. She wiped her lips and mouth with her fingers and wiped the vomit from her eyes. Since she had not slapped Nicolas, he assumed she was giving him a huge come-on and relieved his belly of another tank full of vomit-blood.

Allyra rocked on his lap, which thickened the girth pressing against her ass. She rubbed the vomit from her face and chest, but this simply caused it to stain and spread. Nicolas smiled, happy with his romantic offerings,
‘I have decided that you may attend the tavern tonight for a short time, and I will seek you out for further courting later today, and also tonight.’
‘You have decided, have you?’
‘No need to thank me. I am a gracious lord, providing you are amicable to my good selves.’

Allyra sighed,
‘So, we have moved from third person singular to first person plural?’
‘Indeed, we have. Now that we know each other more intimately, we feel we can be ourselves.’
Allyra thought for a moment, and decided to use Nicolas’s bizarre admiration to her advantage,
‘Nic?’
‘Yes.’
‘Are you going to kill me like the others? Is this part of what you do?’
Nicolas’s eyes widened, and his jaw dropped,
‘Indeed no. How could you even think such a thing?’
‘Because that is the purpose of this whole charade, isn’t it?’
Nicolas took a moment to lick her again, dripping more rancid, dribble and blood over her skin,
‘I do not care for the charade. We have chosen our bride. Nicolas will not let anything happen to her because Nicolas would be sad and that is what matters.’

A long silence fell upon the room. Nicolas spent the silence tilting his head whilst staring at Allyra. He shifted beneath her, primarily because inflexible things were getting a little uncomfortable, then the muttering started,
‘Felippe, go to the mirror,’ he said, ‘take one of the tributes from the embassy’s dungeon… Of course not this side. The other side. No, the other side.’ Nicolas tutted, sighed and then added, ‘Hurry up about it.’ He then smirked at Allyra, who had resolved not to give the Nicolas show anymore attention, and said, ‘Does the lady have any objections to a small dalliance?’
‘A dalliance?’
‘Yes,’ Nicolas said as one arm loosened and his hand dropped between her legs.
‘It isn’t permitted,’ Allyra replied.
Nicolas leaned forward as his fingers gently brushed against her,
‘I won’t mention it to anyone!’
‘Nic, I am not sleeping with you,’ Allyra said through deepening breaths.

Nicolas’s fingers pressed harder and his lips brushed against her neck,
‘Of course you are not,’ he added as his mouth rose to meet hers. His hand withdraw, loosened her trousers and drifted down the front of her thong. Allyra involuntarily parted her legs, and the weight of her body pressed into the arm securing her.

Behind the office’s two-way mirror, in a small secret room, Felippe sat on a throne facing the mirror. The tribute that accompanied him knelt between his legs and he lowered his trousers, forcing his cock into her readily open mouth. His fingers grasped her hair and he used the motion of his hand to direct her oral gait.

Nicolas glanced at the mirror and smiled. His middle finger bled into Allyra’s need and he strummed it up and down, increasing the pace until every last element of Allyra’s resistance left her body. He then peeled the trousers off of her flesh and pushed her body supine across the width of his desk, so that her head hung over the edge. His mouth found her with haste, replacing the errant finger. His tongue locked onto her flesh, lengthened and circled her causing her to moan, cry out, then writhe against his hunger.

Felippe’s wrist increased in both pressure and speed, forcing the tribute to take him deeper into her throat. Felippe felt it. Nicolas felt it. Both could taste the musky scent of their future bride.

Nicolas’s finger found its way inside of Allyra and she pressed against it, then another followed, and a third. Allyra shook under his touch,
‘Fuck me, Nic,’ she pleaded. Nicolas did not respond, opting instead to maintain the current motion of both his tongue and his hand. His body moved rhythmically as if being pumped into an invisible guest. He groaned. Felippe groaned. Nicolas flicked the index finger of his free hand at the mirror and Felippe pulled himself from the tribute’s mouth. He dragged her to her feet and pressed her face against the glass before entering her with a spiteful and harsh thrust.

Allyra wrapped her legs about Nicolas’s neck and rolled her hips backwards and forwards with each lick,
‘Please, Nic, take me.’
Nicolas had no intention of being commanded to do anything and was quite happy where he was. Allyra groaned again and her body clenched around Nicolas’s fingers.

Felippe held the back of the tribute’s neck and slammed in and out of her at haste. His teeth tore chunks of flesh from her neck and shoulders as his excitement built. The experience reverberated within Nicolas. He could taste the tribute’s blood just as he could taste Allyra.

As Allyra’s moaning filled the embassy, Chives quietly opened the door, drank in the scene for a while, then closed it again.

Felippe pressed his weight down on the tribute’s shoulders and she dropped to the floor. His body sprawled across hers. The palms of his hands pressed into the wooden boards. His face elongated. Nicolas’s face elongated, but Allyra did not notice. Felippe pushed his own body weight up, and his massive form arched over the still living body of his victim. Savagely, his teeth ripped chunks from the tribute’s cheek, her back, her arms and her delightful neck. She tried to scream, but talons ripped the vocal cords from her throat before any sound was released. They were consumed at haste and his teeth returned to her body.

Allyra’s stomach knotted and waved. She moved more aggressively and wantonly against her nemesis’s mouth, quite forgetting her dignity and position. Nicolas’s tongue lengthened further and knotted about her entirety.

Felippe’s talons drifted to the tribute’s sternum. The strong nails pressed inward breaking through the flesh. They hooked beneath either side of her rib cage as Felippe shifted to a kneeling position. His prey was dragged upwards. He gripped her ribs and yanked outwards tearing them open and wrenching them from her body.

Nicolas could not hold back. His hand and tongue worked Allyra harder. Her body clenched and ached. She tried to resist the painful climax, but nothing could stop it. The electric pulses raged through her and she yelled Nicolas’s name through gritted teeth as she surrendered herself to his touch.

The tribute shook and trembled. She gasped for air. Her eyes lost their shine, and as the last light left her body both Felippe and Nicolas spent their pent up fury.

Felippe despised waste, it was an environmental travesty, so, as Nicolas licked his lips and fingers clean, Felippe ate the remains of his tribute. Once Nicolas had finished snacking on whatever was coating his hand, he pulled The Busty Bride from his inside pocket and turned the pages whilst Allyra dressed herself.

‘Mmmm, yes. No, I don’t think so,’ Nicolas muttered.
Allyra secured her trousers and sat on the desk,
‘What’s the matter with you now?’
