text:
Her bare feet, blistered from a combination of electric shocks and Webster’s flooring, throbbed and stung with each step. Mirrors pulsated and moved about her as she darted through the labyrinth; a rabbit in an alien warren. Screams cried out from within the void of the glass. Some mirrors were devoid of her reflection, others distorted it into hideous creatures. Behind each creature another inmate screamed and writhed against their bondage.

‘Look how the bunny hops,’ Nicolas’s voice echoed. She turned but could not see him.
‘Run rabbit, run rabbit, run rabbit, run rabbit.’ Archie’s voice pulsed in a sombre rhythm.

The pain in Lucia’s feet shifted to an agonising throb. Her whimpers excited Nicolas. She entered another passage gilded with mirrors. She veered right and left, constantly checking behind her. She pressed against the mirrors, hoping and praying for a secret exit. Her breath quickened. She could not see the monsters. She turned and walked backwards, then, once she was assured that they were far behind her she turned again. Her chest thudded against something hard, Nicolas’s body,
‘Boo!’ He mocked, driving the hare back.
‘This is quite fun, isn’t it?’ Demize chuckled, gliding over her.
‘She definitely has more spirit that our last lady, but I can’t wait to see our bride run!’ Nicolas replied. That comment was at least half true.

The music ceased. Lucia spun out of the glass rooms and into a corridor full of clocks, each louder and clunkier than the last. None told the exact same time. Some thesapiens lay alive but drained on gurneys randomly scattered about the hall. Lucia looked up and down, the realisation hit her, the Electi really had given her no understanding of the Immortalis. She was taught that they were nobility of the vampire classes. She had never been prepared for the level of cruelty she had experienced under Nicolas’s hand, nor the power wielded by him.

The Pauci Electi, being old men quite removed from reality, based everything they knew on tomes written by previous old men who were also on a different wavelength to everyone else, and their equally foolish predecessors who had misinformed them. A lot of the information shared with the Immolesses was, Lucia found to her detriment, not only misguided, but inherently wrong. Indeed, she had noted the latter observation when chained to Nicolas’s breaking wheel by Chester before being dumped in the dungeons. Irkalla, it seemed, revelled in suffering and taking, in accordance with its cold, bloodless ledger.

Lucia eventually found a small, rear spiral stairwell, one she attributed, wrongly of course, to servant usage. She hurried down the steps hoping to find an exit. Another corridor met her below, and this corridor was also adorned with clocks.

She did not notice the sneaky side room until she was passing by it. Her feet stopped dead. Twenty-seven Nicolases sat around a large oak table covered in tribute remains, each sipping individual glasses of thick red blood. They all turned to her, the blood dripping down their chins, and raised their glasses in a toast. She shuddered and forced herself to run further into the heart of Corax, in spite of the gaping blisters on her feet which had stretched into cuts and oozed with every step.

The clocks stopped, then all chimed at once in one monotonous groan. Lucia covered her ears. The chimes beat against her eardrums, accompanied by the howls of the inmates as another surge of electricity bounced wildly from cell to cell.

The music resumed. This time it was one repetitive chord on a poorly tuned piano. The Nicolai sipped again on their wine.

Nicolas used his secret corridors to pursue Lucia rather than disturb the feeding horde. As he danced through the narrow corridors he opened his pocket watch. Webster spoke through its mirror,
‘Is this going to go on all day?’
Nicolas admired his beauty in the bespoke mirror, alongside Webster, seemingly in no rush to pursue Lucia through the maze that was Corax.
‘Who knows?’ Nicolas chimed in response. ‘Am I boring you?’
‘You are boring him! Webster the killjoy!’ Demize spluttered from behind Webster’s image, ‘Webster has places to be, quite the man about town.’
‘Do you have somewhere else to be?’ Nicolas asked.
‘My lab!’ Webster responded, ‘Unless you want the horses unmanageable.’
‘Ten more minutes!’ Nicolas replied.
Webster frowned holding his hand to his chin,
‘I must insist, Nicolas, that you resolve this now!’

Lucia inadvertently ran from the corridor into an alcove that led into the chapel. The chapel was a crumbling, decimated mess filled with overturned chairs, old golden icons, and a decaying pulpit. In the centre, however, stood a well-maintained sarcophagus. One word was etched into it, ‘Elena.’ Lucia breathed a sigh of relief. Her destiny stood before her. She had trained to usurp the Immortalis by releasing the ghost of Ducissa Elena, the true owner of Corax, and now the opportunity presented itself.

Rumour had it that Nicolas had tricked Elena out of her rightful ownership of Corax and had had her killed. No one could prove it. No one tried to, but Lucia was taught that bringing the ghost forth in all of its vengeance and glory would redress Nicolas’s power. This was not true; it was just nonsense made up by The Electi. The Electi were not concerned with truth, they were concerned with the rituals required to keep the population happy, and that their tithes and taxes were paid.

Lucia closed her eyes and laid her hands on the sarcophagus. She breathed in deeply and focused on Elena. Her head throbbed. Her pulse sang. She directed all of her energies on touching hands with Elena and releasing her spirit. In the darkness of her mind, she could see a swirling white form. The form stepped closer, surely this was the ghost of Elena. It was an extraordinary sight; a woman, a beautiful image of forlorn white wisps, and pale lashes and lips. Her eyes were melancholy and downturned. Lucia stretched out her arms to the seemingly benevolent spirit. Elena reached back, a tear rolled down her cheek. Lucia stretched harder, her head thumping, but as much as she reached out their fingers just could not meet.

From the darkness a head dropped down between the two beings. Nicolas’s auburn hair hung wildly, but the top hat remained unmoved. He slowly spun between them as if suspended upside down from an invisible rope. Lucia gasped, pounded by awe and dread. Nicolas stopped spinning and locked eyes with her,
‘Madam, I have been informed that we must hurry this along, so if you wouldn’t mind!’ He tapped his cane against her forehead in an unnecessarily rough manner.

Lucia was instantly thrust into her senses and fell backwards, sprawling on the floor of the chapel. Nicolas sat on Elena’s tomb smiling,
‘Did you really think I would keep my fair patron in a coffin with her name on it?’ He huffed, ‘The Electi really are slacking. Last centuries Immolesses made a lot more effort! But, I guess, we get what we pay for!’
‘You don’t pay!’ Demize cackled.
‘And we don’t get either,’ Nicolas pointed out, ‘It’s becoming a chore. I really must write to The Electi.’ He turned to the mirrors hanging on the chapel’s west wall, ‘Webster, make a note, write a letter of complaint about sloppy social engineering to Solis.’
Webster nodded, but did not bother writing it down, as he knew Nicolas would soon lose interest and find something else to be distracted with.

Lucia attempted to stand,
‘SIT!’ Two voices roared from Nicolas’s mouth. An invisible weight forced Lucia to the stone floor.

Webster watched Nicolas as Nicolas debated with himself about the next course of action. Archie had lost interest entirely and was busy prodding the inmates in the cells with the point of his compass. He would experience Lucia’s fall vicariously through Nicolas anyway.

Nicolas’s waffling continued, and this muttering soliloquy soon became tiresome, so Webster interjected,
‘Horses, Nicolas!’ He snapped, ‘If they don’t get their inhibitors, we will have vampire horses running rampant, and complete anarchy. AGAIN!!’
‘I heard you the first time,’ Nicolas scoffed.
‘Let me remind you, Nicolas, that if that happens that nice supply of Togaduine red-headed tributes you like to make last will dry up, and you will sink into one of your moods.’

Nicolas frowned, clicked his fingers, then crouched down and pushed his face close to Lucia’s,
‘He is, of course correct.’
Lucia opted not to ask who Nicolas was talking to, as any interaction seemed to cause his moods to swing.

Lucia could neither see nor hear Webster as Nicolas had, some three weeks previously, mesmerised Allyra not to see Demize or Webster with the intention of causing her later confusion. The endeavour amused him so much that he extended the privilege to Lucia and Stacia.

‘Nicolas,’ a voice roared. Nicolas turned, and Meatcleaver Pierre bounded into the chapel, ‘hurry up. We ‘ave ze new tributes incoming and I need ze inventory of who is on ze newbie menu for tonight!’
‘Fine,’ Nicolas sighed.

Nicolas returned his attention to Lucia,
‘We had better move this circus along.’
‘Make her walk the tight rope,’ Demize grinned.
‘We don’t have a tight rope,’ Nicolas replied, ‘CHIVES! A tight rope for the theatre or the circus, butler’s choice.’
Nicolas did not even bother to see if Chives was present and just assumed that somehow his demands would be met.

Lucia attempted to drag herself away from the madness. Her feet, now beyond repair, could not carry her, so she rolled onto her front and dragged her body along the floor. Nicolas allowed her to crawl on her belly for a while, until Webster took to banging on the glass. Nicolas then, with mild irritation, as he was enjoying the spectacle, grabbed her by the ankle, pulled himself to his full height and dragged her through corridors and down the set of stairs that led to his chambers. Lucia did not welcome this uncomfortable experience as the stone steps caused a separation between parts of her scalp and her skull.

Once in his chambers, Nicolas opened a closet door and wheeled out a pulley. He then hung Lucia upside down by her knees.

‘Chives!’ Nicolas called, trying to ignore the potent, tasty blood dripping from Lucia’s head.
‘Rosemary!’ Nicolas called again, his eyes fogging with the scent of emerald. Chives was late, and Nicolas could not help himself. His teeth sunk into the hanging shoulder of his victim, and he fed voraciously. Nicolas would have preferred it if Chives put an appearance before he had to shout but was thankful for any excuse to gorge himself on blood. He also hated shouting as it drew unnecessary attention to his fine, and somewhat elusive self.

He released Lucia,
‘CHIVES!’
Nicolas pulled Lucia’s head back by her hair, forcing her to look him in the eye,
‘You just cannot get good service.’ The Long-Faced Demon in him barked at Lucia, ‘I’m sure after a very short lifetime with the Electi, you know this yourself.’

Chives entered the room with haste,
‘Yes Sir, what is it now?’
‘I don’t like his tone!’ Demize grumped. Nicolas waved a hand at the headless spectre silencing its intended roll.
‘Chives, do not summon Robert yet.’ Nicolas said, then, as Chives left the room, turned back to Lucia, ‘I had to listen to Robert moaning after the last Immoless debacle, and he made a mess of my dungeons.’ Nicolas tapped Lucia’s bloody head with his cane again and added, ‘And we don’t want a repeat of that now, do we?’

Nicolas had decided, whilst listening to Lucia’s screams as her head had hit the stone steps, that he might like to inspect her without clothes. Nicolas found clothes such an inconvenience, at least on the ladies he admired or even simply wanted to sample. He decided that Lucia was no exception to the rule, even though she was blonde. Nicolas rationalised that she could be hiding some secret weapon under what was left of her dress, and decided after weighing up all matters, to strip her.

Nicolas was in the process of removing Lucia’s gown with his talons when Chives knocked and entered his chambers putting Nicolas in a filthy mood,
‘Have you no decency, man!’ He snapped, ‘This Immoless is not dressed!’
‘Indeed Sir,’ Chives muttered, ‘However, I thought it may interest you to know that Ghorab has just relayed a message, hence my delay, for which I am truly sorry and beg for your forgiveness.’
‘Just get on with it,’ Nicolas said, swinging Lucia back and forth.

‘Bigglesworth had an incident with the third Immoless and once again she is in the sea with Rachnoc.’
Nicolas ripped off Lucia’s gown completely, discarded it on the floor, then reprimanded Lucia,
‘Don’t you think you should cover yourself up when there are gentlemen present?’
Lucia did not answer. Her head continued to bleed, and Nicolas licked the blood from her scalp.
‘The Jester thinks he’s a dog,’ Demize laughed as he sat on Chives’ head.
Nicolas stopped licking, and looked at the head,
‘You do make an excellent hat. I would wear you myself if you didn’t smell so bad.’
‘Are you talking to me, Sir?’ Chives asked.
‘Chives, we discussed you not being a hat earlier. Do try to pay attention.’

Chives ignored the Nicolai nonsense and returned to the matter in hand,
‘But getting back to the issue of the third Immoless.’
‘Yes, she is in the sea, Chives. I am not deaf.’
Demize rocked back and forward on the head of the weary henchmen,
‘You may not be deaf, but looking at that suit, you are clearly blind.’
‘I told you, this is the fashion!’ Nicolas replied, ‘Everyone will be wearing plaid soon, you will see!’
‘I stand with Demize on this one,’ Webster interjected, ‘The plaid has got to go!’
‘The plaid stays, and that is not up for discussion,’ Nicolas said whilst licking Lucia’s nipples.

‘Sir.’ Chives interrupted again. It was always an epic task to get through to Nicolas, and not one for the weak-willed or feint hearted and Nicolas was getting pithy,
‘Chives you are growing tedious now.’ He groaned, but his attention was still fixed on Lucia’s bare breasts.
‘Yes Sir,’ Chives said humbly, ‘However, Bigglesworth shot his canons before landing the ship’
‘That’s his problem, isn’t it?’
‘Ummm, not exactly, Sir, since according to the porters the Commodore said your bride mistook him for you.’
‘Oh marvellous!’ Nicolas sighed, ‘Now she thinks I’m trigger happy. That’s just great. Never mind, I will straighten this all out today with my magnificent self.’
‘Are you going to tell her about your moods, Sir?’ Chives asked. Chives found it more comfortable to refer to the Nicolai as moods as opposed to a swarm of repulsive goblins.
‘No Chives she doesn’t need to know about the Nicolai yet. I think we have done enough damage without adding more problems.’
‘Very good, Sir.’

Chives went to leave then stopped and fidgeted from one gammy foot to the other,
‘Might it not be easier just to tell her everything from the outset, Sir?’
Nicolas shook his head,
‘Don’t be absurd, Chives, you know nothing about love. Now, do we have salt?’ He asked, ignoring the ghoul’s concerns. ‘Salt, and my best carving knife.’
Chives shuffled away, muttering, and returned, muttering, with the salt and knife. Nicolas lifted the head of Lucia and shook the salt all over the deep, bleeding gashes in her scalp. The stinging sensation forced a scream from her mouth.
‘That amount of noise is unnecessary,’ Nicolas snapped. He then carved a strip of the remaining skin from her skull, dropped it into his hands and sat on the floor ramming it in his mouth,
‘Chives,’ he said, talking with his mouth full, ‘take this one back to the dungeon.’ He then turned to Webster, ‘Time to don the great disguise!’
Webster sighed and closed his eyes.

Scene VI: The Tenacious Millipede

The 2nd Day of the 4th Moon, 1536 P.V.
Sapari Port

Hector’s morning had proved quite challenging. Hector was not only Allyra’s friend, but an old, strong fisherman, whose small operation launched from Sapari Head every morning without fail. He travelled alone, as he had done for most of his life, and dragged ring nets in hope of catching a few irate fish for his lunch, some for the market, and on a good day, some surplus for tea to go with his rum. He liked cod and trout, but despised salmon because the smell reminded him of his ex-wife.

The day had been crudely interrupted by a fleet of ships needlessly and excitedly gallivanting out of the port, barging Hector out of the way, and prancing into the deep blue. The ships spent the early part of the morning gossiping on the horizon, and Hector paid them no more attention. On the plus side, the fish, that had been minding their own business, were so disgruntled by the horde of ships that they changed their course and swam towards Sapari. This pleased Hector, and by mid-morning he had more than enough cod and trout to be getting on with.

He was just about to finish up for the day and enjoy a well-earned beverage in the Sapari Tavern, when his net closed on what appeared to be quite a big catch. His wrinkled and spotted arms exploded from his slicker and made a conscious effort to reel the beast in. The beast was, however, not a fish. It was a young lady dressed in a shiny, black and revealing catsuit. Her red and black streaked hair hung to one side revealing a sharp undercut, and her heavy smoky eye make-up formed tracks down her face. Her swarthy skin glinted in the dusk light, and she clung to a large empty bottle for dear life.

Hector smiled,
‘Morning Lyra, rough night?’
Allyra looked at the bottle in her hand,
‘Must have been.’
Hector reached out his hand and Allyra grabbed it firmly. He hauled in his little demonic catch, and she vaulted into the boat.
‘You want a ride to port?’
Allyra pulled the large black bag from her back and rummaged through it, chucking her trinkets around the boat before she found her silver pocket watch. She flicked it open and gasped,
‘Yes please. I am late.’
Hector laughed as Allyra stuffed her trinkets back into her kleptobag,
‘When are you not late?’
Allyra smiled and checked her smoke tin to make sure her Ashurrel leaf had not dampened and then checked her belt-sheathes to ensure her shuriken and dagger were still in place. Once happy Allyra addressed Hector,
‘If I was early, you would not have the pleasure of my company in the Rachnoc.’
‘That’s an odd term?’ Hector observed, ‘Don’t you mean morning?’
Allyra shrugged,
‘Must still be the whiskey talking.’
‘Must be.’

The boat chudded along, turned, and headed towards land. Hector did not go out too far. He did not want to be intercepted by the miners travelling to and from Thanata, and he had heard rumours of an unruly and difficult necromancer that lived on the archipelago of Sihr beyond Thanata. Legend had it, the necromancer did not like malarkey in his waters. No one knew exactly what ‘malarkey’ consisted of, but considering Elyas ate two tributes from Thanata on a weekly basis, no one really wanted to know.

Allyra sat on the gunwale staring behind her.
‘Still dreaming of Sihr are we?’
Allyra nodded,
‘I hear the skies and sea are so clear that they almost kiss each other under the light of the two suns.’
Hector took to chopping heads off of the still living fish as they spoke, and Allyra was kind enough to assist by pressing and pulling their guts from the bodies.
‘Why do you want to go to Sihr anyway?’ Hector asked as one of the cod danced about with half his head still on. Allyra gave the cod a quick clump and he settled down,
‘To be alone. To spend my life in tranquillity without the Electi planning my death day in and day out.’
Hector lowered his head. He was old enough and wise enough to know that there was something not quite right about the breeding and sacrificing of women as if they were goats or cattle.
‘Sorry Lyra,’ he said at length.
Allyra laughed,
‘You have nothing to be sorry for, old man. Without you, I would have drifted off the map years ago. I would be halfway around the world now, probably sold as a slave to some wealthy tyrant.’
Hector did not laugh.

Allyra threw the fish guts over the side of the boat, attracting a murder of crows and an unkindness of ravens. The sea was once a place where seagulls would tread, but during The War Before the Dusk a conspiracy of ravens and crows took the opportunity to declare war on the seagulls of The Deep, and after a lengthy battle the seagulls migrated south to warmer shores. Legend had it that the ravens and crows had acquired an armoury of porcupines and, as such, had an unfair advantage. Allyra put this down to fabrication, but she was wrong.

One raven pulled away from the conspiracy and perched itself next to Allyra,
‘Hello, little fella,’ she whispered, ‘aren’t you adorable?’
She leaned her head into the raven, and the raven leaned his head to hers. Hector frowned and sighed but said nothing. Allyra’s eyes momentarily flashed white, then returned to their usual dark brown. Hector elected not to mention that either.

Allyra stroked the raven’s head and beak and asked,
‘What’s your name?’ As if he was going to answer. Hector rolled his eyes. Hector’s ex-wife Florence spoke to animals like that and it was a bad omen. One day they had a nice quaint two bedroom wee-house by the sea, the next day they had a zoo alive with cats, dogs and rats that he did not want, armadillos and aardvarks, which he really did not want, and an open-topped aquarium.

The final straw came for Hector when, one night, he was awoken by a cacophony of miaows and bangs. As he walked towards the gas light, to illuminate the subject, something squidgy splooshed between his toes. Once the light was lit, he saw a still flapping koi, that should not have been in a fish tank of any kind, splattered all over his feet. That very same day both Florence and her dowry were dispatched to Corax Asylum where she was rapidly declared insane, just as Hector thought, and Drs Demus, Smythe and Riesigerschwanz committed her to a day in the brazen bull. The creatures were given to the children who were poncing around Sapari on All Hallow’s Eve, and Hector never followed up about the success or failure of the therapy. In later years Nicolas did visit Hector, but with regards to quite another matter.

The raven opted not to tell Allyra its business and flew away in disgust at the constant questioning. As the raven disappeared, the small boat chugged into port. It moped along, feeling a little depressed, in the shadows of the trawlers, and found its way to the derelict end of the port where the shipwreck Solis sat.

Allyra looked up the quayside,
‘The doctor’s office is gone!’ She observed.
‘Hmm?’ Hector replied.
‘Dr Smythe’s office is gone. It looks like it exploded.’
Hector cast a weary gaze up and down the port,
‘There’s no doctor’s office here, Lyra.’
‘You took me there, yesterday.’
‘Yesterday?’ Hector asked.
‘Yes, yesterday.’
‘Never been a doctor’s office on the quayside, love,’ Hector mumbled sadly as he took a swift drink of rum hoping to dodge Allyra’s persistent noise,
‘Your doctor. Dr Smythe.’
Hector shook his head,
‘You’re confused again.’

Allyra was confused.

Hector moored at a stone stairway and Allyra threw her kleptobag back on her back,
‘Thanks Hector. I’m sure we shall meet again soon.’
Hector sighed wearily,
‘I do hope so, Love.’
Allyra nodded as she leapt onto the steps muttering,
‘I feel trapped in some deja confusing fucking vu!’

The steps offered a short climb. As Allyra reached the summit, she noticed a bizarre looking man hovering around by The Solis. She knew that the Electi would already be inside drinking whatever obnoxious spirit Pater Solis, head of the Electi, had condescended to bring, and that they would not have noticed the malingerer. Most people did not malinger around The Solis as they did not want to involve themselves in Electi business. It was mainly out of fear that Nicolas might have killed one of the Electi, as he was known for doing, and they would be drawn into taking the dead man’s place.

Allyra stepped onto the quayside, then slowly walked towards the man. He was tall with broad shoulders, but far from fat. He wore a plaid jacket, which was not very fashionable, an unusually tall top hat, and burgundy silk tie over his black waistcoat. What was most unusual was the mitre that sat on top of his top hat, the obviously fake moustache, the sunglasses at dusk and the sign he was holding up that read, ‘Down with Count Pompous!’

Allyra stopped dead in front of him and looked closer. The man leaned back as if offended. Allyra circled him, then stared into his face again. Nicolas shook his sign and coughed,
‘Madam, I am here petitioning on behalf of our great lord and saviour Nicolas of Corax. Nicolas has been infested with constant complaints from the tyrannical and unduly elevated Count Pompous who sits on his ass in his gruesome tower whining about those of us who actually make an effort to bring this beloved land to great flourishment and excess with no bounds.’

Allyra narrowed her eyes,
‘What?’

‘Are you a hat?’
‘No Sir, but who are you talking to?’
‘You know full well who I am talking to, Chives, but I do like your ever-growing cantankerous demeanour.’
‘His name is Demetri, Nicolas. You know his name is Demetri, you read his resume,’ Webster sighed.
Nicolas looked Chives up and down and screwed up his nose,
‘His name is Chives.’
‘His name is Demetri…’
‘His name is CHIVES!’ Nicolas bellowed in three deep voices, ‘Case closed, end of story, moving on. And Parsley, you may leave.’
‘Very good, Sir,’ Chives replied, then shuffled out of the door, closed it, and stood close by in case the shouting started again.

‘Theaten, Robert, treats his ghoul, Klouthe, with respect,’ Webster mumbled.
Nicolas rubbed his ears,
‘WHAT?’
‘Never mind, tell us the new plan.’
‘Yes,’ Demize said as he settled on the gramophone and spun the turntable, ‘tell us.’
The needle dropped and a soft classical melody of inmate screams offered a comforting background noise to Nicolas’s ears.

‘I shall show you,’ Nicolas smirked, then yelled, ‘CHIVES!’
The ghoul knocked again and hauled himself back into Nicolas’s chambers without having been invited,
‘Yes Sir?’
‘The suit if you will.’
Chives shuffled to Nicolas’s bed, that Nicolas could quite easily have managed to walk to himself, and pulled a drawer from beneath it. He lifted a new clothing bag, unzipped it and pulled out a remarkably repulsive yellow and black plaid suit with just a hint of burgundy. The same suit he had recently procured. The same suit made to order from the milliner.

All of the best suits were made by the milliner as there had been quite a debacle between the tailor, the cobbler and the milliner that left Sapari, Nicolas’s favourite place to shop, with only a milliner who took on all three jobs.

In the second moon of 1522 P.V., Norick Stensible, a lower vampire from Sapari, was seen leaving the milliner Slaty McQuick's shop wearing a noticeably taller hat than Nicolas. No one wore a taller top hat than Nicolas. Two days later, the sign outside of the Sapari Tavern mysteriously disappeared only to be replaced by the milliner's severed head. Slaty's daughter, Rua, vanished that same week.

Thereafter, no one wore a taller top hat than Nicolas, except, on occasion, Chester, but since Chester was Nicolas, Nicolas could not reasonably complain about it.

Rumours spread throughout Sapari about who had replaced the tavern sign, but Nicolas was not one to indulge in gossip and paid the speculation no attention. Following Slaty's disappearance, Emilia Victor became Sapari's new milliner.

In 1528 P.V., Nicolas commissioned Emilia Victor to make him a suit from Thesapien skin. Emilia patiently explained that she was a milliner, not a tailor, and that she certainly did not make garments from mortal skin. Nicolas regarded her response as compelling evidence of insanity and immediately ordered a psychiatric assessment. Naturally, Nicolas conducted the assessment himself, and his findings were seconded by the eminent psychiatrist Dr Riesigerschwanz. Equally naturally, Nicolas declared Emilia Victor insane before the assessment had even begun.

Her replacement was a middle-aged Thesapien woman named Claudia McBurrow, an experienced milliner who had trained in Threnodyl. Wishing to ensure she could satisfy any of Nicolas's increasingly unpredictable requests, Claudia undertook a rapid apprenticeship with the tailor Mr Occasionally Green and the cobbler Clanky Harris.

Nicolas was deeply unimpressed. He had not granted permission for the milliner to broaden her professional expertise and considered such initiative grossly presumptuous. Mr Occasionally Green disappeared shortly afterwards. Two days later, Claudia entered the tailor's workshop to find an impeccably stitched suit of Mr Green’s skin hanging from one of the mannequins.

Nicolas allowed Clanky Harris to live. He simply had Demus and Smythe remove his hands. Several weeks later, Nicolas visited the cobbler's shop intending to commission an exquisite pair of blue-and-yellow Jesus Creepers, only to discover that the business had closed permanently.

Thereafter, the milliner, Claudia, was granted permission to act as Nicolas’s tailor, cobbler and milliner, whilst retaining the title of milliner only. In view of the recent events, she made the sensible decision not to argue the matter.

Chives removed the suit from its hanger and passed it to Nicolas. Nicolas managed to struggle to put on his own clothes, like a big boy, because he did not like being touched. He especially did not like being touched by Chives as he was concerned the old ghoul’s fingers may drop off forcing Nicolas into unwanted surgical work.

Nicolas put on the black shirt and black waistcoat first. He then slid on the plaid trousers that matched the yellow, black and burgundy plaid jacket, then slowly slid the jacket on to impress his small audience. He tied a silk burgundy scarf about his neck, then adjusted the knot, and clicked at Chives to pass the new top hat.

Nicolas lowered the black hat onto his head and stared into the mirror. His reflection sat beside Webster’s smirking face and Nicolas admired himself,
‘Devastatingly handsome!’ He muttered.

He hesitated, looking again at his clean hair, ‘One adjustment.’
He removed the hat, a little quicker than he had put it on and scooped a large handful of cooking oil out of the vat left by Chives and Meatcleaver. He rubbed the oil between his fingers and worked it through his hair. Webster’s mouth opened,
‘That’s vile, Nicolai.’
Nicolas took another handful and added another layer, then gave further instruction to Chives,
‘Rosemary, you may return the vat to Meatcleaver. I’m sure he can use it for the inmates.’
Chives stumbled towards Nicolas.

‘Wait,’ Nicolas said, raising his hand, ‘this is hilarious.’ Nicolas lowered his new trousers just enough to reveal some rather unflattering plaid boxers, with equally unflattering and highly questionable stains, unzipped the fly and turned his back to his henchman.

Webster watched in disgust as Nicolas relieved his bladder into the oil. Demize snorted back a giggle. It took Nicolas some time to finish as a few sprays, drips and drops followed the primary gush,
‘Now you can take the oil to Meatcleaver. Tell him inmates only. If I find out the Nicolai are fed from that vat, Chives, guess who will be operating with only one eye?’
‘Very good Sir,’ Chives groaned, heaving the vat from the floor.
‘And don’t dally. I may need you.’
‘Very good sir,’ Chives wheezed again as he struggled out of the door.

‘What business is on the cards today?’ Webster asked, unwilling to discuss what had just occurred.
Nicolas smiled, he almost looked genuinely happy,
‘I am preparing for our nuptials.’
Webster sighed,
‘This again. Nicolas, until you improve your approach to the Immoless there will be no nuptials.’
Nicolas banged his cane on the glass,
‘There most certainly will. I have a new plan.’
Webster lowered his glasses, breathed on his side of the mirror and polished it with the cuff of his jacket,
‘And what, pray tell, is this new plan?’
‘I shall visit the third Immoless again and tell her if she marries me, I will spare her life.’
‘That’s your plan, is it?’

‘Another stupid idea to match a stupider suit!’ Demize laughed. The head lifted from the gramophone and floated above Nicolas, ‘Why did you order that suit? You look like a fool.’
Nicolas tilted his hat slightly, adjusting his hair to sit behind his ears. His ears pinged outwards in response and made him look like a teapot. Nicolas shook his head and readjusted his hair again and shifted his hat to hide the monstrous ears,
‘This suit is the height of fashion, and my plan is airtight. She cannot refuse.’
The head roared with laughter,
‘She may not, but Behmor will.’
Nicolas knew that Demize was correct, after all, Demize was the critical Nicolai, and
Behmor would only endorse legal contracts, not contracts riddled with duress and issues of capacity. Nicolas thought momentarily then raised his right index finger,
‘I will tell her not to raise the matter with him.’

Webster shook his head,
‘So, let me get this straight, your plan is to coerce the Immoless into marriage by saying if she does not marry you, you will kill her, and then you are going to force her to lie to the king of Irkalla? That’s your plan? Does that make sense to you, Nicolas?’
‘It most certainly does.’

Demize snorted and sniggered,
‘Why not take her on a date?’
‘A what now?’ Nicolas asked, leaning into the floating head.
‘To a restaurant or a theatre.’
Nicolas’s face lit up,
‘What a marvellous idea, I shall build her a theatre here in Corax.’
‘That’s absolutely not what I said!’ Demize chided as he lit another cigar with his vocal cords.
‘Yes, we shall build a theatre, and then she will fall hopelessly in love with my good taste…’
‘Are you in love with her?’ Webster interrupted, ‘Are we in love with her?’
‘That’s neither here nor there, I am sick of being…’ Nicolas stopped talking and returned to fiddling with his hair and ears.

Demize floated around Nicolas’s head, glaring at him,
‘He can’t say it. He can’t say what we all know to be true. Nicolas is…’
Nicolas’s cane swatted Demize before he could complete his sentence. The head flew across the bed chamber, shattered against the bars at the window, fell to the floor, and then drew itself back together,
‘Haha! Missed!’

Nicolas ignored the head, and resumed part of the conversation,
‘What we need for the theatre is a great play written by our good selves, and of course we need the theatre itself. Perhaps we shall build it in the chapel. The chapel isn’t put to any good use anyway, and…’ Nicolas said as he swayed from side to side, ‘We need a flying serial killer with skills in the thespian arts.’
Webster nodded, a little intrigued,
‘Do you know where we can get one?’
‘I know of one. I will find out his whereabouts.’
‘And who will build the theatre?’ Demize asked.
Nicolas thought for a moment then began yelling,
‘Chives! Chives!’
‘His name,’ Webster interrupted, ‘Is Demitri, as you full well know.’
‘His name is Chives.’ Nicolas snapped, ‘CHIIIIIVVVVEEES. Why don’t you take the cotton buds out of your four-eyed, bug ears and listen for once!’

The only reply forthcoming was a knock at the door.
‘Entaaarrr,’ Nicolas hummed.
Chives creaked the door open and slopped into the chamber,
‘You called, Sir?’
‘Yes, indeed I did. I have a few commissions that might interest you, well one commission broken into three parts.’ Chives was not interested, but Nicolas continued anyway, ‘We would like the chapel turned into a theatre, I am sure you and Archie can do that. Hire some builders from The Kingdom of Tepes, it will annoy Count Pompous and send Bink my way so he can work on the script. Oh, and I will speak to you again about catching a flying serial killer, but let’s not rush ahead of ourselves, we have much work to do.’

‘We, Sir?’
Nicolas turned and narrowed his eyes at Chives. Chives not acknowledging the Nicolai beyond table sittings was starting to cause annoyance. He was obliged to speak to the chef, Meatcleaver, as Nicolas told him that he would spend a century wearing his balls for earrings if he did not. He even tolerated the clusters sitting at meals, but otherwise he only really spoke to Chester.

Nicolas huffed,
‘Yes, we Chives, since there are three of us.’ Chives ignored the rotting head and the devious reflection, and changed the subject,
‘Is this for the future Mrs DeSilva?’
‘It most certainly is, Chives.’
‘Sir, have you ever come across the term consent?’ Chives asked, scratching his chin.
‘Of course I have, man, I’m not an imbecile. It is a nonsense word created by The Vigilante Milkmaids to castrate us. I will not be castrated, and nor will Webster. Demize is shit out of luck, but the rest of us stand firm on this matter, and I mean hard!’
‘Very good Sir, you clearly know what you are doing, given all of your previous successes.’
The cane was launched at Chives’s face before he could duck causing Demize to let out a cheer,
‘Bullseye! Your aim never fails to amuse, Nicolas.’
‘Another excellent idea, I should demonstrate my knife throwing skills on the Immoless.’
Demize frowned, and a pair of dark glasses appeared on his head and dropped to his nose,
‘Again, not what I said.’
‘She will be impressed by my prowess and drop to her knees…’
‘Nicolas, stop,’ Webster ordered softly, ‘we have one end goal, Plan BAT, and if you get over-excited, the plan will fail, like all of the other plans. You need to reel it in a bit.’

Nicolas’s lower lip jutted out, and he threw himself on his bed with his hands behind his head,
‘Any news on the second Immoless, Chives?’
‘Yes Sir, I thought I might release her into the hall of mirrors when the first Immoless leaves us and get Chester on the case when he returns from Neferaten.’
‘Good old Ches,’ Nicolas smiled, ‘The Pied Piper always catches the beaver. That man has got the most prolific flute you know?’
‘Yes, you have mentioned it, Sir.’
‘Ladies like a big flute, Chives.’
‘Indeed, Sir.’

Nicolas turned his attention from waving his metaphorical cock at Chives to eyeing Demize’s dark glasses, he raised his hand again and leapt from the bed, dancing. Chives changed the music to the sound of tributes being lashed, and Webster sent four bolts of electricity through the cells and dungeons and allowed the screams to echo through the two-way speaker he had devised for Nicolas’s bedside table.

‘Nicolas?’ Webster asked, interrupting his poor dance skills.
‘Yes?’
‘How exactly does a repulsive plaid suit trigger Plan BAT and attract the Immoless, it’s hardly peacock material?’
‘It’s better than that orange and green mess he was wearing,’ Demize hummed.
‘Firstly,’ Nicolas began, ‘the plaid suit is to show off my god-like physique, secondly the suit comes with a cunning disguise.’
He sauntered over to his desk, opened a drawer and pulled out a small black box, then returned to the mirror opening the box as he moved.

Nicolas took out a pair of round-rimmed dark glasses and a fake moustache that looked a little bit like a French slug. He popped on the glasses, then clawed at a small tube of superglue in an attempt to get the lid off, his black leather gloves, however, inhibited the conquest.

After a while Nicolas opened his mouth and allowed his canines to extend into ghastly fangs. The fangs bit at the tube and glue squirted onto Nicolas’s tongue. Demize lit another cigar,
‘Fool!’
Nicolas wiped the glue from his tongue, and applied it to his top lip, then added the moustache.

‘Fangth in or fangth out?’ Nicolas asked.
‘For what?’ Webster queried.
‘To theduth the Immoleth.’
‘Oh! Definitely fangs out.’
‘Thath what I thought.’
Webster peered over his glasses,
‘Yes, that way the Immoless can see what an absolute weeble you really are.’
Nicolas’s expression dropped and the fangs retracted.

‘Look, Nicolai,’ Webster added, ‘even if you do succeed in seducing the Immoless, which I don’t have high hopes for, you still have the first two Immolesses living in the asylum. The Electi will not send a third until they know the first two matters have been resolved.’
Nicolas nodded,
‘Way ahead of you, no need to panic, these matters shall be resolved early today, and later I shall conquer the third. In fact, Robert should be on route to collect the first Immoless if I am not mistaken.’
Demize cackled,
‘He doesn’t know his own brother’s name. What a goober!’
Webster looked down,
‘Mmmm.’
‘Mmmm what?’ Nicolas asked as he removed the moustache along with a thick layer of skin from his upper lip.
‘I was on watch before you returned and the first Immoless was complaining about the cold.’
Nicolas shook his head,
‘We can’t have that, can we? The comfort of our guests is at the centre of Corax’s manifesto.’ He raised a finger and pointed to the slimy ceiling,
‘I know, I shall warm her up and prepare her for my beloved brother, Robert.’

Scene IV: Interlude I, The Flying Serial Killer

The 2nd Day of the 3rd Moon, 21 A.V.
The Varjoleto Forest, Near Togaduine.

Feilecann lay by the Kapparu river. Her black hair spread about her body with wisps falling over the purple mask covering her eyes. Beside her lay the body of the morning’s feed, a plump milkmaid with auburn locks. Her eyes glazed a deathly white, and her buxom chest trailed paths of blood from the furious bite marks. Her skin was as white as her eyes and she looked a little surprised, as is often the case when a flying vampire-butterfly hybrid appears from nowhere and eats someone. Especially if you are that someone.

Feilecann gave the body a gentle push. It fell into the river and the mariposa watched as it floated downstream elegantly. A few of the milkmaids washing further along the river let out howls of fear and sorrow causing Feilecann to chuckle.

‘Nicely done,’ a deep voice growled from behind her. Feilecann turned. Her rugged lover Dyerbolique stood in black robes, finery Feilecann had stolen from a travelling prince seeking his bride. The prince concerned never found his bride. He found Dyerbolique instead. The travelling Prince, Prince Klaatu also found himself paralysed after Dyerbolique’s blade severed his spine and, thereafter, Prince Klaatu found himself growing mushrooms in a shallow grave.

Prince Klaatu complained about the matter for a while, but Feilecann addressed his concerns by eating his vocal cords, then vomiting blood on the wound so that the prince could enjoy watching the fungi takeover his own body.

‘I have two gifts for you, my beloved,’ Dyerbolique smiled, offering her his hand. She took his hand in hers and stood, glowing with the hue only true love can bestow.
‘You need not bother, Dyer.’
Dyerbolique pulled her into his arms,
‘There is no bother when it comes to you, my queen.’

He led her from the river to his horse, a fine black stallion called Nikto, also procured from Prince Klaatu, and helped Feilecann mount before mounting behind her, then mounting her.

Dyerbolique’s desire did not take long to sate and, once Feilecann had a nice damp patch soaking her gusset, he was more than ready to take his beloved on an adventure that she would never forget. Dyerbolique took the reins and kicked the horse on. It galloped through the village of Doloros, then veered east at Ashurrel into the Varjoleto forest. Nikto followed the forest path for a solid two hours, relentless in his stride, until Dyerbolique changed the steed’s direction and they entered the surrounding shadowy overgrowth.

Nikto slowed as he moved through rugged terrain. and navigated rocks and woodland floor debris. Finally, Dyerbolique pulled the reins at the mouth of an almost vertical cave with steps burrowed within.

He dismounted, and tethered his horse, before assisting Feilecann by lifting her down. Dyerbolique took her white hand, and led her into the cave’s mouth, then guided her one step at a time into the darkness.

As the light disappeared, Dyerbolique lit a flaming torch and the couple followed the steps into a chamber, then through a very tight crevice into a second chamber. The second chamber was lit by flaming torches and candles. In the centre of the chamber, on a rock, lay three women, triplets, all chained naked side by side.

Their heads were completely shaved. Their locks of blonde hair rested in a star that had been painted on the cavern floor with the first triplets’ blood. Each woman’s legs and arms were flayed and spread. The skin from each of their backs was cut into two wings and distributed behind them, and on each of their bellies an image sat carved with daring accuracy. The first woman adorned the portrait of a caterpillar, the second a chrysalis, and the third a magnificent butterfly.

‘They are still alive,’ Dyerbolique muttered, ‘just about, but still breathing. My gift to you.’
Feilecann’s hands touched her lips in symmetry,
‘Such a gift. Such an offering.’
‘I love you more than life my mariposa, and if you would have me as your immortal equal, I would share these creatures with you.’ Dyerbolique bowed his head, ‘Otherwise I respect your decision and watching you feast will suffice.’
Feilecann stared at Dyerbolique, then whispered,
‘I alone shall partake of your offering.’
Dyerbolique nodded.

Feilecann circled her sacrifices. Her hands ran across their bodies, paused on the flayed raw flesh, then moved to their breasts. One after another she touched her prey. Felt their warmth. Delighted in the flesh. Her fangs grew and she took the first triplet biting into her thigh, ripping through the femoral artery. Blood sprayed and pumped at speed, soaking Feilecann’s mouth and face. She licked and swallowed as her prey’s sisters screamed and pleaded for their lives. The death was quick.

Feilecann moved to the triplet in the centre of the rock, crawled up her body and tore into her throat. She choked and spluttered, then gagged and struggled for air as Feilecann fed. Finally, the mariposa turned her attentions to the sobbing wretch still alive. Her powerful teeth acted as tools, circling the girl’s skull until the top of the bone loosened. The cap was pulled back. Feilecann used her talons to scoop out the delicious brain, and she ate it one gruelling handful at a time.

Once the triplets were silent and still, the last mariposa drew a blade from her stocking and severed and ate each head until only the bodies remained. She then signalled to Dyerbolique,
‘You have proved loyalty and love, but you must prove you can feed before any metamorphosis.’
Dyerbolique nodded, but displayed no emotion. Feilecann handed him her blade.

Dyerbolique had always had a thing for offal. He was raised in a house that deemed every night ‘Offal Night,’ so he opened each of the women’s stomachs with a fervour, peeling back the flesh to reveal the organs. He started with the livers, then the lungs, and finally the hearts. The hearts were a little chewy but eventually all of the chosen organs were devoured.

He handed the knife back to Feilecann. She licked the blood and tissue from it, and replaced it,
‘Before we proceed, what is my second gift?’
Dyerbolique’s face lit up,
‘Come,’ he said, taking her by the hand again.
He led her back up the stairs with great care, then untethered Nikto, helped her mount and followed suit.

Nikto rode back to the main path and galloped north through the forest until they hit a clearing. There, two overlapping trees blocked their path. Both dismounted, and Dyerbolique led her between the trees. Before her eyes, a great tower manifested.
‘I had this built. For us,’ Dyerbolique whispered, ‘there is no door only a high window and an internal palace. Safe, secure and hidden by magic.’
‘How?’ Feilecann asked.
Dyerbolique stroked her hair and kissed her cheek,
‘The Djinn Ibliss,’ he replied, then added, ‘but you must carry me as I have no wings.’
‘You will have soon,’ Feilecann nodded, lifting her lover from the ground.

The lovers flew to the window, and Feilecann was not disappointed by the tower’s palatial rooms and well-stocked food supplies maintained in the icy cellar. There were three floors above the cellar. The master bedroom at the top, and a second bedroom below, both fitted with rustic beds and dressing tables, and above the cellar sat the dark drawing room with side washrooms.

After her exploration of the tower, Dyerbolique led Feilecann back to the master bedroom, where he lay her on the bed and whispered,
‘I love you, always.’
Feilecann smiled as he lay next to her,
‘I love you too; I have loved you from the moment I laid eyes on you.’

Dyerbolique cupped her face in his large hands and kissed her. First a peck, then another, then his lips parted and moved against her mouth. She returned his admiration, slipping her tongue between his lips to meet with his. Feilecann unbuttoned Dyerbolique’s shirt gliding her hands over his hairy chest,
‘Promise I will always be safe.’
‘I promise,’ Dyerbolique whispered as his hand lifted off her mask to reveal her porcelain skin and glowing eyes, ‘I promise I will keep you secure and safe from the world.’

His hands pulled at the lace on her dress’s bodice and freed her ample breasts. His head dropped to her nipples, but his eyes remained locked on hers. He licked her buds with a desperate hunger, then returned his mouth to her lips.

Feilecann reached for his trousers and slowly undid them before easing her hand in and caressing his stiff cock,
‘Make love to me, Dyer,’ she pleaded.
Dyerbolique lifted her skirt and petticoats, slipped down her laces and climbed between her legs. He moved slowly and carefully against her desire. His mouth teased her throat and ears. Feilecann moaned as he steadily circled his body about hers. Her legs lifted allowing him to enter more fully, deeper and with a greater passion.

Dyerbolique held back. Waited for her to beg for more, then continued before stopping again. He rolled onto his back pulling her on top of him.

Scene III: The Jester’s New Suit

The 2nd Day of the 4th Moon, 1536 P.V.
Corax Asylum, Togaduine

Nicolas’s mood over Behmor’s interference passed in no time. Deep down, Nicolas enjoyed spending time with his son, and sometimes even bombarded Irkalla with pigeons to force Behmor to pay him a visit. He did not care that the visit was only to complain, he was simply happy to see his son, at least as happy as Nicolas could be given the Nicolai problem that needed resolving.

Nicolas’s deeper problem was that he wanted Allyra not only to marry him, but to love him unconditionally and for who he was. The total success of Plan BAT depended upon it, but Nicolas had no intention of changing who he was in any way, shape, or form. This, of course, exacerbated the problem.

Nicolas did not share all his plans with Behmor, as Behmor had a habit of interfering. Behmor was certainly more or less in the dark about Nicolas’s current plan. Nicolas had fed Chives just enough information to lay the path for Behmor’s slow desensitisation to Nicolas’s Plan BAT, and paid Chives with tribute arms to act as a double agent. It was akin to throwing a dog a bone.

Nicolas decided to leave his Immoless to Bigglesworth for the time being and spent the early hours prowling around his asylum whilst waiting for his new suit.

Nicolas believed that Allyra would be far more attracted to him if he wore something more fashionable than a worn, torn suit that allowed his nob to escape every few minutes. He considered having Ariadne’s bones whipped for the inconvenience caused by tearing his old suit but instead sent the bones to Kane, with Demus, who had a bit of Charmaine thigh saved for Kane too.

Nicolas desperately wanted Allyra to visit Corax so she could fall in love with his home and believed that this would help her in her journey to fall in love with him. Afterall, Fanu’s princesses always found themselves more open to marriage when a wealthy husband was on the cards. Webster proposed that this was not the greatest idea Nicolas had ever come up with, but Nicolas could not, for the life of him, understand why.

Corax was, as far as Nicolas was concerned, a state of the art institution. He maintained a perfectly filthy crypt-level dungeon, with multiple cells, which housed the vampires. Each cell contained a bed with straps and cuffs, chains that hung from the walls, a barred opening panel within the door, so that he could stick his head through to intimidate the inmates, a hidden door in the brickwork that led to and from his secret passages, a shoot for food, a disgustingly mouldy mattress, and a trapdoor on the ceiling.

Beyond the dungeons, the cellar’s damp corridor held an immaculately kept surgical instrument rack, housing the least sterile and most rusty scalpels, scissors, bone saws, and trephines Allyra would ever be fortunate enough to see. The shelves also housed an array of whips and birches. Nicolas did enjoy his petty tortures and fully intended to flog Allyra for her pleasure of course.

The ground floor held a banqueting suite, that only the Nicolai were allowed to use, and a library, that only the Nicolai were allowed to use, and an office that only Nicolas was allowed to use. These stood in the west wing, close to Nicolas’s chambers.

The east wing contained further cells, each was equal to the dungeon cells in its pristine décor, and each contained one or five inmates, depending on how uncomfortable Nicolas wanted them to feel. The first line of cells, as previously explained, held his favourite tributes, for quick and easy access. There were also soiled gurneys, and horrifically over-sized wheelchairs strewn around the corridors with unfortunate tortured beings strapped into them, and sometimes, the remains of unfortunate beings strapped into them.

The beings held in the wheelchairs were not unfairly tortured. They were punished for attempting to escape. Legs and eyes were commonly removed for such transgressions, thus requiring the innovative Billyboxes commissioned by Nicolas and created by Webster. In the spirit of fairness, legs were removed on the first escape attempt and eyes on the second, and filthy bandages were provided to mask the hideous empty orifices.

The inmates consisted of a diverse population of general thesapien inmates, lower vampires, and thesapien tributes. Red-haired tributes were Nicolas’s favourite of course.

There was also a meeting hall and chapel on the ground floor. Nicolas insisted on a meeting hall, so that he could randomly round up the inmates and give pointless speeches or make meaningless announcements. Nicolas was quite sure that Allyra would enjoy his lengthy speeches on how marvellous he was.

All corridors in Corax were covered in mirrors and loudly clanging clocks, and Nicolas’s modest office sat by the great front entrance.

Nicolas had traded six of his finest tributes, after inflicting Moons of debauchery on them, with Irkalla in exchange for his medical license, and recognition by The Thesapien Medical Board that he was, indeed, a Doctor of Psychiatry. Of course, Nicolas had no intention of learning either medicine or psychiatry as he found cure was bad for business.

This hellish elevation allowed Nicolas to declare anyone he saw fit as insane and lock them up against their will. He would then make a concerted effort to drive them insane, therefore proving that they deserved locking up in the first place. Once the inmates were completely bonkers, Nicolas would use the corrective facilities to correct them.

Initially, this was not an ideal situation, as it undermined the thesapien sacrificial tribute service. Nicolas did not care, and Behmor eventually accepted it as in the long run Nicolas would tire of one inmate or another and end their lives, giving them a one-way ticket to Irkalla.

Behmor would always find a home for them in Mortraxis, or Judicara. Occasionally he would receive an intelligent soul who would be allocated a menial and tiresome job in Irkalla’s civil service. This suited everyone, especially Behmor who spent more time finding ways to avoid work than actually doing it.

The ground floor also offered special facilities for the Nicolai including the games room, the Nicolai lounge and the south wing. The south wing was out of bounds, but rumour had it, that it was a lavish suite of rooms dedicated to Nicolas’s Nicolai. No one knew exactly what the Nicolai did in there, only that they spent a lot of time in there away from the smelly inmates. The first floor of the asylum held a series of torture chambers, designed by Nicolas, Archie and Webster.

Nicolas loved the corrective facilities and was especially proud of the bespoke iron maiden, the brazen bull, and his hall of mirrors. The iron maiden had been home to a single inmate for some fifteen centuries, and Webster had devised a series of drips to ensure such longevity.

Nicolas knew that Allyra had been boiling his vampires and assumed that she too would fall in love with his corrective facilities.

Above the corrective facilities was a second floor known as ‘The Second Floor.’ The apartment on the second floor was off limits. Only Nicolas used it, and no one knew what lay beyond the padlocked door.

Above the second floor was a third floor which the Nicolai used for undisclosed reasons, everyone assumed it was their sleeping quarters, and the attic held the washrooms. The washrooms were an open plan series of rooms that spewed out sewage for the inmates to wash in. Nicolas liked to cut the thesapiens beforehand to ensure that they received the best treatment possible, and as such, infection was rife. Nicolas found the sweet smell of infection most pleasing.

Nicolas occasionally earmarked an inmate for special treatment. The special treatment consisted of one thousand small lacerations followed by prolonged exposure to the sewage. He would have Chives chain the inmates concerned under the sewage and would visit everyday to watch their slow and obscene decline.

Nicolas did not sleep much, or at all, and was wandering about waiting for Stacia to injure herself in some way in the dark room. He desperately wanted to speed things along with the first two immolesses so he could focus all of his attentions on bullying Allyra into loving him.

In his boredom, Nicolas spent an hour tinkering with one of his pocket watches. He prided himself on his mastery of horology, and whilst concentrating on the tiny, intricate mechanisms he found that the voices in his head would settle down.

He then turned his attentions to his troublesome chair.

The chair in Nicolas’s chambers had been levitating for two weeks. Nicolas loved to write, he constantly collected old blank parchments and bound them, then wrote on them in red or yellow ink. He considered himself the greatest author in The Deep but never showed anyone his work as he hated sharing. The sudden urge of the chair to float had made writing somewhat more difficult. When Nicolas sat on it, it also spun around, so that Nicolas was obliged to write quickly at each turn. This slowed his prose and he decided to share his concerns with anyone who would listen.

Nicolas tried to get the inmates to listen to his problems first. He crawled on all fours, like a tiger, from cell to cell complaining about the levitating chair. The inmates were not as interested as he had hoped, largely because most were in a frightfully bloody state, asleep, had chunks missing from their bodies, were in a coma, or dead.

Nicolas did not move the dead; he left that to Chives. Chives would take them to the scullery for preparation. The smell did not worry Nicolas, he considered it a luxurious perk to the overall ambience of the asylum, and an odour that Allyra would come to appreciate.

Discouraged by the lack of interest from the inmates, Nicolas decided instead to write a letter of complaint. He wrote the letter in his office which housed a much more reasonable chair, folded it in half and stuck the ends together with a bit of tribute-brain that had been lodged between his teeth. The letter was addressed to Behmor and read,

‘B,

The second Immoless arrived far too early and I am inundated with floating chairs. The inmates are being unreasonably hostile, and Robert is late as usual.

Love Dad.’

Nicolas’s letters were always prone to exaggeration, nonsense, and theatrics, and often accompanied a new self-portrait which Behmor would either use as a target for archery practice or as fuel for his roaring open fire. Sometimes Nicolas would send a HORRIFIC self-portrait of his elongated face with a splash of Chester, which Behmor was always thrilled to receive. Occasionally the portraits held little notes like, ‘Don’t burn this one! Love, Dad.’

Nicolas sent his best raven, Ghorab, to carry the message directly to Irkalla. The message was immediately passed to Behmor, as no one in The Deep or in Irkalla wanted to put Nicolas in a tetchy mood. Behmor read it, noted it, and threw it on the fire.

Once Nicolas realised that Behmor was ignoring him, he created a series of notices on individual parchments. Each read
‘I Declare you Insane.’ He returned to the cells and hung them outside of every door. The inmates did not care about that either and Nicolas had misjudged the number of notices required, so there were several parchments left over.

He returned to his chambers climbed up to the barred window and dropped the lot into the drains below.

As Nicolas stared into the blocked drains, he made the strange decision to have a shower. He only washed once a century and though it was not time, he felt that making some level of effort for his bride would not hurt. Needless to say, he did not use the inmate washrooms.

Nicolas despised cleanliness, but to prevent the maggots setting in, once a century he forced himself to stand beneath the constant flow of water that poured into his wetroom. His wetroom was an ensuite, attached to what Nicolas called his ‘chambers.’ Although, on inspection, one would find that Nicolas’s chambers were not as lavish as the words would imply.

The ‘Chambers’ consisted of one large room. The room was an annexe attached to Corax Asylum and could be accessed by a passageway on the spiral stone steps that led from the dungeons to the ground floor. Nicolas had no intention of living in the filth of Corax as people would talk.

The chamber consisted of an unnecessarily large, and unnecessarily filthy bed with yellow and black plaid sheets, blankets and duvets. The pillows matched the bedding as did the curtains. The stains and grub on the bed matched the mould and damp dripping down the walls, and the bars that secured his window aperture offered a heavy claustrophobic feel to the overall aesthetic.

The hallway that led from the annexe’s door and past the ensuite to Nicolas’s bedroom was needlessly narrow, and clocks cluttered the walls, all telling different times.

Inside his room, the window and bed leaned coldly against the lefthand side wall, and a mirror sat on a rickety old dressing table under the window. Another huge mirror, hung on the wall opposite, and next to that an office desk and chair resided, perpetually covered in red and yellow ink, quills and parchments.

The oddity of the room, overlooking the two smaller doors to the far end that were padlocked, bolted and chained shut, was the gramophone that sat on a table next to the wall mirror.

You may wonder why a gramophone would be deemed odd, but this gramophone was quite different to other gramophones.

This gramophone had a rotting head living on it. A skull with a top hat, sunglasses, the odd cigar, a litre of whisky and vocal cords that wandered about of their own accord.

Nicolas had, some forty years before, taken the head of Demize the First, high priest of the DarkBadb at the time. He found Demize’s ongoing interest in his life disconcerting and felt that Demize would gain some propriety in his behaviour in the absence of a body. In other words, Nicolas lopped Demize’s head off for poking his nose in Nicolas’s business.

Other than the Nicolai and Kane, Nicolas had no friends, for reasons that shall become apparent, and found running an asylum a lonely occupation. The head gave him company. The DarkBadb did not request the return of the head, so Nicolas placed it on his gramophone, and he and Archie applied a little magical surgery allowing the head to be possessed by a Nicolai.

After his shower, Nicolas stared at himself in the wall mirror for some time. He was tall and could have been considered goodlooking with his sharp jawline and emerald eyes, but for the wayward globs of blood about his mouth and a thick film of soap avoidance that drenched his skin.

He tilted his head, not impressed with what he saw. The cleanliness of his long, dark-auburn hair that he had just washed, failed to match the overall aesthetic of his skin, that he had not washed. He considered the problem for a moment and then let out a rampant yell,

‘CHIVES! CHIVES!’

A knock came at the door, and the small, wizened ghoul hobbled in. Ghouls were immortals, but unlike other immortals they could not seem to dodge the ageing process.

Chives, having reached his two thousand and forty-seventh birthday, declined on a daily basis. His skin was so thin it was barely visible, his face was gaunt, and his nose had slipped slightly. His eyes were lopsided and he had a rather inconspicuous hump on his back, and a slight limp.
‘Yes, Sir?’ Chives asked.
‘Ahh,’ Nicolas replied, ‘there you are. You’re late, I have been calling for hours.’
Chives hobbled into the chambers, and we will call them chambers for Nicolas’s sake.
‘Sir, I came as soon as you called.’

Chives had turned punctuality into an artform on account of Nicolas stapling his left foot to his right knee and leaving it there throughout the second century P.V. This, Nicolas considered, was a lesson in the consequences of being late.

Chives, having only been in Nicolas’s employee for some one hundred and twelve years at the time proved to be a slow learner. You see, when Nicolas called, he expected his ghoul to know that he would call beforehand and arrive at the moment his dulcet tones bellowed throughout his dwelling. He also expected his ghoul to be somewhat psychic and pre-empt his every demand, however ridiculous.

‘Chives, go to the kitchen and ask Meatcleaver for some used cooking oil!’ Nicolas ordered.
‘Sir?’
‘Did I stutter, Chives?’
Chives sighed. He tried his best to ignore Nicolas’s alters on account of the workload involved in chasing two hundred and sixteen Nicolas’s about all day. One was more than enough.
‘No sir, but…’
‘Goats butt, Chives. You have ten minutes, and if you are late consider it five!’
Chives limped towards the door,
‘Very good, sir.’

Nicolas stared harder into the mirror, then rapped on the glass,
‘WEB-STAR!’
His reflection faded, and a new reflection filled the glass. The man looking back was dressed in a black waistcoat and black shirt and looked a little like Nicolas, only this man had short, slicked back blond hair and wore glasses at all times, occasionally his veins formed spidery webs over his skin,
‘Nicolas. Good dusk,’ Nicolai-Webster nodded.
‘Good dusk to you Webster, now, without dallying, I need to address some recent problems with Plan BAT and our Immoless.’
Nicolai-Webster took off his glasses, breathed on them, polished them on his jacket and slid them back on his nose,
‘What went wrong this time? Make a cunt of yourself again, did you?’

‘That is a most unpleasant word to use, Webster,’ Nicolas began, ‘and no, I did not make anything of myself. It was HER fault. She over-reacted.’
Webster leaned towards the glass. Nicolas reciprocated until the two were nose to nose. Webster smiled,
‘Is that a lump on your head, Nicolai?’
‘No. No. It is a…’
‘Lump!’ Webster looked over the giant purple mountain where Allyra had beaten Nicolas earlier that night, ‘I take it courting failed yet again. What did you do?’
‘Me?’ Nicolas asked, surprised at such a cruel allegation, ‘Why I was the perfect gentleman. I waited until she and Chester had finished their first coital alignment post-Chester’s return’
‘You mean having sex?’ Webster asked, shaking his head.
‘So crude, so crude, but yes. And then I waited a little longer until Chester was asleep. I did not want to alarm the Immoless, so I put my hood over my eyes, unfortunately…’
‘Here we go!’

‘UNFORTUNATELY, the Immoless tricked me and deceived me by placing errant plant pots about her window.’
Webster’s hand slapped onto his forehead,
‘You made a cunt of yourself, didn’t you?’ He groaned.
Nicolas held his head up, and turned his hand over,
‘I made a gallant entrance through her fruity bushes, then inadvertently tripped a few times, but then I saw her approach and surprised her with my divine self.’
Webster shook his head, as he did the skull on the gramophone opened its weary eyes, and took a swig of whisky before lighting his cigar with his vocal cords,
‘Another failure I hear!’ He cackled, before rising above the gramophone, and joining Nicolas in staring into the mirror, ‘Webster, Bigglesworth would be the better man to send.’
‘Bigglesworth indeed!’ Nicolas snapped. ‘He would fall hopelessly in love with her and read her poetry until she died of boredom. That is not in line with the plan, is it Demize?’
‘You’re not doing much better, Nicolai!’ Nicolai-Demize laughed, circling his head. ‘Useless, useless man.’
He puffed a fog of smoke into Nicolas’s face causing Nicolas to choke.

Webster waited until Demize had finished laughing, and Nicolas had finished choking to continue,
‘I want to get this straight, you were creeping around in the bushes, then you fell over, and then you spoke to her at the window. Then what happened?’
‘She seemed mildly alarmed by my presence and hit me with a lump of metal.’
‘That was not in the plan, was it?’ Webster frowned.
‘No, but it is a declaration of love! And that is exactly what we want isn’t it?’
Demize swallowed his cigar, and it instantly dropped out of the remains of his collarbone and onto the floor. Nicolas swatted at the skull, but Demize was far too quick for him,
‘You little freak, you’re going to burn Corax to the ground one of these days.’
Webster thumped on the mirror,
‘Nicolas, put it out!’ He yelled, ‘NOW!’
Nicolas trod on the cigar with his boot, then swatted at Demize again, the agile skull jumped out of his reach and laughed until he vomited whisky from nowhere.

‘Gentlemen,’ Webster interjected, ‘if you have quite finished, we need a new approach.’
‘I did take her to The Sombre and I was pleasant but then I was summoned back with Behmor complaining,’ Nicolas moaned.
‘You sent Chives to Irkalla too early, Dumbass,’ Demize chided.
Just as he spoke a knock came at the door.

‘Enter!’ Webster called. Chives ignored him.
‘Enter you facetious gremlin,’ Nicolas ordered.
Chives entered, but he was not alone. He was accompanied by an angry chef who looked identical to Nicolas except for his dress. He was dressed in a yellow and black plaid chef’s uniform and hat, and carrying a vat of rather unpleasant and overused oil,
‘Why you ask ze old one to carry ze oil?’
‘Good dusk to you too, Meatcleaver!’ Nicolas grinned.
‘I ‘ave enough to do feeding the Nicolai and your lunatics without carrying around oil like a crazy milkmaid,’ Nicolai-Meatcleaver Pierre moaned.
‘That’s why we have Chives!’ Webster explained, calmly.
‘Chives is a weeble is ze not?’ Meatcleaver replied.
‘He’s not a weeble until he’s in a Billybox with wheels,’ Nicolas snapped, ‘until then he carries whatever I tell him to carry.’
‘So wrong, Nicolas. The way you speak is so wrong,’ Webster muttered.
‘I think it’s funny!’ Demize said as he flew about Chives’ head.

Chives ignored the skull and pretended he could not see him. Nicolas pulled a pocket watch from his inside pocket,
‘Meatcleaver, breakfast starts shortly, long day ahead. Perhaps you have other things to be doing? Things that don’t involve arguing with me and my good selves!’
‘I am a good self, am I not?’
‘Of course, you are but go and be a good self in the kitchen.’
‘Fine, be zat way!’ Meatcleaver muttered, then walked out mumbling to himself in some made up language to sound exotic.

‘Lumpy,’ Demize sang, ‘Lumpy, Lumpy,’ he circled about Chives’ head staring at Nicolas’s love wounds, ‘Lumpy, Lumpy.’
Nicolas glared at Demize,
‘You’re only saying that because you are out of reach, however,’ he observed Demize’s position above Chives’ head, ‘I should like to wear you as a hat!’
‘Me Sir?’ Chives asked.
Nicolas hated it when Chives interrupted

text:
Sun Tzu said the highest form of war is to attack the enemy's strategy, and the next best is to attack his alliances.

Read Putin's offer after Shenzhen with that in mind. He invites European leaders to Moscow for direct talks and says he has no plans to attack Europe, yet gives no sign of easing his demands. Within hours, Kyiv was under a mass missile attack.

An invitation to Moscow is not a peace plan. It is an attempt to split Europe from Washington, and Europe from Kyiv, by letting each believe it can get a better deal alone.

Europe's answer from Berlin was sensible: ready to talk, but together, and with Ukraine in the room. Zelenskyy was honest that there is still no shared view of what Article 5 style guarantees would mean. That gap is the real battlefield now.

My forecast: talks come in the new year, and the side that holds its coalition together through winter sets the terms. Alliances, not offers, decide endings. Worth watching how @WIONews, @CNNnews18 and @republic frame Moscow's invitation for Indian viewers.
