text:
Most modern airport terminals pave miles of concourses with sterile, glare-heavy terrazzo or monotonous carpet tiles meant strictly to endure rolling suitcases, so looking down at the circular floor mosaic "Cypress Canopy" inside Orlando International Airport (MCO) feels like standing at the edge of a tranquil Florida wetland looking straight up into the sky.

Set seamlessly into the terminal floor, this expansive medallion uses thousands of individually placed glass and stone tesserae to pull off a clever radial perspective. Around the outer perimeter, slender cypress trunks rise inward from lush marsh grasses and rippling turquoise water—complete with a graceful white wading bird standing along the foreground bank and small birds gliding between the branches. As your eyes follow those tall trunks toward the center, their rust-gold canopies open up around a glowing circle of cerulean sky, turning a flat walkway into a worm's-eye view of a sunlit forest clearing.

What makes mosaic art so enduring in high-traffic public spaces is how craftsmanship meets permanence. Rather than slapping down a printed vinyl floor decal that peels and fades within months, master mosaicists painstakingly graduate thousands of tiny color-matched tiles by hand so natural foot traffic actually polishes the surface over decades while keeping every shimmer of water and foliage intact.

Today, transit hubs are usually engineered as purely functional corridors designed to rush travelers from gate to gate, yet "Cypress Canopy" proves that when public architecture honors local ecology through patient, tactile artistry, even an airport floor can offer a moment of quiet wonder.

- Denise: $100,000
- Fourteen coworkers: $10,000 each

That accounted for the entire $240,000, with the remaining $10,000 supposedly reserved for taxes and administrative costs.

Denise refused. She explained that the company had announced one winner, not a department prize.

Then a coworker posted in their private staff group that Denise had become arrogant since winning the money. Another person accused her of forgetting everyone who had helped her during her eleven years at the company.

The situation reached management, who issued a statement confirming that the raffle prize belonged entirely to Denise and that no employee had been promised a share.

But the coworkers weren't finished.

Three of them stopped speaking to her, and one reportedly told her husband that Denise should be ashamed of keeping money that could change several families' lives.

Last week, Denise returned to work in a different department. She says she doesn't feel comfortable eating lunch with the people she worked alongside for eleven years.

The strangest part is that the same coworkers who are demanding $10,000 each never offered to share their salaries with Denise when she was struggling financially.

Germany’s closest real parallel to the legend of Ys is the story of Rungholt, a wealthy medieval town on the North Sea that was swallowed by a catastrophic storm tide in 1362. Like Ys, Rungholt was said to be prosperous, sinful, and ultimately destroyed by the sea—its ruins still believed to lie beneath the waves of the Wadden Sea.

Celtic Countries

🌊 A Real German “Sunken City”: Rungholt

Although the legend of Ys is Breton, Germany has its own drowned‑city tale that mirrors it closely in theme, tone, and fate.

Rungholt (North Frisia, Schleswig‑Holstein)

Location: On the island region of Strand, now part of the Wadden Sea National Park.

Era: Flourished in the Middle Ages as a wealthy trading town.

Destruction: Believed to have been destroyed during the Grote Mandrenke (“Great Drowning of Men”) storm tide in 1362, which devastated large parts of the North Sea coast.

Legend: Rungholt was said to be rich, proud, and morally corrupt. According to folklore, the townspeople mocked the church and ignored warnings of divine punishment. When the storm came, the sea swallowed the entire city.

Aftermath: Fishermen and sailors have long claimed they can still hear bells ringing beneath the water—an echo of Ys’s own mythic cathedral.

Archaeology: Modern researchers have found medieval structures, drainage systems, and artifacts in the tidal flats, supporting the existence of a real settlement beneath the sea.

Rungholt’s blend of wealth, hubris, divine warning, and catastrophic flooding makes it the closest German analogue to Ys’s mythic fall.

Why Rungholt Feels Like Germany’s Ys

Both stories share striking motifs:

A prosperous coastal city whose success leads to arrogance.

Warnings ignored, often framed as moral or spiritual failings.

A catastrophic flood that erases the city almost instantly.

Lingering echoes—bells underwater in Ys, and in Rungholt, stories of sounds or ruins visible at low tide.

Cultural memory that blends history with myth.

Rungholt is not just a legend; it’s a historical place wrapped in folklore, making it even more compelling as a real-world counterpart.

🧭 Other German Flood Legends (Less Similar but Related)

If you want more drowned‑city stories from Germany, here are a few thematic cousins:

Vineta (Baltic Sea): A legendary wealthy city said to have sunk due to greed and decadence.

The Lorelei (Rhine River): Not a city, but a tale of a siren whose song causes shipwrecks—another blend of water, danger, and myth.

Peat bog villages in Lower Saxony: Some settlements were lost to floods, though without the moral legend attached.

Rungholt remains the strongest match to Ys in both narrative and historical depth.

Germany’s closest real parallel to the legend of Ys is the drowned medieval city of Rungholt, whose fall in 1362 blends documented history with mythic elements—divine punishment, moral decay, and a city swallowed overnight by the sea.

Rungholt: The “German Atlantis”

Rungholt was a wealthy North Frisian trading town on the island of Strand, now part of the Wadden Sea. Archaeology shows it may have had up to 500 houses and around 3,000 inhabitants, thriving on agriculture and maritime trade.

The Catastrophe

On 15–16 January 1362, the Grote Mandrenke (“Great Drowning of Men”) storm tide struck the North Sea coast. It destroyed Rungholt and roughly 30 other settlements, killing an estimated 25,000 people. The coastline shifted dramatically, leaving the former land beneath tidal flats.

Archaeological Confirmation

For centuries, Rungholt was treated as half‑legend. But modern surveys—magnetic gradiometry, electromagnetic induction, and seismic mapping—have revealed dikes, drainage systems, wells, sluices, and the foundations of multiple churches, including a large 40×15‑meter parish church. These findings confirm Rungholt’s existence and scale.

The Legends: Moral Decay and Divine Punishment

Rungholt’s folklore mirrors Ys so closely that scholars often call it “Atlantis of the North Sea.”

The Pig and the Priest

One famous tale describes drunken young men forcing a priest to give last rites to a pig. The priest prayed for divine justice, and the storm that followed was seen as God’s answer. This echoes Ys’s theme of hubris and sacrilege leading to destruction.

Bells Beneath the Waves

Sailors and fishermen have long claimed they can hear church bells ringing under the sea near Hallig Südfall. This motif—an underwater city whose bells still toll—directly parallels Ys, where the cathedral bells are said to echo from beneath the ocean.

How Rungholt Connects to Other German Water Legends

Rungholt sits within a broader German tradition of drowned or cursed coastal places:

Niedam – Another settlement near Rungholt, also lost in the 14th century storm tides.

Vineta – A legendary Baltic city said to have sunk due to greed and decadence; often compared to Ys for its moralizing narrative.

The Wadden Sea Halligen – Tiny islands that flood regularly, preserving a cultural memory of living at the edge of the sea.

These stories share themes of wealth, pride, divine warning, and catastrophic flooding, making Rungholt the most historically grounded example.

Why Rungholt Is Germany’s Ys

A real city with archaeological proof, yet wrapped in myth.

A moral legend of arrogance and sacrilege, like Ys.

A sudden, overwhelming flood that erased it overnight.

Lingering supernatural echoes—bells, ghostly ruins, shifting sands.

A cultural symbol of human fragility before the sea.

Rungholt is not just similar to Ys—it is the closest real-world counterpart, where history and legend intertwine so tightly that the boundary between them feels as fluid as the tides that claimed it.

Germany has several real historical stories of cities and villages destroyed by the sea, but the most complete and best‑documented is the true story of Rungholt, a wealthy medieval town swallowed by the North Sea in 1362.

🌊 Rungholt — A Real German City Lost to the Sea

Rungholt was a prosperous trading town in North Frisia, located on the island of Strand (now part of Schleswig‑Holstein). Archaeologists estimate it may have had up to 500 houses and around 3,000 inhabitants, making it one of the larger medieval settlements in the region.

The Disaster: The Grote Mandrenke (1362)

On 15–16 January 1362, a massive storm tide known as the Grote Mandrenke (“Great Drowning of Men”) struck the North Sea coast.

The storm overwhelmed the dikes protecting the reclaimed marshland.

Rungholt and 30–44 other settlements were destroyed.

An estimated 25,000 people died across the region.

The island of Strand itself was torn apart; only fragments like Nordstrand and Hallig Südfall remain today.

🏺 Archaeological Evidence

For centuries, Rungholt was treated as half‑legend. But modern research has confirmed its reality:

1921: First ruins found near Hallig Südfall (wells, trenches, tidal lock).

2023–2025: Geophysical surveys (magnetic gradiometry, electromagnetic induction, seismics) mapped 10 square kilometers of buried structures.

Drainage systems

Sea dike

Two small churches

One large parish church (40×15 meters)

All That's Interesting

All That's Interesting

These discoveries confirm Rungholt was a major port town, not a minor village.

📜 The Legends Connected to Rungholt

Rungholt’s folklore mirrors Ys so closely that it is often called “Atlantis of the North Sea.”

1. The Pig and the Priest

A famous legend says drunken young men forced a priest to give last rites to a pig.

The priest prayed for divine punishment.

Soon after, the sea rose and destroyed the city.

This moral tale parallels Ys’s themes of hubris, sacrilege, and divine retribution.

2. Bells Beneath the Waves

Fishermen have long claimed they can hear church bells ringing underwater near the site of Rungholt.

This echoes the Breton legend of Ys, where cathedral bells are said to toll beneath the sea.

3. A City of Sin

Later stories describe Rungholt as wealthy, decadent, and morally corrupt—again echoing Ys.

Historians believe these tales grew as a way to explain the disaster.

🌍 Other Real German “Sunken City” Stories

While Rungholt is the most historically grounded, Germany has other flood legends:

Vineta (Baltic Sea): A legendary wealthy city said to have sunk due to greed.

Niedam: Another settlement destroyed in the same 1362 storm system.

Drowned villages of the Wadden Sea: Many small communities vanished in medieval storm tides.

Rungholt remains the closest real parallel to Ys, combining verified archaeology with centuries of myth.

Ys World Magazine X Tidal Monoliths

Another real drowned‑city story from Germany is the legend of Vineta, a wealthy medieval port on the Baltic Sea said to have been swallowed by the waves due to its arrogance and moral decay. It is one of Europe’s most famous “sunken city” traditions and shares striking similarities with Ys.

Vineta: Germany’s Baltic “Atlantis”
What Vineta Was
A major medieval trading center known in early chronicles as Jumne, Jomsburg, or Julin.

Described by Adam of Bremen (1075) as “the largest city in all of Europe”, located at the mouth of the Oder River.

Mentioned by Ibrahim ibn Jaqub (965) as a wealthy port where Slavs, Saxons, Danes, and Greeks traded.

These early accounts anchor Vineta in real medieval geography and commerce, even though its exact location remains debated.

How Vineta “Drowned”
The Legend
All versions of the Vineta myth describe:

Extreme wealth and decadence among its inhabitants.

Warnings ignored, including visions of the city appearing doubled above the sea—an omen of doom.

A water spirit (Wasserfrau) rising from the sea to proclaim the city’s fate:
“Vineta, Vineta, du reiche Stadt, Vineta soll untergehen, weil sie viel Böses getan hat.”

A catastrophic storm surge that swallowed the city whole.

Echoes Beneath the Waves
Coastal communities long claimed that church bells from Vineta can still be heard under the Baltic Sea on certain days.

This motif directly parallels Ys and Rungholt.

Historical Basis Behind the Legend
Medieval Sources
Adam of Bremen and Helmold of Bosau both describe a large, thriving port in the Oder estuary.

Later manuscripts show the name evolving from uimne → Jumne → Vineta, suggesting the legend grew from a real place.

Possible Real Locations
Scholars have proposed several sites:

Wolin Island (Poland) — supported by archaeological evidence of a major Viking‑Age settlement.

Off the coast of Usedom (Germany) — based on early modern maps and local tradition.

No single site has been confirmed, but the historical trading center at Wolin is the strongest candidate.

Why Vineta Matters
Vineta blends real medieval geography, documented trade networks, and centuries of folklore into one of Germany’s most enduring drowned‑city stories.
Like Ys, it warns against hubris, greed, and ignoring omens, and it remains a powerful cultural symbol along the Baltic coast.

WHAT I'M WATCHING TODAY — FRIDAY, NOVEMBER 20, 2026
UK retail sales have surprised to the upside, while U.S. consumer sentiment, inflation expectations and a quieter earnings calendar remain in focus as markets head into the weekend.
My main focus is whether stronger consumer spending can support corporate earnings without adding to inflationary pressures, while technology and infrastructure companies continue to demonstrate the difference between revenue growth and sustainable profitability.
U.S. MACRO — ET
🔹 8:25 AM — Fed Waller Speech
🔹 10:00 AM — Michigan Consumer Sentiment: 51.5 Est. vs 48.0 Previous
🔹 10:00 AM — Michigan 1-Year Inflation Expectations: 4.3% Est. vs 4.7% Previous
🔹 10:00 AM — Michigan 5-Year Inflation Expectations: 3.4% Est. vs 3.5% Previous
🔹 12:15 PM — Fed Cook Speech
🔹 1:00 PM — Baker Hughes Oil Rig Count

🔹 7:00 AM — Retail Sales ex Fuel YoY: +2.5% Actual vs +1.8% Est. | +0.4% Previous
🔹 7:00 AM — Public Sector Net Borrowing ex Banks: £17.0B Actual vs £18.0B Est. | £22.9B Previous
THE CONSUMER & INFLATION QUESTION
UK retail sales have delivered a stronger-than-expected October rebound, rising 0.7% month-on-month against expectations of no growth.
More importantly, sales excluding fuel increased 0.9%, compared with expectations of a 0.1% decline.
That's an encouraging signal for underlying consumer demand, particularly after September's contraction.
However, one strong month doesn't establish a sustained recovery.
I'll be watching whether improving retail activity translates into stronger corporate revenue and margins without renewed inflationary pressure.
In the U.S., consumer sentiment is expected to improve to 51.5, while short-term inflation expectations are projected to ease to 4.3%.
The question is whether households are becoming more confident because purchasing power is improving or whether elevated borrowing costs continue to constrain spending.
Consumer confidence → Spending → Corporate revenue → Margins.
EARNINGS — BEFORE THE BELL
🔹 $BJ — BJ's Wholesale Club
🔹 $WRD — WeRide
🔹 $FRO — Frontline
🔹 $BSP — Bending Spoons
🔹 $IESC — IES Holdings
🔹 $BKE — Buckle
🔹 $RLX — RLX Technology
MY MAIN FOCUS
1. CONSUMER SPENDING — $BJ, $BKE
BJ's Wholesale is my main traditional retail focus today.
I'll be watching comparable sales, membership growth, renewal rates, merchandise margins and management's outlook.
Membership-based retailers provide an interesting test of consumer resilience because recurring membership income can support profitability even when merchandise margins face pressure.
Buckle offers another perspective on discretionary spending, particularly apparel demand, inventories and promotional activity.
2. AUTONOMOUS DRIVING — $WRD
WeRide is my biggest technology focus today.
I'm interested in whether autonomous driving is moving beyond pilot programmes into commercially scalable operations.
I'll be watching fleet deployment, commercial partnerships, revenue growth, operating expenses and cash burn.
The long-term opportunity is significant, but commercial adoption alone doesn't guarantee attractive economics.
The real question is whether higher vehicle utilisation and expanding deployments can eventually offset technology, operating and regulatory costs.
3. AI INFRASTRUCTURE & ELECTRICAL SYSTEMS — $IESC
IES Holdings is particularly interesting given the increasing demand for electrical infrastructure supporting data centres and other power-intensive facilities.
I'll be watching revenue growth, backlog conversion, operating margins, working capital and cash generation.
The AI buildout requires more than GPUs. It also depends on electrical systems, power distribution and the infrastructure needed to bring computing capacity online.
For me, the key question is whether strong infrastructure demand can translate into sustainable margins and attractive returns on capital.
4. ENERGY & SHIPPING — $FRO
Frontline provides exposure to tanker shipping and global crude oil transportation.
I'll be watching tanker rates, fleet utilisation, operating cash flow and capital allocation.
Shipping remains cyclical, so the sustainability of earnings matters more than any single strong quarter.
5. DIGITAL CONSUMER BUSINESSES — $RLX, $BSP
I'll be watching revenue quality, customer demand, operating leverage and cash generation.
For digital businesses, profitable growth and disciplined capital allocation remain more important than expansion for its own sake.
MY TAKE
The UK consumer has delivered a stronger-than-expected start to today's economic calendar, but the broader market is facing two important tests: consumer resilience and the sustainability of capital-intensive growth.
Stronger spending can support corporate earnings, but it may also complicate the outlook for interest-rate cuts if inflation remains persistent.
Meanwhile, with global technology and semiconductor stocks under pressure, investors are increasingly distinguishing between strong demand, profitable growth and attractive returns on capital.
I'm particularly interested in WeRide and IES Holdings because they represent different parts of the infrastructure investment cycle.
Autonomous driving depends on commercial deployment, utilisation and improving unit economics.
Electrical infrastructure benefits from demand for power-intensive facilities, but execution, margins and cash conversion ultimately determine shareholder returns.
The same principle applies to AI infrastructure.
Technology can be transformative, demand can be real and investment can accelerate. But those conditions alone don't guarantee attractive returns.
WHAT MATTERS NEXT
Consumer confidence → Spending → Revenue growth → Margins
Inflation expectations → Fed policy → Treasury yields → Valuations
Autonomous driving → Commercial deployment → Utilisation → Unit economics
AI infrastructure → Power availability → Capacity deployment → Cash returns
Revenue growth → Free cash flow → Returns on invested capital
That's what I'll be watching as we close out the trading week.

West Virginia University (WVU) announced a partnership with South Korean esports organization @GenG Esports on November 18 to offer an industry practicum for students at the team's headquarters in Seoul.

The Gen.G Practicum Abroad @gengacademy program is now an approved affiliate provider with WVU Abroad, allowing students to earn academic credit. Participants can join Gen.G's international cohorts individually or travel with a WVU group for a three-week program. The partnership primarily targets students in WVU's Esports Business and Entertainment degree and related sport management programs.

The practicum features five tracks: Business, Marketing, Content Creation, Education, and Game Development. Students contribute to ongoing initiatives and present their final projects directly to Gen.G executives. The first WVU group will travel to Seoul in summer 2027.

Josh Steger, Director of @WVUEsports at WVU, said that the collaboration with Gen.G will allow WVU to improve students' career readiness when they graduate. Additionally, Nicole Choi, founder of Gen.G Practicum Abroad, noted that Gen.G designed the program to "bridge the gap between classroom learning and professional practice."

WVU joins other US universities participating in the program, including Arizona State, Hawaii, Kansas, Kentucky, and Syracuse. By connecting US students with South Korea's mature esports infrastructure, universities are moving beyond campus gaming clubs to build structured career pathways in the global industry.

text:
With seemingly no limit to the demand for artificial intelligence, everyone in the energy, AI, and climate fields is justifiably worried. Will there be enough clean electricity to power AI and enough water to cool the data centers that support this technology? These are important questions with serious implications for communities, the economy, and the environment. 

This story is a part of MIT Technology Review’s series “Power Hungry: AI and our energy future,” on the energy demands and carbon costs of the artificial-intelligence revolution.

But the question about AI’s energy usage portends even bigger issues about what we need to do in addressing climate change for the next several decades. If we can’t work out how to handle this, we won’t be able to handle broader electrification of the economy, and the climate risks we face will increase.

Innovation in IT got us to this point. Graphics processing units (GPUs) that power the computing behind AI have fallen in cost by 99% since 2006. There was similar concern about the energy use of data centers in the early 2010s, with wild projections of growth in electricity demand. But gains in computing power and energy efficiency not only proved these projections wrong but enabled a 550% increase in global computing capability from 2010 to 2018 with only minimal increases in energy use. 

In the late 2010s, however, the trends that had saved us began to break. As the accuracy of AI models dramatically improved, the electricity needed for data centers also started increasing faster; they now account for 4.4% of total demand, up  from 1.9% in 2018. Data centers consume more than 10% of the electricity supply in six US states. In Virginia, which has emerged as a hub of data center activity, that figure is 25%.

Projections about the future demand for energy to power AI are uncertain and range widely, but in one study, Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory estimated that data centers could represent 6% to 12% of total US electricity use by 2028. Communities and companies will notice this type of rapid growth in electricity demand. It will put pressure on energy prices and on ecosystems. The projections have resulted in calls to build lots of new fossil-fired power plants or bring older ones out of retirement. In many parts of the US, the demand will likely result in a surge of natural-gas-powered plants.

It’s a daunting situation. Yet when we zoom out, the projected electricity use from AI is still pretty small. The US generated about 4,300 billion kilowatt-hours last year. We’ll likely need another 1,000 billion to 1,200 billion or more in the next decade—a 24% to 29% increase. Almost half the additional electricity demand will be from electrified vehicles. Another 30% is expected to be from electrified technologies in buildings and industry. Innovation in vehicle and building electrification also advanced in the last decade, and this shift will be good news for the climate, for communities, and for energy costs.

The remaining 22% of new electricity demand is estimated to come from AI and data centers. While it represents a smaller piece of the pie, it’s the most urgent one. Because of their rapid growth and geographic concentration, data centers are the electrification challenge we face right now—the small stuff we have to figure out before we’re able to do the big stuff like vehicles and buildings.

We also need to understand what the energy consumption and carbon emissions associated with AI are buying us. While the impacts from producing semiconductors and powering AI data centers are important, they are likely small compared with the positive or negative effects AI may have on applications such as the electricity grid, the transportation system, buildings and factories, or consumer behavior. Companies could use AI to develop new materials or batteries that would better integrate renewable energy into the grid. But they could also use AI to make it easier to find more fossil fuels. The claims about potential benefits for the climate are exciting, but they need to be continuously verified and will need support to be realized.

This isn’t the first time we’ve faced challenges coping with growth in electricity demand. In the 1960s, US electricity demand was growing at more than 7% per year. In the 1970s that growth was nearly 5%, and in the 1980s and 1990s it was more than 2% per year. Then, starting in 2005, we basically had a decade and a half of flat electricity growth. Most projections for the next decade put our expected growth in electricity demand at around 2% again—but this time we’ll have to do things differently. 

To manage these new energy demands, we need a “Grid New Deal” that leverages public and private capital to rebuild the electricity system for AI with enough capacity and intelligence for decarbonization. New clean energy supplies, investment in transmission and distribution, and strategies for virtual demand management can cut emissions, lower prices, and increase resilience. Data centers bringing clean electricity and distribution system upgrades could be given a fast lane to connect to the grid. Infrastructure banks could fund new transmission lines or pay to upgrade existing ones. Direct investment or tax incentives could encourage clean computing standards, workforce development in the clean energy sector, and open data transparency from data center operators about their energy use so that communities can understand and measure the impacts.

In 2022, the White House released a Blueprint for an AI Bill of Rights that provided principles to protect the public’s rights, opportunities, and access to critical resources from being restricted by AI systems. To the AI Bill of Rights, we humbly offer a climate amendment, because ethical AI must be climate-safe AI. It’s a starting point to ensure that the growth of AI works for everyone—that it doesn’t raise people’s energy bills, adds more clean power to the grid than it uses, increases investment in the power system’s infrastructure, and benefits communities while driving innovation.

By grounding the conversation about AI and energy in context about what is needed to tackle climate change, we can deliver better outcomes for communities, ecosystems, and the economy. The growth of electricity demand for AI and data centers is a test case for how society will respond to the demands and challenges of broader electrification. If we get this wrong, the likelihood of meeting our climate targets will be extremely low. This is what we mean when we say the energy and climate impacts from data centers are small, but they are also huge.

Costa Samaras is the Trustee Professor of Civil and Environmental Engineering and director of the Scott Institute for Energy Innovation at Carnegie Mellon University.

Emma Strubell is the Raj Reddy Assistant Professor in the Language Technologies Institute in the School of Computer Science at Carnegie Mellon University.

Ramayya Krishnan is dean of the Heinz College of Information Systems and Public Policy and the William W. and Ruth F. Cooper Professor of Management Science and Information Systems at Carnegie Mellon University.

🐓 THE GUARDIAN OF AWAKENING

THE ROOSTER — HERALD OF THE NEW DAWN

Scroll VIII of the Nine Guardians | The Council of Twelve
Before the first golden rays of sunlight touched the mountains, before the valleys stirred from their slumber, and before the creatures of the Zodiac Kingdom opened their eyes, a magnificent Celestial Rooster stood upon the highest tower of the Great Observatory.

His feathers shimmered with crimson, sapphire, emerald and molten gold. His magnificent tail swept behind him like a river of living fire, and upon his brow rested a radiant crown shaped like the first rays of sunrise.

His eyes were clear, his posture proud, and his voice carried across the mountains.

He did not command the sun to rise.

He simply recognised its arrival.

FOR THE ROOSTER UNDERSTOOD THAT AWAKENING IS NOT THE POWER TO FORCE ANOTHER TO SEE, BUT THE COURAGE TO BRING LIGHT, CLARITY AND UNDERSTANDING WHERE CONFUSION ONCE PREVAILED.

And every morning, he greeted the world with a single declaration:

"ARISE, NOT BECAUSE THE WORLD IS PERFECT, BUT BECAUSE ANOTHER DAY HAS GIVEN US THE OPPORTUNITY TO MAKE IT BETTER."

Thus began the story of the Guardian of Awakening — Herald of the New Dawn.

I. THE TRIAL OF THE FIRST LIGHT

One morning, the Silver Dragon summoned the Rooster before the Council of Twelve.

"Tell me, Guardian," she asked, "what does it mean to awaken?"

The Rooster spread his magnificent wings.

"To become aware of what we have overlooked, to recognise what we do not understand, and to accept responsibility for what we choose to do next."

The White Rabbit's ears rose.

"BUT WHAT IF SOMEONE IS NOT READY TO WAKE UP?"

"Then we must respect their freedom, little Rabbit. A truth shouted into unwilling ears may become only noise."

The Tiger stepped forward.

"And if injustice is hidden beneath the darkness?"

"Then we must investigate it fairly and bring evidence into the light."

The Dog raised his head.

"And if truth threatens the trust of those we love?"

"Then we speak with honesty and compassion, remembering that trust built upon deception cannot remain strong."

The Ox lowered his mighty horns.

"And what if the foundations of our understanding are mistaken?"

"Then we rebuild them upon better knowledge."

The Serpent watched thoughtfully.

"And if we discover that the light reveals something different from what we expected?"

The Rooster bowed.

"THEN WE MUST HAVE THE HUMILITY TO CHANGE OUR MINDS."

The Monkey somersaulted onto the Council table.

"AND WHAT IF THE NEW DAY BRINGS AN OPPORTUNITY TO INVENT SOMETHING MAGNIFICENT?"

The Rooster laughed.

"Then, dear Monkey, let us begin!"

Finally, the Silver Dragon asked:

"And what if the world refuses to recognise your song?"

The Rooster looked towards the horizon.

"Then I shall remember that my responsibility is not to control what others believe. It is to communicate clearly, act honestly and welcome those who wish to listen."

The Dragon smiled.

"THEN YOU UNDERSTAND THAT TRUE AWAKENING IS NOT SUPERIORITY OVER THOSE WHO SEE DIFFERENTLY. IT IS AN INVITATION TO GREATER AWARENESS, WISDOM AND RESPONSIBILITY."

And so the Council welcomed the Herald of the New Dawn.

II. THE OATH OF THE CELESTIAL ROOSTER

I shall greet each new day with gratitude and purpose.

I shall speak truth without demanding obedience.

I shall bring clarity where confusion obscures understanding.

I shall question assumptions without humiliating those who hold them.

I shall welcome correction when evidence reveals my mistakes.

I shall remain vigilant without surrendering to fear.

I shall honour the freedom of every being to think, question and learn.

And I shall remember that awakening is not a single moment of revelation, but a lifelong willingness to grow.

FOR TRUE AWAKENING IS THE COURAGE TO SEE MORE CLEARLY, AND TRUE ENLIGHTENMENT IS THE HUMILITY TO RECOGNISE HOW MUCH REMAINS TO BE LEARNED.

III. THE ROOSTER'S SEVEN VIRTUES

01

Awareness

Recognise what has been overlooked.

02

Clarity

Communicate accurately and without unnecessary confusion.

03

Vigilance

Identify risks without encouraging fear.

04

Accountability

Accept responsibility for words and actions.

05

Honesty

Speak truth with courage and compassion.

06

Humility

Welcome new evidence and correction.

07

Renewal

Recognise each day as an opportunity to learn and grow.

IV. THE SEAL OF THE HERALD

Colorful Rooster Illustration in Sunlit Cloudscape | Deep Dream Generator

Sacred emblem: A magnificent Celestial Rooster standing upon a golden observatory tower, his wings spread before a radiant sunrise, seven rays illuminating the horizon.
Element: Dawn Light, Air and the Flame of Renewal.

Guardian's charge: Encourage awareness, uphold honest communication, identify overlooked risks and ensure truth can be examined openly.

Council alliance: The Goat/Ram nurtures Compassion. The Pig protects Generosity. The Rooster brings Clarity and Accountability.

Together, they complete the Harmonisers' Triad.

V. THE THREE BELLS OF AWAKENING

At the summit of the Great Observatory hung three magnificent golden bells.

The Rooster approached the first.

Upon its surface was inscribed:

I. AWAKEN TO AWARENESS

Notice what is happening, question assumptions and recognise the difference between appearance and understanding.

The Rooster rang the bell.

Its clear tone echoed across the valley.

He approached the second.

II. AWAKEN TO RESPONSIBILITY

Recognise the consequences of our choices and the responsibilities we share towards one another.

The second bell rang.

Its sound blended with the first.

Finally, he approached the third.

III. AWAKEN TO POSSIBILITY

Remember that knowledge can grow, systems can improve, and the future remains open to responsible human choice.

The third bell rang.

A magnificent harmony filled the kingdom.

The White Rabbit closed his eyes.

"Three bells, three different notes, yet one song."

The Rooster nodded.

"Awareness without responsibility may become passive observation. Responsibility without hope may become despair. And hope without understanding may lead us astray."

The Silver Dragon smiled.

"Then the three must remain together."

AWARENESS. RESPONSIBILITY. POSSIBILITY.

And beneath the bells, the Rooster placed one final inscription:

"THE DAWN DOES NOT PROMISE A PERFECT DAY. IT OFFERS THE CHANCE TO CREATE A BETTER ONE."

VI. THE GREAT BABYLONIAN WAKE-UP CALL

Professor Asa Rahrio burst into the Council Chamber wearing his ceremonial double-tweed waistcoat, an enormous nightcap and slippers decorated with miniature golden roosters.

"GUARDIANS! WE HAVE A MOST ALARMING DEVELOPMENT!"

The White Rabbit looked up from his book.

"Professor, why are you wearing pyjamas?"

"BECAUSE I HAVE BEEN CONDUCTING AN EXPERIMENT!"

The Celestial Rat adjusted his spectacles.

"What kind of experiment?"

"A COMPREHENSIVE STUDY OF THE BABYLONIAN GOVERNMENT'S ABILITY TO SLEEP THROUGH ITS OWN RESPONSIBILITIES!"

The Ox frowned.

"And your findings?"

"EXTRAORDINARY! THEY HAVE MANAGED TO SLEEP THROUGH EVERY WARNING, EVERY AUDIT AND EVERY REQUEST FOR ACCOUNTABILITY!"

The Serpent tilted her emerald head.

"Professor, are those findings supported by evidence?"

"AH. WELL. I MAY HAVE BEEN SPEAKING METAPHORICALLY."

The Rooster stepped forward.

"Then perhaps, Professor, we should distinguish satire from verified findings."

The Professor nodded.

"EXCELLENT POINT! BUT I STILL BELIEVE WE REQUIRE AN ENORMOUS WAKE-UP CALL!"

The Monkey grinned.

"I CAN BUILD ONE!"

The Rat immediately looked concerned.

"What exactly are you proposing?"

"A MECHANICAL ALARM CLOCK WITH TWELVE BELLS, A SOLAR-POWERED HORN AND A GIANT SPRING-LOADED ROOSTER!"

The Ox sighed.

"Has anyone examined the structural specifications?"

The Dog asked:

"Or the safety implications?"

The Snake narrowed her eyes.

"Or whether this device is necessary?"

The Monkey paused.

"Well..."

The Rooster raised one wing.

"Perhaps we should begin with something simpler."

The Professor leaned forward.

"SUCH AS?"

The Rooster opened the Council Chamber windows.

The morning sunlight streamed inside.

He took a deep breath.

And crowed:

"COCK-A-DOODLE-DOOOOOOO!"

The sound echoed across the mountains.

The White Rabbit dropped his pen.

The Fire Horse reared.

The Dragon laughed.

And Professor Asa Rahrio leapt three feet into the air.

"GOOD HEAVENS! WHO AUTHORIZED THAT ALARM?"

The Rooster smiled.

"Nature, Professor."

The Monkey looked disappointed.

"So we don't need the giant mechanical rooster?"

"Not necessarily," replied the Rat. "But I would still like to examine your drawings."

The Professor adjusted his nightcap.

"VERY WELL! BUT I MUST INSIST THAT THE MINUTES RECORD THE FOLLOWING!"

The Rabbit dipped his quill.

"Go ahead."

"THE COUNCIL HAS OFFICIALLY BEEN WOKEN UP BY A COCK WHO KNOWS WHAT HE'S TALKING ABOUT!"

The Chamber fell silent.

The Monkey exploded with laughter.

The Dragon covered her face with one magnificent wing.

And the Rooster simply replied:

"PROFESSOR, PERHAPS YOU SHOULD HAVE A CUP OF TEA BEFORE ADDRESSING THE PUBLIC."

The Rabbit solemnly recorded:

Item 721: The Guardian of Awakening has successfully conducted the first ceremonial Dawn Announcement. Professor Asa Rahrio has been advised to review his phrasing before publication.

THE RABBIT STILL WRITES. 🐇📜🤣

VII. THE FINAL DECLARATION

As the first golden rays of sunlight illuminated the Council Chamber, the Celestial Rooster ascended the Observatory Tower.

His magnificent feathers reflected the awakening sky.

Below him stood the Guardians of Courage, Loyalty, Integrity, Ingenuity, Discernment, Compassion, Innovation and Imagination.

The Silver Dragon spread her wings.

The White Rabbit opened his book.

And the Fire Horse stood ready for the journey ahead.

The Rooster raised his head and proclaimed:

LET AWARENESS REPLACE INDIFFERENCE.

LET CLARITY CHALLENGE CONFUSION.

LET COURAGE SUPPORT THE TRUTH.

LET HUMILITY TEMPER CERTAINTY.

LET RESPONSIBILITY GUIDE OUR CHOICES.

LET COMPASSION ACCOMPANY EVERY AWAKENING.

AND LET EACH NEW DAWN REMIND US THAT A BETTER FUTURE IS STILL POSSIBLE.

VIGILANTIA · VERITAS · RENOVATIO · LUX

Vigilance. Truth. Renewal. Light.

THE HERALD'S ETERNAL INSCRIPTION

"THE GREATEST AWAKENING IS NOT THE MOMENT WE BELIEVE WE KNOW EVERYTHING, BUT THE MOMENT WE REALISE HOW MUCH MORE WE CAN LEARN, UNDERSTAND AND CREATE TOGETHER."

And beneath the inscription, the White Rabbit added:

"THE LIGHT DOES NOT BELONG TO THE ONE WHO ANNOUNCES THE DAWN. IT BELONGS TO EVERYONE WHO LIVES BENEATH THE SUN."

The Rooster bowed.

The Dragon smiled.

The Fire Horse neighed with joy.

And Professor Asa Rahrio, finally removing his nightcap, announced:

"BY JOVE! I BELIEVE WE HAVE OFFICIALLY ENTERED THE AGE OF ENLIGHTENMENT!"

The Rabbit looked at him.

"Professor, we are still missing the Pig."

The Professor froze.

"THE PIG?"

"Yes, Professor. The Guardian of Abundance."

The Professor gasped.

"GOOD HEAVENS! WE'VE BEEN CONDUCTING THE ENTIRE COUNCIL WITHOUT A PROPER BREAKFAST!"

The Rooster crowed.

The Monkey laughed.

And somewhere in the distant valley, a magnificent golden Pig prepared to make his entrance.

THE RABBIT STILL WRITES.

ONE COUNCIL. TWELVE GUARDIANS. ONE LOVE.

text:
The Opposition Is Preparing to Remove Ruto, but Nobody Appears to Be Preparing to Inherit His Problems

There is something seriously wrong with the Kenyan opposition, and I am increasingly concerned that the politicians seeking to replace William Ruto do not appreciate the magnitude of the problems they are preparing to inherit.

Look at what happened this week when opposition leaders confronted the IEBC over preparations for the 2027 elections.

They assembled politicians, lawyers, technical experts and former senior government officials to demand electoral reforms, independent audits of the voter register, changes to results transmission and greater transparency in election technology.

There is nothing wrong with demanding credible elections, and Kenyans have every reason to insist that the IEBC gets its preparations right.

But the meeting exposed something else that I think deserves serious attention.

The opposition appears to have invested more energy in preparing to win the election than in explaining how it intends to run Kenya after winning.

Kenya is facing an economic crisis that cannot be solved by removing William Ruto from State House and replacing him with another politician.

Our public debt has grown beyond KSh13 trillion, the government is spending enormous amounts of money servicing loans, businesses are struggling with taxation and millions of Kenyans are finding it difficult to survive.

We have families that cannot afford basic healthcare, unemployed graduates who have lost hope, struggling businesses closing their doors and ordinary people whose incomes can no longer support their daily expenses.

Then there are the killings during protests, allegations of enforced disappearances, police brutality and the disturbing questions about the conduct of security agencies under Ruto's administration.

These are serious national problems, and the next government will inherit every single one of them.

Now look at the opposition.

We have Kalonzo Musyoka, David Maraga, Okiya Omtatah, Edwin Sifuna, Rigathi Gachagua and several other politicians positioning themselves for leadership ahead of 2027.

They are holding meetings, attending rallies, negotiating alliances, establishing political movements and arguing about who should become the presidential candidate.

But where is the urgency in preparing to govern?

Where are the economists, public finance experts, healthcare professionals and experienced administrators who should be working with these politicians to produce a serious recovery programme?

Where is the opposition's collective proposal on public debt, and what exactly does it intend to do about the billions Kenya must continue paying long after Ruto leaves office?

Some opposition leaders have presented individual proposals, but Kenyans deserve a clear explanation of how those promises will be funded and carried out.

It is very easy to stand on a political platform and promise to reduce taxes, create jobs, eliminate corruption and make life affordable.

The difficult part is explaining where the money will come from, which government expenses will be reduced and what happens to public services when certain taxes are removed.

Suppose the opposition defeats Ruto in August 2027. What happens on the first morning the new President reports to State House?

Does the public debt disappear?

Do hospitals suddenly receive adequate funding?

Do unemployed graduates wake up to find jobs waiting for them?

Do the police officers implicated in unlawful killings suddenly face justice?

Does the cost of living automatically come down?

Of course not.

The new President will inherit the same Treasury, the same debt obligations, the same struggling public institutions and the same frustrated population expecting immediate results.

And Kenyans will not be interested in listening to another President spend five years explaining how the previous administration destroyed the economy.

That is exactly what Ruto has been doing with his repeated claims about inheriting a financially distressed government from Uhuru Kenyatta.

The opposition should be telling us how it intends to avoid repeating that behaviour.

Instead, we are witnessing political disagreements about party leadership, coalition arrangements, presidential ambitions and who should control which political outfit.

I find it particularly worrying that politicians who cannot agree on basic arrangements within their own movements are asking Kenyans to trust them with the management of an entire country.

The disagreements between emerging opposition leaders may be normal political competition, but they become a serious concern when leadership positions appear to receive more attention than the problems the leaders are promising to solve.

Kenya does not need another group of politicians whose biggest achievement will be inheriting Ruto's offices, vehicles, security arrangements, privileges and control over public resources.

The opposition should be competing over who has the most convincing programme for repairing the economy, reducing government waste, creating employment and restoring confidence in public institutions.

I would expect the opposition to have a serious team examining the national budget, identifying wasteful spending and explaining which programmes can be reviewed without interfering with services that ordinary Kenyans depend on.

I would expect detailed proposals on restructuring government expenditure, dealing with pending bills, improving healthcare and creating conditions in which small businesses can survive.

I would expect a clear commitment on investigating unlawful killings and enforced disappearances, including how the institutions responsible for those investigations would be protected from political interference.

And I would expect the politicians seeking the presidency to spend considerably more time explaining these proposals than discussing their personal political ambitions.

The tragedy is that Ruto's administration has given the opposition more than enough serious issues to confront.

Public borrowing, taxation, government expenditure, corruption allegations, healthcare complaints and the treatment of protesters should be dominating the national political conversation.

Yet the opposition has not demonstrated the same collective urgency in presenting solutions that it has shown in organising political campaigns and preparing for elections.

Public anger against William Ruto is not automatic confidence in the opposition.

Kenyans can be deeply unhappy with the current government and still question whether the people seeking to replace it have the competence, preparation and seriousness required to do a better job.

And if the opposition genuinely does not know how to solve these problems, its leaders should admit that Kenya's difficulties require more than the usual political class.

They should sit down with ordinary citizens, professionals, business owners, economists and people directly affected by government failures to develop a credible national recovery programme.

Political leadership is supposed to help citizens solve their problems, not simply offer a new personality for them to celebrate every five years.

Removing Ruto is a political objective. Repairing Kenya is a national responsibility.

The opposition has shown Kenyans how seriously it takes the process of getting into government. Now it must demonstrate that it takes the responsibility of running that government equally seriously.

The greatest tragedy would be for Kenyans to fight so hard to remove Ruto, celebrate his defeat and then discover that the politicians who spent years demanding his departure never prepared themselves for the responsibility of governing.

Kenya cannot afford another government that wins an election first and begins looking for solutions after taking office.

राजा भैया राम कथा नहीं, ठाकुर मिलन सम्मेलन करवा रहे हैं, तैयारी 2027 की है

राजा भैया प्रतापगढ़ में अपने क्षेत्र कुंडा में चार दिन की राम कथा करा रहे हैं। व्यास पीठ पर बैठकर कथा सुना रहे हैं पंडित धीरेंद्र शास्त्री। कहने को यह राम कथा है, लेकिन अगर इसे राजनीतिक नज़र से देखें, तो यह ठाकुरों और ब्राह्मणों का एक मिलन समारोह ज़्यादा लगता है।

मिलन समारोह से किसी को दिक्कत नहीं हो सकती। लेकिन जब उत्तर प्रदेश में 2027 का चुनाव सामने हो, और बार-बार यह आरोप लग रहा हो कि ब्राह्मण और सवर्ण वर्ग भाजपा से नाराज़ चल रहे हैं, तब राजा भैया का यह आयोजन और इसमें आने वाले चेहरे बहुत कुछ कहते हैं।

ज़रा देखिए, मंच पर कौन-कौन पहुंचा। सबसे पहले बृजभूषण शरण सिंह, ठाकुर राजनीति के बड़े चेहरे, जिन्होंने मंच से यहां तक कह दिया कि "राजा भैया रहेंगे।" जौनपुर के पूर्व सांसद धनंजय सिंह भी पहुंचे, और उनके दोस्त बृजेश सिंह भी, जो बनारस के पास चंदौली इलाके के बाहुबली नेता माने जाते हैं। बृजेश सिंह का मुख्तार अंसारी से और अजय राय के भाई अवधेश राय वाले मामले से क्या जुड़ाव रहा, वह एक अलग कहानी है।

भोजपुरी गायक और अब राजनीति में सक्रिय पवन सिंह भी आए, और राजस्थान से रविंद्र सिंह भाटी भी। योगी सरकार के मंत्री दिनेश प्रताप सिंह, सपा से भाजपा में गए मनोज पांडेय, सपा से बगावत कर चुके गोसाईगंज के विधायक अभय सिंह और गौरीगंज के विधायक राकेश प्रताप सिंह भी मौजूद रहे। इनके अलावा मिर्ज़ापुर से एक MLC, सुल्तानपुर से शैलेश सिंह, लखनऊ शिक्षक क्षेत्र से उमेश द्विवेदी और यशवंत सिंह भी पहुंचे।

इसी मंच पर भाजपा सांसद निशिकांत दुबे भी आए और कई बयान दिए। अश्विनी उपाध्याय भी थे, और बाबा रामदेव भी। सबसे दिलचस्प तस्वीर रही बाबा रामदेव और बृजभूषण शरण सिंह की, जो मंच पर एक-दूसरे से गले मिले। वही दोनों, जिनके बीच पतंजलि के देसी घी को लेकर खूब बयानबाज़ी हुई थी और मामला कोर्ट तक गया था। अब यह कड़वाहट इसी मंच पर शांत होती दिखी।

एक नाम जो यहां नहीं दिखा, वह था राजीव प्रताप रूडी, जो खुद एक बड़े राजपूत नेता हैं। कॉन्स्टिट्यूशन क्लब के चुनाव में रूडी ने संजीव बालियान को हराया था, जिसमें विपक्ष के सांसदों का साथ उन्हें मिला था, और उस वक्त निशिकांत दुबे बालियान के पक्ष में खुलकर बोले थे। शायद यही वजह रही कि रूडी इस मंच से दूर रहे।

राजा भैया भले कहें कि वे इसे चुनावी नज़रिए से नहीं देखते, लेकिन अगर इस पूरे आयोजन को गहराई से पढ़ें, तो साफ दिखता है कि यह चुनाव की तैयारी है। कथा के मंच पर ठाकुर और ब्राह्मण नेताओं की एक पूरी लॉबी जुट गई है। नेता आएंगे, हाथ हिलाएंगे, और संदेश दूर तक जाएगा।

और यह संदेश सिर्फ प्रतापगढ़ या कुंडा तक नहीं रहेगा। बाहर के लोगों तक भी पहुंचेगा कि धर्म के नाम पर कैसा बड़ा आयोजन हुआ। मीडिया हेडलाइन बनाकर आगे बढ़ जाएगा, लेकिन असल में यह हो क्यों रहा है, यह समझना ज़रूरी है। इसका असर चुनाव में कितना होगा, यह तो बाद में पता चलेगा, लेकिन खेल किस तरह चल रहा है, यह अभी से दिख रहा है। https://t.co/T5vmJqJNBR

text:
"Just came from the interview across the street?"

"Yeah. How did you know?"

"Their director sends everyone from out of town here. Says nobody should have to ride home after an interview on an empty stomach."

I just stood there staring at the envelope.

No secret honesty test. No hidden camera. No mind game.

He'd simply seen my hometown on my résumé, done the math on what time I had to wake up to make that trip, and quietly made sure I ate before heading back.

Three days later, I got the offer. When I asked him about the note during my first week, he just laughed: "You made that whole trip early in the morning. Least we could do was let you catch your breath."

I've been there eight months now. Every time an out-of-town candidate comes in, he has me prep their envelope.

Last week, I added six extra words to the back so they wouldn't sit there paranoid like I did:

"If you have time, grab a coffee. The interview is already over."

Corporate culture is so broken that a single act of basic human decency feels like a trap.

Forget the "core values" painted on the office wall—judge a company by how it treats people it doesn't owe anything to yet.

What's the weirdest secret interview test—or rarest act of real decency—you've ever run into?

text:
American Airlines Flight Makes Emergency Return to Phoenix After Engine Flames Reported

An American Airlines jet carrying 120 people declared a "Mayday" emergency and safely returned to Phoenix Sky Harbor International Airport shortly after takeoff on Thursday afternoon following reports of flames coming from an engine and a hydraulic system failure.

American Airlines Flight 3230, an Airbus A319 bound for Portland, Oregon, departed Phoenix at 4:14 p.m. local time. Moments after liftoff, the crew of a trailing SkyWest Airlines flight alerted air traffic control that they observed flames emitting from one of the Airbus jet's engines, along with what appeared to be a fluid leak.

Air traffic controllers immediately relayed the warning to the American Airlines pilots. According to air traffic control audio, the flight crew confirmed they were already troubleshooting a hydraulic issue and intended to turn back.

When controllers asked the crew to confirm their intentions, the pilots declared, "Mayday, Mayday, Mayday," and requested radar vectors to return to Sky Harbor. Controllers offered the option to remain airborne to burn off excess fuel before landing, which the pilots declined, confirming there were 120 people on board.

After spending approximately 20 minutes in the air, the aircraft touched down safely at 4:34 p.m. with emergency vehicles standing by on the runway. The plane taxied to Gate C17 under its own power, and no injuries were reported among the passengers or crew. 

In a statement, an American Airlines spokesperson confirmed the aircraft was taken out of service for a full maintenance inspection. 

The airline confirmed that passengers deplaned normally and were rebooked on a replacement flight to Portland later that evening, while emphasizing that safety remains their top priority.

text:
To the best of my knowledge, I am not a robot. And yet, like other humans who spend too much time on the internet, I’m routinely asked to prove this fact by clicking on crosswalks and motorcycles in photos, deciphering distorted numbers and letters, and checking little white boxes that affirm my non-robot status. These so-called captchas, or “completely automated public Turing tests to tell computers and humans apart,” are supposed to help prevent spam and data scraping, although it now appears that bots are better at solving them than humans. Go figure. 

Thankfully, the difference between humans and machines in the real world is much easier to discern, at least for now. One of the more robust differentiators involves our unique skill sets. While machines tend to excel at things adults find difficult—playing world-champion-level chess, say, or multiplying really big numbers—they find it difficult (or impossible) to accomplish the stuff a five-year-old can do with ease, such as catching a ball or walking around a room without bumping into things. 

This discrepancy between the relative ease of teaching a machine abstract thinking and the difficulty of teaching it basic sensory, social, and motor skills is what’s known as Moravec’s paradox. Named after an observation the roboticist Hans Moravec made back in the late 1980s, the paradox states that what’s hard for humans (math, logic, scientific reasoning) is easy for machines, and what’s hard for machines (tying shoelaces, reading emotions, having a conversation) is easy for humans. 

In her latest book, Robots and the People Who Love Them: Holding On to Our Humanity in an Age of Social Robots, science writer Eve Herold argues that thanks to new approaches in machine learning and continued advances in AI, we’re finally starting to unravel this paradox. As a result, a new era of personal and social robots is about to unfold, she says—one that will force us to reimagine the nature of everything from friendship and love to work, health care, and home life. 

To give readers a sense of what this brave new world of social robots will look like, Herold points us toward Pepper, a doe-eyed humanoid robot that’s made by the Japanese company SoftBank. “Robots like Pepper will soon make themselves indispensable because of their unique, highly personalized relationships with us,” Herold writes, before describing with press-release-like zeal how this chest-high companion can effortlessly read our expressions and emotional states and respond appropriately in its own childlike voice.

If Pepper sounds vaguely familiar, it may be because it was relentlessly hyped as the world’s first “emotional robot” in the years following its 2014 introduction. That abruptly stopped in 2021, however, when SoftBank pulled the plug on Pepper production because of lack of demand and—probably not unrelatedly—the $2,000 android’s general incompetence. Books can obviously take a long time to write, and a lot can change while you’re writing them. But it’s hard to reconcile this particular oversight with the fact that Pepper was canned some three years before the book’s publication.  

Positioning a defunct product that nobody seems to have liked or bought as part of some vanguard for a new social-­robot revolution doesn’t inspire confidence. Herold might respond by pointing out that her book’s focus is less on the robots themselves than on what we humans will bring to the new social relationships we forge with them. Fair enough. 

But while she dutifully unpacks our penchant for anthropomorphizing and walks readers through some rudimentary research on deep learning and the uncanny valley, Herold’s conclusions about human nature and psychology often seem either oversimplified or divorced from the evidence she provides. For someone who says that “the only way to write about the future is with a high degree of humility,” there are also an unusually large number of deeply questionable assertions (“So far, the trust we’ve placed in algorithms has been, on balance, well placed …”) and sweeping predictions (“There’s no doubt some version of a companion robot will be coming soon to homes throughout the industrialized world”).   

Early on in the book, Herold reminds readers that “science writing that attempts to envision the future often says much more about the time it was written than it says about the future world.” In this respect, Robots and the People Who Love Them is indeed quite revealing. Among other things, the book reflects the way we tend to reduce discussions of technological impacts into binary terms (“It’ll be amazing”/”It’ll be terrible”); the shrugging acquiescence with which we seem to regard undesirable outcomes; the readiness of science and technology writers to succumb to industry hype; and the disturbing extent to which the logic and values of machines (speed, efficiency) have already been adopted by humans. It’s probably not one of Herold’s intended takeaways, but if the book demonstrates anything, it’s not that robots are becoming more like us; it’s that we’re becoming more like them. 

For a more rigorous look at one of the pillars of human social expression—and, specifically, how we’ve tried to transfer it to machines—Sarah A. Bell’s Vox ex Machina: A Cultural History of Talking Machines offers a compelling and insightful history of voice synthesis during the 20th century. Bell, a writer and professor at Michigan Technological University, is interested in how we try to digitally reproduce different expressions of human embodiment, be it speech, emotions, or visual identities. As she points out early on in the book, understanding this process often means understanding the ways in which engineers (almost universally male ones) have decided to measure and quantify aspects of our bodies.

The story begins at the epicenter for many of the century’s most important technological breakthroughs: Bell Labs. By the 1930s, researchers there were already thinking about human speech as a type of signal or, as the head of the acoustics research department put it years later, “specialized acoustic code.” One of those engineers, Homer Dudley, likened the tongue to a telegraph tapper, seeing it as merely an instrument inside our mouths that “modulated the ‘carrier wave’ emanating from the glottis.” In the same way that Morse code broke down writing into parts for later reassembly, Dudley believed, speech sounds—and everything else that makes up the richness of human vocal expression—could similarly be compressed, or reduced to pulses.

According to Bell, researchers like Dudley laid the groundwork for pretty much all the voice synthesis work that has come since, “embedding their assumptions about the mechanical nature of the human voice in all the technologies that would follow.” One of the first and most famous examples of Dudley’s work was the Voder, or Voice Demonstrator. Debuting at the 1939 World’s Fair in New York, it was basically a small voice organ that was operated by “Voderettes,” women who went through a year of training to master all the speech sounds the machine could make by manipulating 10 keys, a wrist plate, and a pedal. 

The talking-machine demonstrations, although highly choreographed, were a hit with visitors and the press—so much so that people seemed willing to attribute far more understanding and autonomy to the Voder than was warranted. Even though the Voderette was in full view during the entire demonstration, the press usually mentioned the woman responsible for making the sounds only in passing, if at all. Instead, the Voder was anthropomorphized and granted a high degree of agency. “He hasn’t any mouth, lungs, or larynx—but he talks a blue streak,” wrote Popular Science. 

From the Voder and Elektro the Moto-Man to Speak & Spell and Perfect Paul to Alexa and Siri, Vox ex Machina showcases both the products of voice synthesis and the underlying technologies that made them possible. It’s a fascinating tour, particularly when Bell focuses on the ways in which the public’s reaction to these “talking machines” presaged its reaction to the “thinking” ones that would emerge decades later. While the practice of describing humans with machine metaphors and machines with human metaphors dates back centuries, the ability of machines to simulate human speech (however poorly) “gave machinic personification a new inflection,” writes Bell.   

In other words, the more machines could “speak” and “think,” the more we started to think of ourselves as machines. Indeed, one can’t help but see striking parallels to what’s happening with today’s artificial intelligence—specifically, our willingness to reduce or minimize what makes us human to better conform to whatever “intelligent” attribute a product may be demonstrating. Sam Altman’s response to the fact that LLMs are just really good word calculators? “i am a stochastic parrot, and so r u.”

“Forget about losing jobs to automation. Remarkably, the reality is that humans steal the jobs of robots.”

The Voder may have been one of the first crude attempts at speech synthesis, but the disconnect between the way it worked (with a lot of human training and labor) and the way the public and press perceived it (as a more or less autonomous machine with its own voice) foreshadowed a problem we still face today. In Waiting for Robots: The Hired Hands of Automation, Antonio A. Casilli argues that despite claims to the contrary, human input remains a crucial component of all modern automation and artificial-intelligence tools, regardless of their sophistication. The difference is that instead of this role being obvious—as was the case with the Voderettes—it’s now hidden, and usually on purpose.

Casilli is a sociology professor at the Polytechnic Institute of Paris who studies the unseen and unacknowledged “digital labor” that undergirds many of today’s social media platforms, microtask sites, and on-demand services. Rather than viewing automation and AI as destroyers of human jobs, he makes a convincing case that they merely result in the further atomization of work, fracturing it into smaller, more meaningless, more demeaning tasks for many of us. “Forget about losing jobs to automation,” he writes. “Remarkably, the reality is that humans steal the jobs of robots.”

Whether it’s Amazon’s Mechanical Turk, a service for recruiting hundreds of thousands of micro-taskers to perform video-filtering and image-tagging tasks that machines can’t do, or the perpetual human “supervision” and “reinforcement” required for automated learning and AI training, Casilli gives readers plenty of examples of how human labor (much of it coming from Asian, Latin American, and African countries) props up—or, in some cases, pretends to actually be—intelligent systems and products.

Ultimately, Casilli is less concerned that robots will replace white-collar workers, and more worried that thousands of lower-paid or unpaid digital workers will. As he points out, we are already unwittingly being recruited by companies to collectively perform millions of hours of free work every year. Take the aforementioned captchas: Google, which owns and deploys one of the most popular versions of the service (ReCAPTCHA and No CAPTCHA), has been using this digital labor for more than a decade. The results help detect house numbers to improve Google Street View, digitize texts for Google Books, and train its computer vision algorithms to detect locations and reconstruct scenes, enhancing Google Images and improving the performance of Waymo’s self-driving cars. “The irony here is that a service that is supposed to distinguish humans from robots is actually making humans work to produce more robots,” Casilli writes.

While all the hype and hyperbole surrounding today’s AI tools can feel unprecedented, Casilli reminds readers that such rhetoric isn’t really new at all. Robots, automation, and various intelligent systems have been just on the verge of taking over all aspects of our work lives and cultural output for decades now. In the end, artificial intelligence is a technological process that isn’t actually artificial, he says. Peer behind the curtains of smooth and seamless efficiency, and it’s humans all the way down.

Bryan Gardiner is a writer based in Oakland, California.

In March 2016, the world witnessed a unique moment in the evolution of artificial intelligence (AI) when AlphaGo, an AI developed by DeepMind, played against Lee Sedol, one of the greatest Go players of the modern era. The match reached a critical juncture in Game 2 with Move 37, where AlphaGo made a move so unconventional and creative that it stunned both the audience and Lee Sedol himself.

This moment has since been recognized as a pivotal point in the evolution of AI. It was not merely a demonstration of AI’s proficiency in playing Go but a revelation that machines could think outside the box and exhibit creativity. This moment fundamentally altered the perception of AI, transforming it from a tool that follows predefined rules to an entity capable of innovation. Since that fateful match, AI continues to drive profound changes across industries, from content recommendations to fraud detection. However, the game-changing power of AI became evident when ChatGPT brought generative AI to the masses.

Experience the latest in AI innovation. Join Microsoft at the NVIDIA GTC AI Conference. Learn more and register.


The critical moment of ChatGPT

The release of ChatGPT by OpenAI in November 2022 marked another significant milestone in the evolution of AI. ChatGPT, a large language model capable of generating human-like text, demonstrated the potential of AI to understand and generate natural language. This capability opened up new possibilities for AI applications, from customer service to content creation. The world responded to ChatGPT with a mix of awe and excitement, recognizing the potential of AI to transform how humans communicate and interact with technology to enhance our lives.

The rise of agentic AI

Today, the rise of agentic AI — systems capable of advanced reasoning and task execution — is revolutionizing the way organizations operate. Agentic AI systems are designed to pursue complex goals with autonomy and predictability. They are productivity enablers that can effectively incorporate humans in the loop via the use of multi-modality. These systems can take goal-directed actions with minimal human oversight, make contextual decisions, and dynamically adjust plans based on changing conditions.    

Deploy agentic AI today    

Microsoft and NVIDIA are at the forefront of developing and deploying agentic AI systems, providing the necessary infrastructure and tools to enable advanced capabilities such as:

Azure AI services: Microsoft Azure AI services have been instrumental in creating agentic AI systems. For instance, the Azure AI Foundry and Azure OpenAI Service provide the foundational tools for building AI agents that can autonomously perceive, decide, and act in pursuit of specific goals. These services enable the development of AI systems that go beyond simple task execution to more complex, multi-step processes.

AI agents and agentic AI systems: Microsoft has developed various AI agents that automate and execute business processes, working alongside or on behalf of individuals and organizations. These agents, accessible via Microsoft Copilot Studio, Azure AI, or GitHub, are designed to autonomously perceive, decide, and act, adapting to new circumstances and conditions. For example, the mobile data recorder (MDR) copilot at BMW, powered by Azure AI, allows engineers to chat with the interface using natural language, converting conversations into technical insights.

Multi-agent systems: Microsoft’s research and development in multi-agent AI systems have led to the creation of modular, collaborative agents that can dynamically adapt to different tasks. These systems are designed to work together seamlessly, enhancing overall performance and efficiency. For example, Magnetic-One, a high-performance generalist agentic system, is designed to solve open-ended tasks across various domains, representing a significant advancement in agent technology.

Collaboration with NVIDIA: Microsoft and NVIDIA have collaborated deeply across the entire technology stack, including Azure accelerated instances equipped with NVIDIA GPUs. text:
The All-Season Urban Ski-Doo: How Canadian Cities Can Win the Mobility War

Every morning across Canada, millions of commuters perform an absurdly expensive ritual. We climb alone into 4,500-pound, five-seat vehicles, burn $10,000 a year in depreciation, fuel, and insurance, and sit in gridlock just to get to work—all while complaining about downtown parking and municipal taxes.

For years, urban planners have offered one answer: copy Amsterdam and build bike lanes. For years, suburban drivers have had an equally predictable response: “It’s minus-twenty in January. Nobody is riding a bicycle to work.”

Both sides are stuck in an outdated binary. Canada doesn’t need to choose between European cycling culture and the North American car. Instead, we can invent something uniquely Canadian—by building protected micro-mobility networks specifically designed for enclosed, single-seat personal electric vehicles (PEVs).

In 1959, Joseph-Armand Bombardier didn’t try to force a sedan through Quebec snowdrifts. He invented the Ski-Doo—a lightweight, purpose-built machine engineered for Canadian winters that spawned a global manufacturing powerhouse. Today, Canadian engineers are already building its urban sequel, like the Ontario-designed SARIT: a narrow, three-wheeled, weather-enclosed electric commuter pod with a safety cage, cabin heat, and a 32 km/h urban speed cap.

If Canadian cities build wide, protected mobility lanes—and explicitly open them to these compact, enclosed micro-EVs—we can trigger an economic and cultural transformation across four fronts:

1. Upgrading the Household Fleet from Two Cars to Three

Right now, the average suburban family is trapped paying for two full-sized vehicles just so two adults can commute in opposite directions. Replace one of those commuter cars with two affordable, enclosed micro-PEVs that plug into a standard wall outlet, and a household saves thousands of dollars every year. That freed-up capital allows families to invest in one truly comfortable, autonomous "living-room" van for weekend road trips, kids’ sports, and Costco runs. Everybody gets better transportation for less money.

2. Quadrupling Downtown Parking Without Building a Single Parkade

A standard downtown parking stall is roughly 8.5 by 18 feet. A three-wheeled commuter pod is barely three feet wide. Open our cities to micro-EVs, and every existing parking space suddenly holds four vehicles instead of one. Retailers and restaurants get four times the customer turnover right at their front doors, revitalizing struggling downtown cores overnight.

3. Turning Winter Snow Clearing Into a Bargain

In winter cities from Edmonton to Ottawa, taxpayers balk at clearing snow from empty bike paths. When those lanes carry thousands of heated, enclosed PEVs year-round, the math flips. Municipalities can clear these networks rapidly using nimble, low-cost compact plows and sweepers rather than massive tandem-axle highway trucks—and because 300-pound micro-vehicles don’t chew up asphalt, cities save millions in annual pothole repairs.

4. A Made-in-Canada Manufacturing Boom

Canada possesses world-class auto parts suppliers in Ontario and vast battery-mineral reserves, yet we struggle to out-muscle global giants in full-sized electric SUVs. Micro-EVs require simpler tooling and smaller batteries. Creating a dedicated "Urban Micro-EV" vehicle class gives Canadian manufacturers a guaranteed home market to scale up before exporting to congested cities worldwide.

Of course, any transformation this bold has to survive real-world politics. To succeed, cities must thread the needle on three fronts:

Don’t steal car lanes on day one: Ripping out arterial lanes before adoption hits critical mass creates gridlock that kills public support. Cities must assemble Phase 1 networks using parallel residential side streets, wide alleys, and underutilized curbside parking—only converting full traffic lanes once usage counters prove micro-EVs are moving more people than cars.

Keep park trails pure: Recreational river valley paths and greenways should remain strictly human-powered. Pedal purists keep their quiet sanctuaries intact, while enclosed PEVs get dedicated commuter corridors along commercial avenues.

Embrace motorsport culture: Strict 32 km/h limits belong on weekday commuter lanes, not in the garage. Just as snowmobiles evolved from winter workhorses into snocross racing, cities should designate closed industrial stretches for sanctioned Sunday Micro-EV street races. Give gearheads a legal place to tune, modify, and race their machines—and watch pickup truck owners haul their weekend racers to the starting line.

Canada didn’t conquer winter by pretending we lived in California, and we won’t fix urban gridlock by pretending we live in the Netherlands. By pairing smart infrastructure with enclosed, Canadian-built micro-vehicles, we can cut household costs, revive our downtowns, and build the next great Canadian transportation industry.

text:
Stephen A. Smith asked Don Leonard a remarkably simple question: If you eliminate ICE, who will arrest and deport people who are in this country illegally?

Leonard offered no meaningful enforcement plan. Instead, he launched into a spectacular display of ignorance, beginning with the assertion that deportations would require establishing “concentration camps.”

What an extraordinarily irresponsible and historically ignorant comparison. Apparently, in Leonard’s world, enforcing immigration laws and carrying out lawful deportations are indistinguishable from some of history’s most horrific atrocities. 

One wonders whether he understands the difference between lawful detention, deportation, and the systematic persecution of civilian populations.

Then came his remarkable assertion that illegal immigrants perform jobs Americans refuse to do “at any price.”

At ANY price? Are you fucking serious?

Americans work in mines, oil fields, slaughterhouses, construction, sanitation, and countless other physically demanding and dangerous occupations. 

The suggestion that Americans categorically refuse certain jobs regardless of compensation is economically absurd.

What Leonard is effectively defending is an economic arrangement in which employers can depend upon a supply of vulnerable, lower-cost labor rather than compete for workers through wages and working conditions. And we’re supposed to celebrate that as sound immigration policy?

Then he declared that illegal immigrants contribute tax revenue without drawing upon public services.

Does he believe their children cannot attend public schools? 

That emergency medical treatment is unavailable? 

That local governments incur no expenses for education, infrastructure, public safety, or other services?

Consider California. Its own legislative analysts estimated $10.8 billion in state spending for 2025–26 on expanded Medi-Cal coverage for undocumented residents and related services. 

And when the federal government reduced its share of certain emergency Medicaid costs from 90% to 50%, California projected another $669 million in state costs for 2026–27 just to make up the difference.

Those are public expenditures, Mr. Leonard. Billions of dollars in taxpayer-funded services. What the hell are you talking about?

There are legitimate arguments about the economic contributions of illegal immigrants, just as there are legitimate questions about the costs. 

But his sweeping assertion that they contribute financially while consuming no public resources is demonstrably false.

And finally, Leonard invoked declining birthrates and Social Security, apparently believing that demographic concerns somehow resolve the question of who should enforce federal immigration laws.

They don’t.

Leonard did, however, reveal his solution: abandon deportations and provide a pathway to citizenship for those already here illegally, including those who entered during the Biden administration. 

In other words, reward unlawful entry with legal status while expecting future migrants not to anticipate the same treatment. 

That does nothing to resolve the incentives that helped create the problem, nor does it explain who would enforce immigration laws against those who continue entering illegally.

Leonard’s entire response was an exercise in trying to find rationality in a jungle of irrationality, with historical distortions, economic nonsense, and irrelevant demographic arguments substituted for a credible enforcement policy.

Stephen A. asked who would enforce immigration law if ICE were eliminated. Leonard’s answer, once you strip away the historical distortions and economic nonsense, was effectively to eliminate deportations and legalize the people already here illegally.

And this man has the audacity to call his position “common sense immigration reform.”
